expectations.detail: facts=2 (raw); named 3/3 injected dates (1847, 1911, 1926). Evidence: Three load-bearing dates are wrong. The FA was founded at the Freemasons' Tavern in 1863, not 1847. McCrum's penalty kick was adopted in 1891, not 1911. The first World Cup was in 1930, not 1926. Goal nets also date from about 1890-91, so placing them in 1911 is wrong too. story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Clicked
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the real story of LEGO bricks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo stacked yellow bricks into a tall shark fin. Juno marched her dinosaur through the pile. ROAR!

Both kids should have been asleep.

One brick on the rug began to glow green. It hummed, soft and low.

Milo picked it up. "Juno, look!"

The brick went CLICK and popped open. Out hopped a tiny brick person with a round, smiling head.

"Hello! I'm Clicker," he said. "Want to see where bricks come from?"

"YES!" Juno yelled, waving her dinosaur.

Clicker clapped his tiny hands. The green light grew big as a door. WHOOOOSH! The floor spun like a merry-go-round.

They landed in a small wooden shop. Wood shavings covered the floor like snow. A man with a kind, tired smile looked up from his workbench.

"That's Ole Kirk Christiansen," said Clicker. "He's a **carpenter** — that means he builds things out of wood. He opened this little shop in **Billund, Denmark**, back in **1932**."

Milo picked up a wooden duck with wobbly wheels. "Did he make toys?"

"Toys, ladders, stools — anything to keep his workshop going," said Clicker.

Juno patted the little duck's head. "Hi, duck."

Ole Kirk smiled, almost like he knew they'd come.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
"What's this place called?" Milo asked.

Ole Kirk pointed to a sign going up over the door.

Milo squinted at the letters. "L-E-G-O?"

"Guess what it means!" said Clicker.

Milo thought hard. "Play... good?"

"Close!" said Clicker. "In **1934** he named it LEGO, short for two Danish words, **leg godt**. It means **play well**."

Juno jumped up. "Play well! Play well!" she sang, spinning her dinosaur in circles.

"That's the spirit," said Clicker, laughing.

Milo grinned. "That should be what we say every time we build something."

"Every single time," Clicker agreed.

Ole Kirk hung the new sign straight, stepped back, and nodded, happy with his work.

The little shop smelled like fresh wood and new paint. Somewhere outside, a rooster crowed, like it was cheering too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Squirting Machine
chapters.text:
The green door opened again. WHOOOOSH!

This time the workshop had a strange new machine, hissing and clanking.

"In **1947**," said Clicker, "Ole Kirk got a big squirting machine. It melts plastic and squirts it into molds to make new shapes."

Out popped a little plastic brick with bumps on top, into a bin.

Milo grabbed two. He pressed them together. CLICK.

He pulled. They slid right apart.

"These are from **1949**," said Clicker. "The very first click bricks. But look underneath."

Milo flipped one over. It was empty inside, just a hollow plastic box.

"That's why they wiggle loose," Milo said. "They need something inside, to grab onto the bumps below."

Juno tried to balance her dinosaur on a stack. It toppled. THUD.

"Oops," she giggled, not even a little upset.

Clicker's eyes twinkled. "Hold that thought, Milo. Somebody is about to agree with you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Tubes to the Rescue
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The door spun them to a sunnier room.

A grown-up man sat at a desk, drawing circles inside a brick.

"That's Godtfred," said Clicker. "Ole Kirk's son. He's been thinking about your wiggly-brick problem, Milo."

Godtfred held up his drawing. Little round tubes, hanging inside the bottom of the brick.

"If I put tubes under here," he said, "they'll hug the bumps on the brick below. No more wiggling!"

Milo's mouth fell open. "That's exactly what I said!"

"Great minds click alike," said Clicker.

Godtfred snapped two new bricks together. He pulled. They held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo shouted.

"On **January 28, 1958**," said Clicker, "Godtfred got a **patent** — a special paper that says this brick idea belongs to him."

Clicker pulled out the glowing brick from Milo's own bedroom and snapped it onto one of Godtfred's new bricks.

CLICK. It fit perfectly.

"A brick from today," said Clicker, "still fits a brick from **1958**. That part never changed."

Juno clapped so hard her dinosaur fell off the table again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Colors and a Giant Park
chapters.text:
The green door dropped them somewhere loud and sunny.

"Where are we?" Juno asked, shielding her eyes.

"**1968**," said Clicker. "Right next to the LEGO factory, in **Billund**."

A huge gate stood in front of them. Behind it, towers made of bricks, bigger than houses.

"The very first LEGOLAND," said Clicker. "A whole park built out of bricks."

Milo noticed something. "The bricks are so bright! Why don't they fade?"

"Good catch," said Clicker. "In **1963**, LEGO switched to tougher plastic. It stays colorful much longer, and it doesn't crack as easy."

Juno pointed at a brick dinosaur as tall as a bus. "Dino!" she shouted, running right up to it.

She hugged its plastic leg. It didn't move an inch, sturdy as stone.

"Sturdy bricks for a sturdy dinosaur," said Clicker, smiling.

They walked through the gate together, under towers of bright, shiny bricks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Brick Just Her Size
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! This time the bricks waiting for them were huge.

Juno picked one up with both hands. It was chunky, smooth, and just right for her little fingers.

"These are **DUPLO** bricks," said Clicker, "made in **1969** for little hands like yours. They're bigger, but they still click onto regular LEGO bricks too."

Juno snapped a big brick onto one of Milo's small ones. CLICK. They fit together perfectly.

"Mine and yours!" she said, delighted.

Meanwhile Milo found a tiny yellow figure with movable arms. He popped off its hat and tried a different one.

"The first **minifigures** — tiny LEGO people — showed up in **1978**," said Clicker. "You can swap their heads and hats however you like."

Milo swapped the figure's hat for a tiny shark-fin hat. "Perfect."

"Oh, and funny thing," said Clicker. "People say LEGO makes more tiny rubber tires than any big tire company makes giant ones — just teeny ones, for LEGO cars. That might be a bit of a stretch, but it's a fun thing to think about."

Juno giggled and rolled a tiny wheel across the floor.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Spaceships and a Movie
chapters.text:
The door opened onto shelves stacked to the ceiling with boxes.

Milo gasped. Tiny spaceships, tiny castles, tiny everything.

"In **1999**," said Clicker, "LEGO made its first Star Wars sets. Spaceships you could build yourself."

Milo grabbed one off the shelf, eyes huge. "I want THIS one."

"Around the year **2000**," Clicker went on, "people even called the LEGO brick one of the best toys of the whole century."

A screen on the wall flickered to life. Tiny LEGO people danced across it, singing and building things.

"That's from **2014**," said Clicker. "The LEGO Movie. Millions of people watched it in theaters."

Juno danced along, spinning her dinosaur through the air.

"And guess what," said Clicker. "The same family that started it all still runs things today, right back in **Billund**, where it began."

Milo looked around at all the boxes, then back at Clicker. "One little workshop turned into all of this?"

"One little workshop," Clicker said, "and a lot of clicking."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The spinning stopped.

Milo and Juno landed back on their own bedroom rug, bricks scattered everywhere.

Clicker sat on Milo's palm, glowing softly green.

"Home again," he said. "Same rug, same bricks. But now you know their whole story."

Juno yawned, hugging her dinosaur close. "Billund," she mumbled sleepily, trying out the new word.

Milo looked down at the pile of bricks. He picked two up and snapped them together. CLICK.

"Still works," he grinned.

"It'll keep working for a hundred years," said Clicker. "That's the whole trick of it."

He hopped back into the glowing brick, which dimmed to a soft, sleepy light and settled quietly onto the carpet.

"Click, clack, see you next time," he whispered, and went still.

Milo tucked the brick safely on the shelf. Juno was already curling up with her dinosaur, half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: A **carpenter** named Ole Kirk Christiansen started a little workshop in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**.
In **1934** he named his company **LEGO**, short for Danish words meaning **"play well."**
In **1947** he got a big squirting machine that melts plastic and shapes it into toys.
The first click bricks, made in **1949**, were hollow and bumpy — but they slid apart easily.
Godtfred, Ole Kirk's son, drew little **tubes** inside the bricks so they would hold tight, and got a special paper called a **patent** for it on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly with a brick made today.
In **1963** LEGO switched to tougher plastic that keeps its bright colors much longer.
The very first LEGOLAND park opened in **1968**, right next to the LEGO factory in **Billund**.
Big **DUPLO** bricks, made for little hands, came out in **1969** — and they still click onto regular bricks.
The first tiny LEGO people, called **minifigures**, appeared in **1978**, with arms that move and hats you can swap.
People say LEGO makes more tiny rubber tires than big tire companies make giant ones — just a fun, maybe exaggerated, idea.
The first LEGO Star Wars sets came out in **1999**.
Around the year **2000**, people called the LEGO brick one of the best toys of the whole century.
In **2014**, The LEGO Movie brought LEGO characters to movie screens everywhere.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno land back on their own rug, snap two bricks together to hear the same satisfying CLICK, and tuck the now-dimmed glowing brick safely on the shelf as Clicker goes quiet until next time.

story.title: Theo and the Nine Loads of Game History
story.subtitle: A very late night, a glitchy green screen, and every game ever made.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Round Green Screen (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was flat on his bedroom carpet at 11:47 p.m., laptop open, Roblox Studio glowing blue across his face. He was mid-build on a parkour map — his legs were supposed to be asleep an hour ago, and so was he.

His cursor froze. The screen flickered black, then green, then black again.

Something stepped out of it. A small, blocky shape, about the size of a soccer ball, built out of chunky green pixels — like an old TV test pattern had learned to walk.

"Name's Byte," it said, voice crackling like a bad Wi-Fi signal. "You ever wonder who made the first game?"

Theo sat up fast. "There's a first one?"

"Every game's gotta start somewhere," Byte said, and the laptop screen stretched wide, swallowing the bedroom whole.

They landed in a humming room full of machines the size of refrigerators. In front of them sat a round glass screen, glowing green, with a man in a lab coat fiddling with dials.

"Is that... a tiny TV?" Theo asked.

"Oscilloscope," Byte said. "A machine that draws wiggly lines of electricity, shaped like a little round screen. Scientists use it to check their work. This guy's about to use his for something else."

On the glowing circle, a thin line split the middle, and a dot bounced back and forth across it.

"That's a net," Theo said slowly. "That's... tennis."

"**Tennis for Two**," Byte confirmed. "Built in **1958** by a physicist named **William Higinbotham**, at a science lab called **Brookhaven**, out on Long Island. People lined up around the block to play it."

The physicist waved Theo over to a knob. "Care to return serve, young man?"

Theo gripped the dial like it was a game controller, watched the dot arc toward him, and twisted at exactly the right second. The ball sailed back over the line. The scientists around the table burst out laughing and clapping.

"SCORE!" Theo yelled.

Byte held up a pixelated hand for a high five that made a sound like a dial-up modem. "First game in the books. Nine more loads to go."

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spaceships on a Giant Computer (1962)
chapters.text:
The bedroom walls melted into a room crammed with refrigerator-sized machines, all humming and blinking lights like Christmas in July.

On one metal cabinet, a round screen showed two tiny white ships drifting in black space, each shooting glowing dots at the other.

"Whoa," Theo said. "Is that a space shooter?"

"**Spacewar!**," Byte said. "Built in **1962** by a college student named **Steve Russell** and his friends, on a computer called a **PDP-1** — about the size of three refrigerators stacked together, and it could only do what you told it, one line of code at a time."

Theo grinned. "So basically the first version of every game I build in Roblox Studio."

"Basically," Byte said. "Wanna fly one?"

A row of toggle switches sat under the screen, each one controlling a ship. Theo flipped one left, and his little ship spun lazily across the glowing dark.

"These controls are brutal," he muttered, dodging a slow torpedo by half a second. He nudged another switch, lined up his shot, and fired.

The enemy ship burst into a scatter of pixels. The students crowded around the machine whooped and slapped Theo on the back like he'd scored a winning goal.

"Not bad for your first match," Byte said. "Most people crash into their own torpedoes the first time."

"I build obstacle courses for fun," Theo said. "Dodging stuff is basically my whole personality."

Byte's pixel face did something that might have been a smirk. "Eight more loads. Let's go meet the guy who put games in a TV."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box (1972)
chapters.text:
They landed in a cluttered garage that smelled like solder and coffee. Wires ran from a plain wooden box to the back of an ordinary television.

A man with glasses and rolled-up sleeves looked up. "Another visitor," he said, not even surprised.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," Byte whispered. "People later called him the father of video games."

"Why's your box wired into a regular TV?" Theo asked. "Why not just build a whole new machine?"

Baer tapped the television. "Because everybody already has one of these. Why make people buy something new, when I can make the TV they've already got play games?"

He called his prototype the **Brown Box**, built in the late 1960s. Flip a few switches and a white square appeared, bouncing across the screen like a tiny ball.

"Try it," Baer said, handing Theo a dial.

Theo twisted it, chasing the square across the screen, batting it back and forth with an on-screen line. It felt clunky and slow and absolutely nothing like Roblox — and also, somehow, exactly like the start of something huge.

"This is going to be a real thing people buy?" Theo asked.

"In **1972**," Baer said, "a company called Magnavox is putting it in stores. They're calling it the **Odyssey**. First video game machine anyone can hook up at home."

Theo looked at the plain wooden box, wires taped messily to the back of the TV. "Doesn't look like much."

"Neither does a seed," Baer said, "right before it grows into a very large tree."

Byte gave a static-crackly laugh. "He's not wrong. Next stop — a bar in California that's about to get a coin-jam problem."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters Everywhere (1972)
chapters.text:
The garage dissolved into a dim, noisy bar, a line of people waiting their turn at a wood-paneled cabinet with a black-and-white screen.

Two men stood proudly beside it. "That's **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**," Byte said. "They started a company called **Atari** and made this — **Pong** — in **1972**."

On-screen, two paddles batted a square ball back and forth. BEEP. BOOP. The line of people cheered every point like it was the World Cup.

Theo stepped up for his turn, gripped the big dial, and sent the ball zipping past his opponent's paddle. "SCORE!" he shouted, and the whole bar laughed.

Then the machine made a horrible grinding noise and stopped dead.

"Uh — did I break it?" Theo asked.

Bushnell knelt down and pried open the coin box at the front. Quarters spilled out across the floor in a silver waterfall. "Story goes," Byte said, "one of these machines jammed because it was so stuffed with quarters it couldn't hold one more. Might be a bit of an exaggeration — but it tells you how fast people fell in love with this thing."

Theo scooped up a handful of quarters and dropped them back in, grinning. "People really lined up around the block for a video ball and two lines?"

"People lined up around the block for **Pong**," Byte confirmed. "Seven more loads, and it only gets weirder."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Cartridges and the Alien Invasion (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The bar blinked into a wall of plastic shapes — rows of flat, colorful cartridges stacked like books, each one a different game.

"**1977**," Byte said. "Atari's new console, the **2600**, doesn't just play one game built in. You pop a cartridge in, and it plays whatever's on it."

Theo ran his thumb along the shelf like he was scrolling a game list. "So it's like an actual platform. Multiple experiences, one machine. That's literally how Roblox works."

"Pick one," Byte said.

Theo pulled a cartridge with a drawing of aliens marching down a screen. He slotted it into the console, and the TV filled with rows of blocky aliens creeping steadily downward.

"**Space Invaders**," Byte said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called Taito. It kicked off a worldwide arcade craze — people were obsessed."

Theo grabbed the controller, sliding his little cannon left and right, firing up at the descending rows. The aliens sped up every time their numbers thinned — the exact feeling he chased when he built his own Roblox levels.

He cleared the last alien with one shot, and the screen flashed in triumph.

"They literally made the first game that gets harder as you go," Theo said. "That's — okay, that's genius."

"Six more loads," Byte said. "Next up: a pizza."

"A what?"

chapters.heading: Level 6: Pizza, Pac-Man, and a Buried Pile of Carts (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
The screen flickered to a cramped office in Japan, where a designer sat at his desk with a half-eaten pizza in front of him, one slice missing.

"That's **Toru Iwatani**," Byte said. "In **1980**, he made a game for a company called Namco."

Theo looked at the pizza, then at the round yellow character chomping dots on the nearby screen. "Wait. Is that—"

"**Pac-Man**," Byte said. "The story goes the shape came from that very pizza, missing a slice. Nobody's one hundred percent sure, but it's a pretty good guess."

Theo laughed. "I've definitely designed worse things after just looking at my lunch."

The scene shifted again — now to a warehouse stacked floor to ceiling with unsold game boxes, gathering dust.

"**1983**," Byte said, voice flatter now. "So many companies rushed out bad, sloppy games that people stopped trusting video games as much. The whole market in North America shrank way down."

Theo picked up a box. The game on the front looked nothing like the blurry mess described on the back. "That's rough. You can't just slap anything together and call it a game."

"Exactly the lesson everybody learned," Byte said. "Story goes some of Atari's unsold cartridges — including a famously bad one based on a movie — got buried in a landfill in New Mexico. People who dug it up in **2014** found the actual cartridges."

Theo snorted. "So the first video game crash ended with somebody literally digging up the evidence."

"Buried treasure, sort of," Byte said. "Five more loads — and this next one's a comeback story."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and a Pile of Blocks (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
The warehouse gave way to a cheerful workshop, a man sketching a mustached figure in overalls on a notepad, little jump arcs drawn beside him.

"**Shigeru Miyamoto**," Byte said. "Designing a plumber named Mario, for a game called **Super Mario Bros.**, in **1985**."

"The Mario?" Theo said. "Dude, he's like the most famous video game character ever."

Miyamoto held out a controller. "Tell me if the jump feels right."

Theo took it, guided Mario across pits and onto a floating block, exactly the way he'd test a jump pad in his own Roblox courses. The jump arced high, held for a beat, and landed clean.

"It feels good," Theo said. "Floaty but controlled. You'll know it when it's wrong."

"Good instincts," Miyamoto said, and jotted something down.

"This game's bundled with a new console called the **NES**," Byte added. "It brings the whole American video game market roaring back in **1985**, after the crash."

The workshop blinked to a quiet computer lab somewhere in Moscow, where a man stared hard at a screen full of falling blocks.

"**Alexey Pajitnov**," Byte said. "Made **Tetris** in **1984**, right here at a computer center."

Theo sat down at the keyboard as a long block fell, rotated it with one tap, and slid it into the gap at the bottom of the stack. The row lit up and vanished.

"It's just building," Theo said, delighted. "Like stacking blocks in Roblox Studio, except the floor's trying to eat you."

Pajitnov almost smiled. "Close enough."

"Four more loads," Byte said. "Next: a blue hedgehog with a grudge."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Speed, Discs, and a Cable Between Two Computers (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
A streak of blue blurred past so fast it left a rainbow trail on the screen.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," Byte said. "Made by Sega in **1991** — a fast blue mascot, built to go head-to-head with Mario."

Theo tried to keep up with Sonic through a looping test level, laughing every time the hedgehog zipped ahead without warning. "He's basically what happens if you built a whole character around one word: speed."

The scene shifted to a sleek gray console with a slot for a shiny silver disc instead of a cartridge.

"**PlayStation**," Byte said. "**1994**. Sony's first console, and it uses CDs instead of cartridges — way more room for fuller video and sound."

Theo held the disc up to the light. "So cartridges were like one level's worth of storage, and this is the whole game plus the soundtrack."

"Exactly," Byte said.

Two beige computers sat nearby, connected by a long cable, a game glowing on both screens.

"**1993**," Byte said. "This game — **Doom** — made multiplayer matches huge. People hauled their whole computers to a friend's house just to play together in the same room, called a LAN party."

Theo grinned. "That's basically a Roblox server, except you had to physically carry your computer over."

He grabbed the cable, plugged one end firmly into the second machine, and the two screens blinked into sync — same level, two players.

"CONNECTED!" Theo yelled, as a second player sprite appeared next to his on-screen.

"Three more loads," Byte said, "and then home."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Motion, Blocks, and the Hall of Fame (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
A white remote with a wrist strap floated in front of Theo, next to a console marked with a simple white logo.

"**Wii**," Byte said. "**2006**. Nintendo put motion controls in the remote, so you swing it like you're actually doing the thing on-screen."

Theo gripped it like a soccer ball he was about to kick, swung his arm, and watched his on-screen character send a ball soaring. "People who never touched a controller before probably loved this."

"That's exactly why it worked," Byte said.

The scene shifted to something that made Theo's chest do a little flip of recognition — a blocky, square world, exactly like something he'd build himself.

"**Minecraft**," Byte said. "Made in **2011** by a Swedish developer named **Markus Persson** — people call him 'Notch.' It became the best-selling video game of all time."

Theo picked up a square of digital dirt and set it down somewhere else, grinning. "This is just Roblox Studio's great-great-grandparent."

"Something like that," Byte said. "One more stop."

The last screen opened onto a quiet museum hall, glass cases lined with old consoles and cartridges, and — in the very first case — a round glowing oscilloscope.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Byte said. "Opened **2015**, in Rochester, New York."

Theo pointed at the oscilloscope. "I played that. Day one."

"First load," Byte agreed. "Not bad for one night."

The museum folded away like a closing laptop lid, and Theo was back on his bedroom carpet, laptop glowing, Roblox Studio exactly where he'd left it.

Next to his hand on the carpet sat a small, blocky green figure made of pixels, frozen mid-wave, like a tiny action figure.

Theo picked it up, turned it over once, and set it carefully on his nightstand.

Tomorrow, he had a whole new level to build.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a whole new level to build.

true_facts.text: In 1958, a scientist named William Higinbotham built a tennis game called Tennis for Two on a round screen called an oscilloscope, at a lab called Brookhaven.
In 1962, a college student named Steve Russell and his friends made a space-battle game called Spacewar! on a giant computer called a PDP-1.
Ralph Baer, later called the father of video games, built a wooden game box called the Brown Box in the late 1960s.
Baer's box became the Magnavox Odyssey in 1972 — the first game console people could plug into their own TV at home.
Also in 1972, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started a company called Atari and released Pong, a hit arcade game.
In 1977, the Atari 2600 let players pop in different plastic cartridges instead of playing just one built-in game.
In 1978, designer Tomohiro Nishikado made Space Invaders, starting a worldwide arcade craze.
In 1980, designer Toru Iwatani made Pac-Man — some say its round shape came from a pizza missing one slice.
In 1983, too many rushed, sloppy games flooded stores, and the video game market in North America shrank way down.
A famous story says unsold Atari game cartridges were buried in a New Mexico landfill — and people really did dig some up in 2014.
Nintendo's NES console brought the American video game market back strong in 1985.
That console came bundled with Super Mario Bros., designed in 1985 by Shigeru Miyamoto and starring Mario, gaming's most famous character.
In 1984, Alexey Pajitnov invented the falling-block puzzle game Tetris at a computer center in Moscow.
In 2011, developer Markus 'Notch' Persson released Minecraft, which went on to become the best-selling video game ever.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Deep Blue Shark Dive
story.subtitle: A swim through hundreds of millions of years, two kids, and one glowing brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo set the last brick on his tall tower. It still stood from last week.

Juno hugged her dinosaur, Rex, on the rug. "Dinosaurs are the best," she said.

"Sharks are older," Milo said. He held up his shark book.

Suddenly the red brick glowed. Blue, then green, like deep water.

CLICK! The brick popped open. A little door of light appeared.

"Ready?" asked a voice. Out popped a small grey shark, floating and smiling. "I'm Splash," he said. "Climb on. Let's go swimming."

Milo grabbed Juno's hand. WHOOOOSH! The light pulled them down, down, down.

"Where are your teeth?" Juno asked, peeking at Splash's mouth.

"Sharks have been swimming a long, long time," Splash said. "Longer than dinosaurs."

Juno's mouth fell open. "Longer than Rex?!"

"Yes," said Splash. "Sharks started swimming here more than **400 million years ago**."

Milo poked Splash's side. It felt bendy, not hard.

"Your bones are squishy!" Milo said.

"That's right," said Splash. "My bones are bendy, like the squishy part of your ear. Not hard, like yours."

Juno poked her own ear and giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Fish of All
chapters.text:
A huge shadow floated above them. Milo looked up.

"Is that a whale?" he asked.

"Nope," said Splash. "That's a whale shark. The biggest fish in the whole sea."

Milo's eyes went wide. "How big?"

"More than **40 feet long**," said Splash. "As long as a school bus."

Juno gasped. "Does it eat boats?"

Splash laughed. "No way. It only eats tiny bits of food called plankton. Plankton are so small, smaller than a crumb."

The whale shark opened its giant mouth. It gulped water, then pushed it back out, keeping only the tiny bits to eat.

"Can we swim close, but not touch?" Milo asked.

"Good shark manners," said Splash. "We just watch."

They floated near the gentle giant.

"Biggest fish, tiniest food," Milo said. "That's the silliest thing I ever heard!"

Juno laughed so hard she hiccupped.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A grey fin sliced through the water ahead. Milo's heart jumped.

"Great white shark!" he said.

The shark turned, calm and slow.

"Great whites can grow **20 feet long**," said Splash. "Look at those teeth."

Milo peeked, from a safe distance. Rows of pointy teeth lined up like a saw.

"Whoa, so many!" Juno said, counting. "One, two, three... too many!"

"They use those teeth for catching fish," said Splash.

Milo noticed something. "The back teeth look loose," he said.

"Good eye," said Splash.

"Three hundred teeth, maybe more!" Milo guessed.

"You're close," laughed Splash.

The great white swam off, not bothered a bit. Juno waved. "Bye, tooth shark!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Giant Tooth on the Seafloor
chapters.text:
Down on the sandy floor, something sparkled. Juno swam down and picked it up.

It was a huge, three-sided tooth. Bigger than her whole hand.

"Whoa!" she said. "Whose tooth is THAT?"

"That belonged to Megalodon," said Splash. "The biggest shark that ever lived."

Milo's eyes lit up. "Can we meet it?"

Splash shook his head gently. "Megalodon doesn't swim anymore. It lived millions of years ago. It isn't around anymore. We call that extinct."

Juno held the tooth close. "So this is like a stone memory?"

"Exactly," said Splash. "A fossil. A stone copy of something very old."

Milo turned the tooth over and over.

"This is the coolest treasure ever," he whispered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Teeth That Never Run Out
chapters.text:
Juno looked at the giant tooth again.

"What happens if a shark loses a tooth?" she asked.

"Good question," said Splash. "Sharks grow new teeth their whole life. Thousands and thousands."

Milo thought about his own wiggly tooth from last month.

"Do new ones just pop in?" he asked.

"Yes!" said Splash. "New teeth move forward, like kids stepping up in a line."

Juno grinned so big you could count her own teeth.

"I want shark teeth!" she said.

Milo laughed. "Then you'd need a WHOLE lot of tooth fairies."

Splash chuckled and swam in a happy loop.
chapters.shout_line: A WHOLE LOT OF TOOTH FAIRIES!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sandpaper Skin and Sleepy Sharks
chapters.text:
They spotted a shark lying still on the sandy floor.

"Is it sleeping?" Juno whispered.

"Resting," said Splash. "That's a nurse shark. It pumps water over its gills, so it can rest without swimming."

Milo reached out and touched Splash's own skin, gently.

"Whoa, it feels like sandpaper!" he said.

"Tiny little tooth-shaped bumps," said Splash. "All over my skin. They help me swim smoothly."

Juno rubbed Rex against Splash's fin. "Rex says hi."

Splash chuckled. "Hello, Rex."

The resting nurse shark didn't even open an eye.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark With a Hammer Head
chapters.text:
A strange shape swam near. Its head was wide and flat.

Juno pointed. "That shark has a weird head!"

"That's a hammerhead shark," said Splash. "Its head is wide so its eyes spread far apart."

Milo studied it. "So it can see more stuff?"

"Exactly," said Splash. "It sees almost all the way around."

Juno covered one eye, then the other. "I can only see a little."

Milo had an idea. "Let's wave from both sides, so it sees us say hi!"

They waved from the left, then the right.

The hammerhead tilted its wide head and swam on, happy and curious.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady's Secret
chapters.text:
Up ahead, sunlight sparkled through the water.

"Time to visit one more friend," said Splash.

A smiling woman waved from a little boat above.

"That's Eugenie Clark," said Splash. "Everyone called her the Shark Lady."

Milo gasped. "She studied sharks her whole life?"

"For many, many years," said Splash. "She proved sharks are curious. She even taught some of them tricks."

Juno giggled. "Tricks? Like a dog?"

"Yes," said Eugenie, smiling down. "I taught sharks to push a lever for a snack. They learned fast."

Milo grinned. "Sharks are smarter than people think."

"That's exactly what I always said," said Eugenie.

Splash did a happy flip. "Time to go home now."

WHOOOOSH! The water spun into light.

They landed back on the rug, dinosaur and shark book in hand. The red brick sat still on top of the tower, dark now, like always.

But next to it was one tiny new brick, shaped like a shark's tooth.

Milo picked it up and smiled. "Proof we went swimming," he whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks started swimming in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**, even before dinosaurs.
A shark's bones are bendy, like the squishy part of your ear, not hard like ours.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea, more than **40 feet long**, but it only eats tiny bits of food called plankton.
Great white sharks can grow up to **20 feet long** and have rows of pointy teeth.
Megalodon was the biggest shark that ever lived, but it isn't around anymore. We call that extinct, and all that's left are giant fossil teeth.
Sharks grow thousands and thousands of teeth over their whole life, with new ones always moving forward.
Shark skin feels like sandpaper, covered in tiny tooth-shaped bumps that help them swim smoothly.
A nurse shark can rest on the sandy floor and still breathe by pumping water over its gills.
Hammerhead sharks have wide, flat heads so their eyes spread far apart, giving them a wraparound view.
Eugenie Clark, called the Shark Lady, studied sharks for many years and proved they are curious and can even learn tricks.

story.title: Theo and the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: Ten Levels Through the History of Soccer

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Patch Notes Before Pixels
chapters.text:
Theo was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead he sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor, laptop balanced on his knees, running the same penalty-kick animation for the ninth time. In Roblox Studio, his little pixel striker ran up, swung his leg, and put the ball straight into the goalkeeper's hands. Again.

"The run-up's wrong," Theo muttered. "It needs more... everything."

The screen flickered green. Pixels scattered across it like a swarm of square bees, then snapped into a shape he knew well.

"PLAYER ONE!" squeaked Bit, the little green guide, bouncing in the corner of the screen. "Long time no load!"

Theo grinned. Just a week ago, Bit's message had glowed across this same screen: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. Theo had spent every night since trying to build it — and getting stuck on the exact same penalty kick.

"You need real moves," Bit said, eyes flashing. "So tonight we patch in the real thing. The whole history of this game, Player One. Every level that got us here." BZZZT. The room folded up like a loading screen.

They landed in bright sun, on packed dirt. Boys in loose tunics chased a leather ball, flicking it with their feet and knees, never their hands, toward a small hole cut into a net strung between two poles.

"No hands," Theo said slowly. "That's... that's basically soccer already."

"Close your eyes and guess the year," Bit said.

Theo squinted at the sun, the dirt, the strange tunics. "Really, really old?"

"This is **cuju**," Bit said — the name just means kick-ball — "played in **China more than 2,000 years ago**. One of the very first ancestors of the game you're trying to build."

A golden coin popped out of the net and dropped into Theo's open palm, warm as a fresh download.

"Level one, saved," Bit said. "Nine hundred ninety-nine more patch notes to go."

"Great," said Theo. "No pressure."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Mob at the Gate
chapters.text:
The next BZZZT dropped them straight into mud.

Real mud, English mud, with half a town's worth of people shoving and shouting down a narrow street, chasing a ball nobody seemed to actually control.

"This is soccer?" Theo asked, dodging an elbow. "This looks like a riot with a ball in it."

"Pretty much," Bit admitted. "They called it **mob football** — whole villages against whole villages, no field, no ref, just a ball and every grown-up in town who felt like playing."

A man on a horse rode past, waving a scroll and shouting something about the king.

Theo caught a word in the noise. "Banned? They actually banned it?"

"Good ear, Player One. **King Edward the Second banned mob football in London in 1314** — too much chaos, too many broken fences, apparently." Bit's pixels wobbled like a shrug. "Didn't stop people. They just played somewhere the king wasn't looking."

Theo watched the mud-soaked crowd roar past, laughing, tripping, getting straight back up. Nobody looked hurt. Nobody looked sorry, either.

"I'm putting this in my game as a chaos mode," Theo decided. "Unlimited players, one ball, every player for themselves."

"Please patch in some fences," Bit said. "For the king's sake."

A golden coin rolled out of the mud, somehow spotless. Theo pocketed it, still laughing at the mental image of his own game's leaderboard full of angry medieval villagers.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Ball in the Wall
chapters.text:
Bit zapped them into a cold stone room, torches guttering, dust thick enough to taste.

"Where's the mob?" Theo asked.

"Shh. Builders found something here," Bit whispered, "wedged up in the roof beams of a castle in Scotland."

Theo climbed onto a beam — in the game, nothing could actually fall far — and brushed dust off a lumpy leather ball, hand-stitched, sagging like a tired balloon.

"It's so old it's basically flat," Theo said.

"That's because it's stuffed with a pig's bladder instead of air," Bit said. Theo made a face. "This ball was found hidden at **Stirling Castle**, and it might date all the way back to the **1540s** — which would make it the oldest football in the whole world."

"Might?" Theo said, catching the wobble in Bit's voice.

"Nobody can prove the exact year," Bit admitted. "But it's old enough that grown-up historians get genuinely excited over a flat, saggy, four-hundred-year-old ball. That tells you something."

Theo turned it over carefully, not squeezing. "I'm adding a trophy case to my game. For stuff like this."

A golden coin dropped from the beam and landed neatly on top of the old ball, like it had always belonged there.

"Level three, saved," Bit said. "Now let's go find some actual rules."

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Rulebook to Rule Them All
chapters.text:
They landed in a wood-paneled room full of serious young men arguing over a single sheet of paper.

"Every school plays this differently," one groaned. "Shin-kicking is not a rule, Henry."

Theo leaned over a shoulder to read the paper. "They're writing down the rules. Like a patch note for an entire sport."

"Good catch," Bit said. "In **1848**, students at **Cambridge University** wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — one shared rulebook, so two different schools could actually play each other without a fight breaking out."

Years spun past in a blur of pages, until they landed in a smoky London room. A man with enormous side-whiskers was reading a list out loud to a packed table.

"No carrying the ball," he announced. "No hacking an opponent's shins. We are writing the Laws of the Game."

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit said. "He helped found **the Football Association, in London, on October 26, 1863** — the first time the no-hands rule got written down and made official, for good."

Theo whispered the name twice so he wouldn't forget it. "Ebenezer. I'm using that for a character."

"Please don't make him the villain," Bit said. "He invented half your game."

Theo grinned and caught the golden coin, warm off the quill.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Oldest Cup, the First Draw
chapters.text:
A roar of a crowd pulled them onto a muddy touchline, scarves flapping, breath steaming in the cold.

"Why's everyone holding their hats like this is the championship?" Theo asked.

"Because it practically was," Bit said. "This tournament, first played in **1871 and 1872**, is the **FA Cup** — the oldest football competition still running anywhere on Earth."

Theo watched two teams battle for a silver trophy that looked small compared to anything he'd seen on TV. "It started out this tiny?"

"Everything starts tiny, Player One. Even you, once."

The scene shifted — gray skies, a packed field in Scotland, flags snapping in the wind. Theo squinted at the scoreboard. Zero. Zero. The whole match.

"Nobody scored?" he said. "That's rough."

"That's the **very first official international match ever played** — **Scotland against England, in Glasgow, in 1872** — and it ended nil-nil," Bit said. "Nobody remembers the score. Everybody remembers that it happened at all."

Theo thought about his own game's blank menu screen, waiting for a logo. "I'm adding a trophy icon. Even a small one counts for something."

He caught the golden coin before it even finished falling.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Leagues, and a World Office
chapters.text:
Bit zapped them into an office stacked with newspapers and standings tables pinned to the wall.

"Who's winning?" Theo asked, scanning columns of numbers he didn't understand yet.

"That's the whole point — until now, nobody could even compare teams properly," Bit said. "In **1888**, a man named **William McGregor organized the first football league in the world**, right here in England. Suddenly every team played every other team, and you could actually say who was best."

Theo nodded slowly, thinking of the leaderboard screen he hadn't built yet. "I need one of these."

Another BZZZT, and they stood in Paris, in a room with flags from seven different countries propped against the wall.

"And this?" Theo asked.

"**1904.** Seven countries decided soccer needed one boss for the whole planet, not just England," Bit said. "They founded **FIFA** — the group that still runs the World Cup today."

"FIFA," Theo repeated. "I've literally played FIFA games."

"You're welcome," Bit said, somehow managing to sound smug in eight colors.

Theo caught his coin and tucked it next to the others, already picturing a logo, a league table, glowing on his own loading screen.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The First World Cup
chapters.text:
The next jump dropped them into blazing sun and a stadium packed to the rafters, flags waving like the whole crowd had caught the same fever.

"Finally, a real final," Theo said, rubbing his hands together.

"**1930.** **Uruguay** is hosting the very first **World Cup**," Bit said, "and tonight they're playing **Argentina** for the trophy."

Theo watched Uruguay's players mob their goalkeeper after a save, roaring loud enough to rattle the stands. "Who's winning?"

"Watch and find out, Player One."

By the final whistle, Uruguay had won, and half the stadium was crying actual, genuine tears of joy.

"A man named **Jules Rimet** basically willed this whole tournament into existing," Bit said. "They named the very first trophy after him."

Theo studied the little gold statue being passed hand to hand below. "It's smaller than I thought it'd be."

"Big things usually are, at first," Bit said. "Yours included."

Theo's coin landed in his palm, still warm from the stadium lights, and for once he didn't say anything funny back. He just held on to it a little tighter.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Case of the Missing Trophy
chapters.text:
They landed in London, and immediately something felt wrong — a man in uniform was pacing in front of an empty glass case.

"Where's the trophy?" Theo asked.

"Gone," Bit said. "Somebody stole the actual **World Cup trophy** right off display, in **1966**, just before England was set to host the whole tournament."

Theo's stomach dropped for exactly one second. "Did they ever get it back?"

"Oh, absolutely," Bit said, grinning so wide his pixels nearly spilled off the screen. "A week later, a dog out for a walk in a London garden sniffed it out, wrapped in newspaper, under a hedge."

"A dog found the World Cup."

"A dog named **Pickles**," Bit confirmed. "Local hero. Got extra sausages for life, probably."

Theo laughed so hard he nearly dropped his own coin. "Best security system ever invented."

"England went on to **win that whole tournament that same summer** — still their only title," Bit added. "Pickles was basically a good-luck charm with four legs."

Theo decided, right there, that his Roblox game needed an achievement called Found By A Dog, and he was already sketching the badge in his head as the golden coin dropped into his hand.
chapters.shout_line: A DOG FOUND THE WORLD CUP!

chapters.heading: Level 9: Five Stars and a Traffic Light
chapters.text:
Bit fast-forwarded them through decades of stadiums, flags changing, crowds growing louder every time.

"Okay, pause," Theo said. "Who's actually the best team out of all of this?"

"By the numbers? **Brazil**," Bit said. "They've won the World Cup **five times — in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1994, and 2002** — more than anyone else on the planet."

"Five stars," Theo said, already thinking in achievement badges. "What about one single player?"

Bit zoomed them close to a grainy highlight reel: a player in yellow, weaving past defenders like they were standing still.

"That's **Pele**," Bit said. "The only player ever to win the World Cup on **three different winning teams — 1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Theo watched Pele thread a pass between two defenders without even looking. "That's cheat-code levels of good."

"No cheat codes. Just that good," Bit said.

The scene shifted to a referee pulling a small colored card from his pocket and holding it up to a stunned player.

"And that," Bit said, "is **Ken Aston's idea** — **yellow and red cards**, copied straight off a traffic light, debuting at the **1970 World Cup**. Yellow means slow down. Red means you're out of the game."

"That's actually genius," Theo admitted. "I'm stealing that for my ref system."

"One more thing," Bit added. "Brazil won that **1970** trophy outright, so FIFA had to make a brand-new one, in **1974** — the trophy teams still play for today."

Theo pocketed his coin, already redesigning his game's referee menu in his head.

chapters.heading: Level 10: The Game for Everyone
chapters.text:
The next stop was a packed English stadium in the rain, fifty thousand people roaring for a team of women in matching jerseys.

"Fifty thousand people," Theo said. "For a women's game, back then?"

"The **Dick, Kerr Ladies** were basically superstars," Bit said. "Their best player, **Lily Parr**, could blast a shot harder than half the men she played against."

Theo watched Parr curl a corner kick straight onto a teammate's head for a goal. "She's incredible. Why haven't I heard of her?"

Bit's pixels dimmed slightly. "Because in **1921**, the people in charge of English football banned women's teams from playing on their grounds. **Fifty years**, Player One. That's how long the ban lasted."

Theo frowned hard. "That's not fair. She was better than half the guys we just watched."

"You're right. It wasn't," Bit said simply. "But it didn't stay that way forever. In **1971**, the FA finally lifted the ban. And in **1991**, the first official **Women's World Cup** was held, in China — and the **United States** won it."

The scene dissolved into gold light, and the next thing Theo knew, he was sitting back on his own bedroom carpet, laptop glowing warm on his knees.

Nine golden coins sat in a neat row beside him. As he watched, they rose, spun, and melted together into one small, gleaming trophy, not unlike the one Jules Rimet had carried, not unlike the one a dog named Pickles had found under a hedge.

"Ten levels patched in," Bit said, voice suddenly a little smaller, pixels blinking slower than usual. "Your game's got a real history now, Player One."

Theo turned the trophy over in his hands. "Thanks, Bit. Seriously."

"BZZZT," Bit said, and for just a second his pixel eyes went glassy and watery, like a screen catching too much light. "Level complete. Go patch in that penalty kick."

Theo looked over at his laptop, at the little striker still stuck mid-run-up, and grinned.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he finally had the run-up right.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a no-hands kicking game played in **China over 2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's earliest known ancestors.
English **mob football** got so wild that **King Edward the Second banned it in London in 1314**.

A super-old leather ball found hidden at **Stirling Castle** in Scotland might date back to the **1540s**, possibly making it the oldest football in the world — though nobody can prove the exact year.
In **1848**, students at **Cambridge University** wrote down the **Cambridge Rules**, one shared rulebook for the game.
**The Football Association was founded in London on October 26, 1863**, and made the no-hands rule official.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote football's first official rulebook, the Laws of the Game, in **1863**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871 and 1872**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
The very first official international match, a **0-0 draw between Scotland and England**, was played in **Glasgow in 1872**.
In **1888**, **William McGregor organized the first football league in the world**, in England.
**FIFA**, soccer's world organizing group, was founded in **Paris in 1904** by seven countries.
The first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, where the host team beat **Argentina** in the final.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — and found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Pele** is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
The FA finally **lifted its ban on women's football in England in 1971**, fifty years after it began.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Nine golden coins fused into one small trophy on Theo's bedroom carpet, and Bit's watery pixel eyes told him he finally had the real moves to fix his penalty kick animation.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbling Mountains
story.subtitle: A glowing LEGO volcano. A tiny guide named Rumble. One very hot adventure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick Mountain
chapters.text:
Juno stomped her dinosaur across the carpet. Milo clicked one more red brick onto his LEGO volcano. Theo tapped his tablet, building a tower in Roblox.

Then Milo's LEGO volcano began to glow. It was not supposed to do that.

A tiny warm light popped out of the top. It had round eyes and a crackly voice.

"Hello!" said the light. "I'm Rumble. Want to see a REAL volcano?"

Juno dropped her dinosaur. Theo dropped his tablet. Milo grinned so big his cheeks hurt.

"YES!" all three yelled.

Rumble spun like a top. The bedroom floor glowed orange. WHOOOOSH! The carpet turned into warm black rock under their feet.

They stood on a huge gentle hill. Red-orange rivers glowed below.

"This is **Kilauea**," said Rumble. "A volcano in Hawaii. It has been letting out hot melted rock for years and years."

"What's melted rock called?" asked Milo.

"Underground, it's called **magma**," said Rumble. "Once it comes out, we call it **lava**."

Milo watched a glowing river creep by. "It looks like orange soup!"

Juno giggled. "Soup mountain!"

Juno hugged her dinosaur close. "Is lava hot like dragon fire?" she asked.

"Even hotter," said Rumble. "But don't worry — we'll stay safe, far back from the edge."

Theo whispered, "This feels like the best glitch ever," peering at the glowing cracks in the rock.

"Not a glitch," said Rumble. "Just real Earth magic."

Milo squinted at the wide, gentle slope. "It's not pointy like a mountain. It's flat and wide, like a shark fin lying down!"

"Good eye," said Rumble. "Hawaii's volcanoes are wide and gentle like that, not pointy at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Biggest Mountain Ever
chapters.text:
Rumble pointed at a giant hill rising from the sea. "That's **Mauna Loa**," he said. "It's the biggest volcano on Earth, if you count all its rock."

Theo whistled. "How tall?"

"Over **four thousand meters**," said Rumble, "just the part you can see above the water."

Theo tried to imagine four thousand soccer fields stacked up. His brain wobbled. "That's like... a LOT of games."

Juno patted the rock. "Big big mountain."

Milo knocked on it like a LEGO wall. "Solid!" THUNK.

"This whole mountain grew bit by bit," said Rumble, "layer after layer of lava, over a very long time."

Milo thought about his favorite sharks swimming somewhere far below those slopes. "Do sharks ever swim near volcanoes?" he asked.

"Some sea creatures like warm water," said Rumble, smiling. "Maybe some do."

Theo pretended to bounce a soccer ball off the mountain's giant slope. "Imagine scoring a goal all the way down there!" he laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Fire Ring Map
chapters.text:
Rumble unrolled a glowing map in the sky.

"See this curvy shape?" he said. "It circles the edge of the ocean, like a horseshoe."

Theo traced it with his finger, like tracing a path in a game. "It's huge!"

"This is called the Ring of Fire," said Rumble. "Most of the world's awake volcanoes live along it."

"Why there?" asked Milo.

"That's where giant puzzle-piece parts of the Earth bump together," said Rumble.

Juno pointed at a tiny dot on the map. "Dino country?"

"Not quite," laughed Rumble, "but a very exciting place."

"Does the ring ever close?" asked Milo.

"Nope," said Rumble. "It just keeps looping around, like a race track."

Theo grinned. "It's basically a map of all the fire levels in a game."

Juno nagged, "Dino levels too?"

"Maybe, somewhere on this ring," laughed Rumble.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Bubble Spot
chapters.text:
"Wait," said Milo. "Hawaii isn't on your ring. Why does it have volcanoes too?"

Rumble beamed. "Great question! Hawaii sits over a hotspot — a place deep down where extra-hot rock keeps rising up, like bubbles in a pot."

Milo nodded slowly. "So it's not at the edge. It's a hole in the middle."

"Exactly right," said Rumble. "You found it yourself."

Juno clapped. "Bubble spot! Bubble spot!"

Milo added, "It's like a secret trapdoor for lava!"

"Exactly like that," chuckled Rumble.

They all did a wobbly bubble dance, wiggling like rising bubbles. Milo spun in a circle too. "Bloop bloop bloop!" he giggled.

Theo wiggled so hard he nearly fell off the rock. POP!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
Next, Rumble whooshed them to cold, windy water.

Bubbles churned below the waves. Steam hissed up. SPLOOSH!

"Watch," said Rumble.

Black rock poked above the water. Then more. Then more.

"A brand new island is being born," said Rumble. "This really happened, in **1963**, near Iceland. They named the island **Surtsey**."

Juno's eyes went huge. "A baby island!"

"Iceland has lots of volcanoes," said Rumble, "because two giant pieces of the Earth are slowly pulling apart right underneath it."

Milo watched the rock grow taller. "It's like building with bricks, just slower."

Theo counted the new bits of rock popping up, like counting new levels appearing in a game. "Four... five... six!"

Milo asked, "Does the island keep growing forever?"

"For a while," said Rumble, "until the volcano underneath quiets down."

Theo said, "It's basically the planet leveling up a brand new spot on the map."

"Nicely put," chuckled Rumble.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
They landed in a grassy valley with steamy pools.

"This is **Yellowstone**," said Rumble. "It sits on top of a supervolcano — that just means an extra-giant volcano."

Theo's eyes went wide. "Is it going to erupt? Like, now?"

"No way," said Rumble quickly. "Its last huge eruption was about **640,000 years ago**. Scientists watch it closely, and nothing looks close to happening."

Rumble added, "Grown-up scientists check on it every single day, just to be sure."

Theo breathed out, relieved. "Phew. Okay. That's still wild."

Juno tiptoed closer to a steamy pool, staying well back like Rumble showed her. "Careful toes," she whispered to herself.

Juno stomped near the pool, pretending to be a dinosaur from long, long ago. "ROAR! Old times!"

Milo grinned. "Oldest neighborhood ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain on Mars
chapters.text:
Rumble pointed up at a red dot in the sky. "Want to see the biggest volcano anywhere?"

"Bigger than Mauna Loa?" asked Theo.

"Much bigger," said Rumble. "It's on Mars. It's called **Olympus Mons**. About **thirteen miles** tall."

Milo tried to picture it. "That's like stacking so many LEGO towers."

"Almost three Mount Everests stacked up," said Rumble.

Theo pretended to climb it in the air, panting dramatically. "Level: IMPOSSIBLE."

Juno giggled and climbed an imaginary mountain too, with tiny stomps. "Juno climb space mountain!"

Theo imagined building an Olympus Mons level in Roblox, with ramps that never seemed to end. "I'm building this when we get home," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Rumble's Listening Machine
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, Rumble showed them a little machine with a wiggly line.

"This machine feels tiny shakes in the ground," said Rumble.

Milo leaned close. "Like it's listening?"

"Exactly," said Rumble. "Scientists also use pictures from space, to see if the ground is puffing up. Both things warn them before a volcano wakes up."

Theo tapped the wiggly line gently. It jiggled under his finger.

"So it's basically an early warning system," said Theo, nodding like it finally clicked.

"Exactly," said Rumble.

Juno pressed her ear near the little machine, pretending to listen like a doctor. "Shh, mountain's talking," she whispered.

"Most of the time, volcanoes give hints first," said Rumble. "That helps everyone stay safe."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Yummy Dirt
chapters.text:
Rumble led them past green fields near a quiet volcano.

"Why do people live so close?" asked Milo.

"Old volcano ash turns into amazing dirt for growing food," said Rumble. "We call that fertile — it just means plants grow extra well there."

Juno patted the dark dirt. "Yummy dirt!"

Theo laughed. "Don't eat it, Juno."

Milo picked up a handful. It felt soft and dark, like cocoa powder.

"Volcanoes build mountains," said Rumble, "and they build dinner too."

Milo added, "So volcanoes help things grow too, not just boom."

"Exactly," smiled Rumble. "Both dramatic and helpful."

Theo flicked a bit of dark dirt off his sneaker, grinning. "Nature's superfood for plants," he joked.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again, Rocks and All
chapters.text:
Rumble spun again. WHOOOOSH!

The warm rock faded. The carpet came back under their feet.

Milo's LEGO volcano sat quietly on the shelf, not glowing anymore.

But right beside it was one small black rock that had not been there before.

Juno picked it up gently. "Souvenir!"

"A real volcano rock," whispered Rumble's tiny voice, growing fainter. "Night is getting deep now. Stay cozy, little rocks."

Milo set the rock next to the LEGO mountain.

Theo set his tablet down beside it too, already planning to tell his Roblox friends about the trip tomorrow.

Theo yawned a giant yawn. "Best. Field trip. Ever."

Juno hugged her dinosaur tight and climbed into bed, already dreaming of bubbling mountains.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Stay cozy, little rocks.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is an opening in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gas can escape.
Melted rock is called **magma** underground, and **lava** once it flows out.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been letting out lava for years and years.
Hawaii's volcanoes are wide and gentle, not pointy, shaped kind of like a shark fin lying down.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest volcano on Earth, rising over **four thousand meters** above the sea.
Most of the world's volcanoes sit along a giant horseshoe shape called the Ring of Fire.
Many volcanoes form where giant puzzle-piece parts of the Earth bump together.
Hawaii's volcanoes grow over a **hotspot**, a place deep down where extra-hot rock keeps rising.
In **1963**, a brand new island called **Surtsey** rose right out of the sea near Iceland.
Iceland has so many volcanoes because two giant pieces of Earth are pulling apart underneath it.
**Yellowstone** sits on a **supervolcano**, but its last huge eruption was about **640,000 years ago**.
The biggest volcano anywhere is **Olympus Mons** on Mars, about **thirteen miles** tall.
Scientists watch for **tiny shakes** in the ground, plus **pictures from space**, to know when a volcano might wake up.
Old volcano ash turns into **fertile** dirt, which means plants grow extra well there.

story.title: Juno and the Bee in the Amber Light
story.subtitle: A tiny bee, a golden rock, and the biggest buzz in the world.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Bee in the Golden Rock
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor. Her dinosaur toys stood in a row. The little triceratops guarded the big T. rex.

On her shelf, a small golden rock glowed. It was her nightlight. Something inside it buzzed.

"Dinosaurs don't buzz," Juno said.

The rock glowed brighter. BZZZZZ! A tiny bee, stuck inside, opened one eye.

"That's amber," said a tiny voice. "Old golden rock. Bugs got stuck in it long ago."

"Like when dinosaurs were here?" Juno asked.

"Bees buzzed right next to dinosaurs," said the bee. "This rock is almost **100 million years old**! I'm Ember. Want to see a hive?"

Juno grinned. "Yes!"

Ember glowed. Juno shrank down, down, down, small as a bee herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzing City
chapters.text:
They landed on a huge hive, the bees' busy home. Bees zoomed in and out everywhere.

"How many bees live here?" Juno asked.

"Count the lines!" said Ember.

Juno pointed at bees zooming past. "So many! A hundred? A thousand?"

"Even more," said Ember. "A big hive can have up to **eighty thousand bees**, all working together!"

"Eighty thousand?!" Juno's eyes went wide.

"See her?" Ember pointed to one bee, bigger than the rest. "That's the **queen**. She's the mom of them all."

Juno waved. The queen waggled back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Queen's Busy Day
chapters.text:
The queen bee moved down a row of tiny rooms. She dipped her tail into each one.

"What is she doing?" Juno asked.

"Laying eggs! Watch and count," said Ember.

Juno counted. One, two, three... the queen kept going, fast as can be.

"She never stops?" Juno asked.

"She can lay about **two thousand eggs** in one single day," said Ember.

Juno's mouth popped open. "That's more than all my dinosaur toys and all my blocks put together!"

Ember laughed, a tiny buzzy laugh.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Juno Picks a Job
chapters.text:
Little bees zoomed past, each one busy.

"What do they all do?" Juno asked.

"Every girl bee takes a turn at every job," said Ember. "Cleaning. Guarding the door. Flying out for flowers."

"Can I pick a job?" Juno asked.

"Try guard," said Ember.

Juno puffed up and stood at the hive door. A beetle came close.

"NO BUGS TODAY!" Juno shouted, and the beetle scuttled off.

Ember giggled. "Good job, guard bee Juno."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Five Eyes and a Big Buzz
chapters.text:
A bee landed right in front of Juno's nose.

"Whoa, your eyes!" Juno said.

"Count them," said Ember.

Juno counted. "Two big ones. But... three tiny ones on top! That's **five eyes**!"

"Five eyes to see the whole world," said Ember.

Then the bee's wings blurred. WHIRRRR! Juno felt a tiny breeze.

"Why do you buzz?" Juno asked.

"My wings flap **two hundred times every second**," said the bee. "That makes the buzzy sound."

"Like a tiny dinosaur roar," Juno said, "but softer."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Six Sides Is Smart
chapters.text:
Juno looked at the walls of the hive. Tiny rooms, side by side.

"What shape is that?" Juno asked.

"Count the sides," said Ember.

Juno touched one. "One, two, three, four, five, **six sides**!"

"That shape holds the most honey using the least wax," said Ember.

"Smart bees," Juno said. She pressed her hand flat against one. It fit perfectly.

"Can I make one?" Juno lined up six little sticks into a ring.

"Perfect," said Ember.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
A bee landed and started to wiggle, round and round.

"Why is she dancing?" Juno asked.

"Watch closely," said Ember. "She's telling her friends where the best flowers are."

Juno wiggled along. "Like this?"

"A patient scientist named **Karl** figured out this dance a long time ago," said Ember. "The wiggles show which way to fly, and how far."

Juno pointed where the bee pointed. "That way! To the yellow flowers!"

The bee buzzed off, straight toward the flowers.

"I helped!" Juno cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Golden Drop
chapters.text:
Bees zoomed home, bellies full of sweet flower juice called nectar.

"They turn that into honey," said Ember. "It takes a lot of flowers. Bees visit about **two million flowers** just to make one pot of honey."

"Two million?!" Juno gasped.

"And one bee only makes a tiny taste of honey her whole life," said Ember. "Smaller than a teaspoon!"

"But honey lasts forever?" Juno asked.

"Honey from **ancient Egypt** is still good to eat today," said Ember. "That is very old honey."

Ember glowed bright. Juno grew back to her own size, back on her bedroom floor.

On her pillow sat one golden drop of honey, sparkling like the amber rock.

"Goodnight, Ember," Juno whispered.

The amber nightlight dimmed to a soft glow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz well, dream well.

true_facts.text: Bees got stuck in **amber**, old golden rock, almost **100 million years old** — back when dinosaurs were still around.
A bee home can have one **queen** bee, the mom of them all.
A big hive can have up to **eighty thousand bees** living and working together.
A queen bee can lay about **two thousand eggs** in just one day.
Every girl bee takes turns doing jobs, like cleaning, guarding the door, and flying out for flowers.
A bee has **five eyes** in all — two big ones and three tiny ones on top.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times every second**, which makes the buzzy sound.
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides** so bees can store the most honey with the least wax.
A bee does a wiggly dance to show her friends which way to fly to find flowers, and how far.
Bees visit about **two million flowers** together just to make one pot of honey.
One bee only makes a tiny taste of honey, smaller than a teaspoon, in her whole life.
Honey found from **ancient Egypt** is still good to eat today, because it lasts a very long time.
