story.title: Theo and the Beep Heard Round the World
story.subtitle: A midnight trip through the space race, one level at a time

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beeping Ball (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was supposed to be asleep.

Instead he was on the floor of his room, laptop balanced on a stack of books, building a rocket inside Roblox Studio. The rocket kept exploding on launch. Again.

He mashed the test button one more time. The screen flickered. Then it didn't just flicker — it went black, then green, with little square blips crawling across it like something out of an old computer museum.

A pixel blinked in the corner. It grew arms. Then legs. Then a blocky astronaut helmet, like an avatar nobody had finished skinning yet.

"Status: online," it said, in a voice like a dial-up modem learning to talk. "Player Theo has joined the server."

Theo blinked at it. "Did I just glitch a guy into existence?"

"Negative," said the blocky avatar. "Call me Ping. I've been parked in this screen since before you were born, waiting for someone who likes building things enough to notice. You built forty rockets tonight. All forty failed." A pause. "I like your odds."

"They weren't failures," Theo said. "They were learning opportunities."

"Good answer," said Ping. "Here's a real one that didn't fail." The green blips arranged themselves into a small, shining ball with four long whiskers of wire trailing behind it. "**October 4, 1957**. The Soviet Union launches this — a satellite called **Sputnik 1**, about the size of a beach ball. **58 centimeters** wide. No camera. No crew. Just a radio."

"A radio that does what?"

"Listen."

A sound crackled out of the speakers: *beep... beep... beep...* — plain, steady, almost boring.

Theo frowned. "That's it? That's the big space moment?"

"That beep," said Ping, "is the first man-made object to ever circle the Earth, talking to anyone on the planet who owned an ordinary radio. People pointed their antennas at the sky and picked it up themselves. No special equipment. Just patience."

Theo's building brain, the one that spent hours figuring out how scripts worked, started breaking the problem into pieces. "So if people everywhere could tune in and hear it going around, you could time it. Figure out how fast it's going. How high."

"Try it," said Ping, and a slider appeared, counting seconds between beeps.

Theo tuned it the way he'd tune anything — patiently, nudging the dial until the rhythm lined up with a pulsing dot circling a cartoon Earth. The orbit snapped into place.

"**WHOOOOSH**," Ping said approvingly, as the dot swept past. "You just found Sputnik's orbit using nothing but a stopwatch and your ears. That's basically what people all over the world did in 1957, except they didn't have a reset button."

Theo grinned. "Beat level one."

"There are more levels," said Ping. "A lot more. Put your shoes on."

"It's midnight."

"It's always midnight somewhere a satellite is passing over," said Ping, which didn't really make sense, but the room was already folding away.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Passenger (1957)
chapters.text:
They landed — if that's the word for however Ping moved things — inside a hush of cold air and the hum of machinery.

A dog sat patiently inside a small capsule, a round window at her eye level, cables looped gently around her like the world's strangest car seat.

"Her name's **Laika**," said Ping. "**November 3, 1957**. One month after Sputnik 1. This is Sputnik 2, and she's about to become the first living creature to orbit the Earth."

Theo crouched by the capsule, the way he'd crouch next to his own dog if she looked nervous before a car ride. "Is she scared?"

"She's trained," said Ping. "But you tell me. Look at the window."

Theo looked. It was small — barely bigger than a porthole — but it was right at paw height. "She can see out," he said slowly. "Somebody built this so she wouldn't just be stuck in the dark."

"Correct," said Ping. "Somebody thought about that. It mattered to them."

Theo sat back on his heels. In Roblox Studio, whenever he built a vehicle, he always put in a window — not because the code needed it, but because it felt wrong to trap a player in a sealed box with no view. He hadn't expected real rocket engineers to think the same way.

"She's about to go higher than anything with a heartbeat has ever gone," Ping said. "Nobody knew for certain what it would do to a living creature. She went anyway — or rather, she was sent, and she handled it."

"That's a lot of pressure for a dog," Theo said.

"She didn't know that," said Ping. "She just knew it was launch day. Which might be the secret to doing anything brave. Don't think about it too hard."

The capsule lit up, and for a second the little window glowed gold with reflected sunrise. Then the room folded away like a loading screen, and the hum of rocket engines faded into something gentler — an office full of blinking consoles.

"She became famous all over the world," Ping said. "Streets, stamps, a statue later on. The first living passenger in space, and she never even had to fill out an application."

Theo laughed despite himself. "I want a statue."

"Build something worth one first," said Ping. "Come on. Next stop, a building that didn't exist yet."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Invisible Belt (1958)
chapters.text:
The console room buzzed with new energy, chairs spinning, coffee cups — so many coffee cups — scattered across desks.

"**October 1, 1958**," said Ping. "The United States starts a brand-new agency to catch up in the sky. They call it **NASA**. Before this, American rocket work was split across different groups, all a little competitive with each other. NASA put it under one roof."

"Catch up how?" Theo asked. "Didn't the US already have rockets?"

"They had rockets," said Ping. "They didn't have a satellite in orbit yet. That changed fast." A model rocket, thin as a pencil compared to the fat Soviet ones Theo had seen, stood on a nearby pad. "**January 31, 1958**. **Explorer 1** launches. First successful American satellite."

"What's it actually for?" Theo said. "Sputnik just beeped. Did this one do more?"

"Good question," said Ping, sounding genuinely pleased, like a teacher whose student had finally asked the thing the whole lesson was building toward. "Explorer 1 carried an instrument that counted radiation — tiny invisible particles — zipping around near Earth. And here's the strange part. As it climbed higher, the counter didn't count more. It went quiet."

Theo thought about debugging scripts, the way a tool sometimes went silent not because nothing was happening, but because *too much* was happening and it maxed out.

"It's not broken," he said slowly. "It's overloaded. There's so much of whatever it's measuring up there that the counter can't keep up."

Ping lit up — literally, a small green glow pulsing across the blocky chest. "Exactly what the scientists figured out. There's a belt of radiation circling the Earth, invisible, way up high, held there by Earth's own magnetism like a giant invisible hula hoop. Nobody knew it was there until Explorer 1's silence told them."

"So the broken instrument was the discovery."

"The **Van Allen radiation belt**," said Ping. "Named for the scientist who figured out what the silence meant. You just worked out, from one small clue, something that took real scientists weeks to untangle. Not bad for someone who can't stay awake through a car ride."

"I was six," Theo said. "That was one time."

"Noted in the logs forever," said Ping. "Now buckle up for real. Next stop is a man about to do something nobody in the history of the species has ever done."

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The console room dissolved into daylight and a launch pad so tall Theo had to tip his head back to see the top.

A man in a round helmet walked toward a silver capsule, smiling like he was heading to a soccer match instead of outer space.

"**Yuri Gagarin**," said Ping. "**April 12, 1961**. First human being to leave the planet. He's about to ride this capsule, called **Vostok 1**, all the way around the Earth once, then come home. **108 minutes**, start to finish."

Theo did the math without meaning to, the way he always did math he actually cared about. "That's less than two hours. He went around the *entire planet* in less than two hours?"

"Fast," said Ping. "Give or take."

"Faster than anything in my game," Theo muttered. "I'd have to rewrite half my movement script."

Gagarin climbed in. The hatch sealed. Somewhere behind them, engineers Theo couldn't see were holding their breath, and the ground began to shake.

"**WHOOOOSH**," Ping said, and meant it this time — the whole set trembled as the rocket climbed, flame beneath it turning the dawn orange.

Then, almost too fast, it was over: a dot on a screen, a parachute, a man walking away from a field somewhere, grinning.

"He just circled the whole world," Theo said, a little stunned. "And came back smiling."

"People said he smiled the entire flight," said Ping. "Twenty-three days later, an American named **Alan Shepard** went up too, in a capsule called **Freedom 7** — shorter flight, no full orbit, but first American off the ground. **May 5, 1961**."

"So the Soviets were still ahead."

"By a lot," Ping agreed. "Which is exactly why, three weeks after that, an American president stood up and said something enormous."

The scene shifted: a stage, cameras, a man at a podium with the calm, deliberate voice of someone who knew the whole country was listening.

"**May 25, 1961**," said Ping. "President **John F. Kennedy** challenges the United States to land a man on the Moon — and bring him home safely — before the decade is out."

Theo stared at the date in his head. "Before 1970. That's not very long."

"They didn't even have a rocket built yet that could do it," Ping said. "Kennedy told an entire country to build something from scratch, on a deadline, with the whole world watching."

"That's every group project I've ever had," Theo said. "Except with more rocket fuel."

"Considerably more," said Ping. "Let's go meet some of the people who actually had to deliver."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Forty-Eight Orbits and Ten Minutes Outside (1963–1965)
chapters.text:
They arrived somewhere that smelled, improbably, like machine oil and fresh bread.

A woman in a flight suit walked briskly across the tarmac, clipboard under one arm, like she had somewhere far more important to be than wherever anyone expected.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Ping. "**June 16, 1963**. First woman in space. Before this she worked in a textile factory and jumped out of planes for fun on weekends."

"Jumped out of planes. For *fun*," Theo repeated.

"For fun," Ping confirmed. "She went up aboard a capsule called **Vostok 6** and orbited Earth **48 times** before she came back down."

Theo tried to picture it — forty-eight full laps of the entire planet, like running laps of a soccer field except the field was the whole world and you never got tired enough to stop.

"What was it like having her up there?" Theo asked.

"Nobody had tested whether a woman's body would handle space any differently," Ping said. "Spoiler: it didn't. She handled it exactly as well as anyone, which at the time was apparently considered news."

"It shouldn't have been," Theo said.

"No," Ping agreed. "It shouldn't have."

The scene flickered, and a new one rose up — a capsule drifting in silent black, a cosmonaut floating just outside it on the end of a long tether, turning slowly like a balloon that had slipped someone's grip.

"**Alexei Leonov**," said Ping. "**March 18, 1965**. First person to leave his capsule entirely and float free in space, tied to the ship called **Voskhod 2** by a safety rope. About **ten minutes** outside."

Theo studied the tether, the way it looped from the capsule to the suit. His builder brain clicked on again. "That's the whole safety system? One rope?"

"One very important rope," said Ping.

"If I built that in Roblox Studio, I'd triple-check the rope never breaks. Probably add backups just in case."

"They checked it plenty," said Ping. "It held. He got back inside — a little late, a little worried about how puffed-up his suit had gotten out there, but he got back inside."

"Puffed-up how?"

"Space doesn't push back on a suit the way air does," said Ping. "It swelled up like a pool floatie. He had to let some air out of it just to squeeze through the hatch again."

Theo laughed, surprised. "Nobody tells you that part."

"Most people don't," said Ping. "Most people just remember the ten minutes of floating. The squeezing-back-in part is the better story."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Secret Chief Designer (1966–1968)
chapters.text:
The next stop was a blueprint room, walls covered floor to ceiling with drawings of rockets Theo didn't recognize.

"Somebody built all the Soviet rockets that kept winning," Theo said. "Who?"

"That," said Ping, "is the best question anyone's asked all night, because for years, nobody outside the program was allowed to know."

"What do you mean, allowed?"

"His name was **Sergei Korolev**," Ping said. "Chief designer behind the Soviet rocket program. Sputnik, Gagarin's flight, all of it ran through his desk. And the Soviet Union kept his identity a secret the entire time he was alive. No photos released. No name in the newspapers. Just 'the Chief Designer.'"

Theo frowned at the blank space where a nameplate should have been on one of the drawings. "So the guy behind the most famous rockets on Earth was basically invisible?"

"Famous achievements, invisible face," Ping said. "Nobody outside the program knew who he was until after he died, in **1966**."

"That feels backwards," Theo said. "Shouldn't the person who does the thing get credit for the thing?"

"You'd think," said Ping. "Meanwhile, on the American side, there was no mystery at all."

The blueprints shifted, and Theo found himself at the foot of something so enormous he had to walk backward three full steps to see the top of it.

"The **Saturn V**," Ping said. "**363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty, if you stood it right next to her. Designed by a team led by **Wernher von Braun**, who'd built rockets years before and brought that experience to NASA."

"That's not a rocket," Theo said. "That's a skyscraper that's mad about something."

"It had to be that big to carry enough fuel to reach the Moon," said Ping. "Three astronauts, one lander, thousands of tons of machinery and fuel, standing on a pad, waiting."

The scene shifted once more — suddenly they were floating, no gravity at all, inside a cramped capsule with a tiny round window. Through it, Earth hung against the black, blue and white and startlingly small.

"**December 1968**," said Ping. "**Apollo 8**. First crew to circle the Moon. Didn't land — just orbited and came home. But look what one of them saw on the way around."

A photo on the console: the grey, cratered edge of the Moon in the foreground, and behind it, rising like a sunrise except it was an entire planet, Earth itself.

"**William Anders** took that picture," said Ping. "They call it **Earthrise**. First time anyone had seen their whole planet like that — small, round, floating alone."

Theo stared at it for a long moment, the kind of quiet that didn't need Ping to fill.

"That's kind of the best screenshot anyone's ever taken," he finally said.

"Nobody's topped it yet," Ping agreed.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Giant Leap and the Long Way Home (1969–1970)
chapters.text:
A ladder. A boot. A dusty grey surface stretching out under a black sky with no stars twinkling in it at all, because up there, they don't twinkle — they just sit, steady and silent.

"**July 20, 1969**," Ping said, voice dropping like even a blocky pixel avatar understood the moment deserved it. "**Apollo 11**. **Neil Armstrong** becomes the first person to walk on the Moon."

The boot touched down. Grey dust puffed outward in slow motion, with nothing to blow it away.

"*That's one small step for man,*" Armstrong's voice crackled, "*one giant leap for mankind.*"

Theo mouthed the last word along with him. He'd heard the line a hundred times, in videos, in memes. Standing here, watching the boot actually hit the ground, it didn't sound like a meme at all.

"**Buzz Aldrin** joined him down there a few minutes later," said Ping. "A third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above the whole time, alone in the ship that would fly them back home — a command module called **Columbia** — circling the Moon and waiting for them to come back up."

"That feels like the worst job," Theo said. "Getting that close and not getting to walk on it."

"Somebody has to fly the ship home," said Ping. "Not every important job gets the ladder."

Theo nodded slowly. He thought of all the times in group builds where he'd done the unglamorous part — the lighting, the backend scripts nobody saw — while somebody else got the screenshots.

"Between **1969 and 1972**," Ping went on, "**twelve** American astronauts walked on the Moon, across six landing missions. Armstrong was just the first."

"Only twelve people, ever, in all of history," Theo said. "That's a smaller number than my soccer team."

"Much smaller," said Ping. "And it almost didn't stay that clean a record. Come here."

The Moon dissolved into the cramped inside of a different capsule, warning lights blinking, a steady alarm tone thinner and more worried than anything Theo had heard yet.

"**1970**. **Apollo 13**," said Ping. "On the way to the Moon, an oxygen tank explodes. Crippled ship, three astronauts, hundreds of thousands of miles from home."

Theo's stomach tightened. "Did they—"

"They made it back," Ping said immediately, cutting straight through the worry. "Every one of them. Engineers on the ground, working around the clock, found a fix using only what the astronauts already had on board. No fancy new parts. No resupply. Just very smart people solving a puzzle under pressure."

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "That's basically the best debugging story ever."

"The best one that mattered this much, certainly," said Ping. "They came home safe. Every single time something went wrong up there, somebody on the ground or in the capsule found a way through it."

"I like that version of space better," Theo said. "The one where everybody gets to come home."

"Funny," said Ping. "That's most of them."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
The capsule dissolved, and for a moment Theo floated in simple black, calm after the alarm of the last stop, waiting to see what came next.

"One more stop," said Ping. "The last one. It's my favorite, honestly."

Two spacecraft drifted toward each other against the dark — one blocky and American, one rounder and Soviet, their shapes completely different, like two different kids had built them in two completely different games.

"**July 17, 1975**," said Ping. "American and Soviet spacecraft dock together in orbit. Crews open the hatch between them and shake hands, right there in space."

Theo watched the hatch creak open, watched an astronaut's gloved hand reach through to meet a cosmonaut's.

"Wait," Theo said. "After everyone was racing each other for like twenty years, they just teamed up?"

"That's how it ended," said Ping. "Not with a winner crossing a finish line first and everyone else going home sad. With two crews from two different countries, shaking hands a hundred miles above the planet, because by then it wasn't really about beating each other anymore. It was about what people could do when they stopped keeping score."

Theo thought about every build he'd ever rage-quit because somebody else's game had better graphics, more players, more everything. He thought about how much better it usually went when he just messaged the other builder and asked how they'd done it.

"That's a pretty good ending," Theo said.

"Best one I know," said Ping.

The black around them folded inward, the way a loading screen folds, and Theo blinked — and he was back on his bedroom floor, laptop glowing in front of him, the clock on the wall reading well past when he should've been asleep.

His rocket was still on the screen. Still mid-explosion, frozen on the last frame before he'd been pulled away.

He looked at it for a second. Then he deleted the whole launch sequence and started again, slower this time, adding a window to the capsule, small and round, right at the front, exactly where a Sputnik-dog or a Moon-walking astronaut or anybody at all would want one.

A tiny green blip pulsed once in the corner of the screen, then went quiet, waiting for the next time Theo stayed up too late building something.

"Status," Theo murmured to the empty room, grinning. "Saved."

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a docking port to build.

true_facts.text: On **October 4, 1957**, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, a satellite about the size of a beach ball.
Sputnik 1 was only **58 centimeters** wide and sent out a steady **beep** anyone with a regular radio could pick up.
The whole contest between the US and the Soviet Union to reach space firsts ran from about **1957 to 1975**.
On **November 3, 1957**, a dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States started a brand-new space agency called **NASA** on **October 1, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and found an invisible ring of radiation around Earth called the **Van Allen belt**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling the whole Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet crews docked their spacecraft together in orbit and shook hands, ending the space race in teamwork.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** challenged the country to land a person on the Moon and bring them home safe before **1970**.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, circling Earth **48 times**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float freely outside his capsule, held by a safety rope for about **ten minutes**.
The Soviet Union's chief rocket designer, **Sergei Korolev**, was kept secret from the public until after he died in **1966**.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon during the **Apollo 11** mission.

story.title: Maya and the Brass Compass: The Night the Titanic Sailed
story.subtitle: A calm, true voyage across one hundred years of water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Boat That Glowed
chapters.text:
Maya sat on her bedroom floor, drawing boats, like she did every single night. Tonight she drew the biggest one yet — four tall funnels, rows of little windows, one tiny flag on top.

She set down her pencil. Something on her shelf began to glow.

It was the small brass compass Grandpa had given her. Its needle spun in slow circles, and soft blue-green light spilled across the carpet.

"Well," said a creaky little voice. "Someone has drawn the Titanic."

Maya jumped. "You can talk?"

"Only when someone draws something worth talking about," said the compass. "Call me Compass. Want to see the real ship — the one in your drawing?"

Maya grabbed her pencil case like a suitcase. "Always."

The light swallowed the room. When it cleared, Maya stood in a noisy **shipyard** — a big outdoor workshop where ships get built — hammers banging all around her.

"Welcome to **Belfast, Ireland**," said Compass. "The year is **1909**."

A giant metal spine stretched across the yard, long as a whole city block.

"That's her **keel**," said Compass. "The bottom bone of the ship. Workers laid it down on **March 31, 1909**, right here at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard."

Maya tipped her head back. The ship already towered over her.

"Someday she'll be **882 feet long**," said Compass. "About as long as nine blue whales nose to tail. The biggest ship in the whole world."

Maya knelt and sketched the keel in the dirt, adding tiny stick-figure workers for scale. "I want to see her finished!"

Compass chuckled, and the needle spun again. They landed beside a river packed with cheering crowds. A huge ship slid into the water with a **SPLOOSH**, splashing Maya's shoes.

"**May 31, 1911**," said Compass. "The day Titanic was launched."

Maya laughed, wringing out her socks. "She splashed me already, and she isn't even finished!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: All Aboard!
chapters.text:
A deep horn blasted, so loud Maya covered her ears. Crowds waved hankies on a busy dock.

"**April 10, 1912**," said Compass. "Titanic's very first trip. She's leaving **Southampton, England**, headed for **New York City**."

Maya counted the funnels sticking up from the deck. "One, two, three, four!"

She squinted. "Wait — that fourth one looks different. It's not smoking like the others."

"Sharp eyes," said Compass. "Titanic had **four funnels**, but only **three** ever puffed real smoke. The fourth was mostly there to look grand."

Maya giggled. "So it's a fake chimney? That's silly."

"People liked big ships to look even bigger," said Compass.

Maya pulled out her pencil and doodled a tiny mustache on her drawing's fourth funnel. "There. Now it looks proud of being pretend."

As the ship pulled away, Compass pointed to two more ships docked nearby, nearly twins of Titanic. "Those are her sisters, **Olympic** and **Britannic**. Three ships built together, like a family."

Maya waved at the matching ships. "Do sisters race each other?"

"Sometimes," said Compass. "But tonight, this one has somewhere to be."

The horn blasted once more, long and proud, and the dock slid away behind them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Unsinkable Rooms
chapters.text:
Maya leaned over the ship's rail, watching the water rush by far below. A worry bubbled up. "Compass, this ship is so heavy. What if it just... sinks?"

"A fair question," said Compass. "Come see something clever."

They slipped down into the ship's belly, where metal walls stretched floor to ceiling in neat rows.

"These are **watertight compartments**," said Compass. "Sixteen separate rooms, each with doors that seal shut tight. If water ever got into one room, the rest would stay dry."

Maya's eyes went wide. "Like an egg carton! If one cup breaks, the others are fine!"

"Exactly like that," said Compass. "People were so impressed, they started calling her 'nearly unsinkable.'"

Maya grinned and drew a row of little sealed boxes in her notebook, labeling them "safe! safe! safe!"

Up on the bridge, a tall man with a neat white beard studied a map calmly.

"That's **Captain Edward Smith**," said Compass. "One of the most experienced captains anywhere. He's sailed this ocean more times than you've had birthdays."

Maya waved up at him. He gave a small nod back, steady as a lighthouse.

"He seems like he knows exactly what he's doing," Maya said.

"He does," said Compass softly. "That's why people trusted him with such a big ship."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Dogs, Dresses, and Molly Brown
chapters.text:
A small bark echoed across the deck. Maya spun around to find a fluffy little dog trotting past on a leash.

"That's a **Pomeranian**," said Compass. "Two of them are aboard, tucked snug in their owners' arms."

Maya crouched low and gave the dog a gentle pat, careful not to startle it. "Hello, little sailor."

Nearby, a cheerful woman in a wide hat was laughing with a group of passengers, telling a story with big, sweeping arm motions.

"That's **Molly Brown**," said Compass. "Remember her name. Later, she'll row her own lifeboat, and people will call her 'the **Unsinkable Molly Brown**.'"

"Unsinkable, like the ship!" Maya said.

"Even better," said Compass. "She earns it herself."

Maya noticed rows of small boats hanging along the deck's edge. She counted on her fingers. "There are so many people on this ship. Are there boats for everyone?"

Compass's light dimmed just a little. "There are lifeboats for about **1,178 people**. Not quite enough for everyone aboard."

Maya frowned, thinking hard. "That doesn't seem fair. Everybody should get a seat."

"You're right," said Compass gently. "Hold onto that thought, Maya. It matters later."

Maya nodded and drew a little boat with extra seats, just in case.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Sea Turned to Glass
chapters.text:
The air turned sharp and cold. The ocean lay flat and still, smooth as glass under a sky full of stars.

"It's so quiet," Maya whispered.

Then — **CRUNCH**. A shudder rolled through the deck under her feet.

Maya grabbed the rail. "What was that?!"

"An iceberg," said Compass calmly. "A giant chunk of floating ice. It's **11:40 p.m.** on **April 14, 1912**. Titanic just scraped along its side."

"Is everyone okay?" Maya asked quickly.

"Everyone on deck is just fine," said Compass. "No one is hurt. But down below, water is starting to come in."

Maya hurried toward a small room crackling with electric buzzes and clicks. Two men bent over a machine, tapping out patterns.

"That's **wireless**," said Compass, "a radio that sends messages through the air using beeps. They're sending a **distress signal** — a call for help — the old way, called **CQD**, and the brand new way, called **SOS**."

Maya tapped her finger along with the rhythm, counting the short beeps and long ones. "Dot, dot, dot — dash, dash, dash — dot, dot, dot!"

"That's it exactly," said Compass. "S-O-S. Help is on its way."

Maya let out a breath. "Good. Someone's coming."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Ship That Came Running
chapters.text:
The deck tilted, just a little, like a seesaw settling. Passengers climbed calmly into the small boats, wrapped in blankets.

From somewhere near the front, soft music drifted across the water — violins, playing on.

"Legend says the ship's band kept playing to help everyone stay calm," said Compass. "We can't be completely sure that's exactly how it happened, but it's a lovely story, and it shows how brave those musicians were."

Maya hummed along quietly, watching the little boats row away from the big ship under the stars.

"By about **2:20 a.m.**," said Compass, "less than three hours after the iceberg, Titanic slipped beneath the water."

Maya's chest felt tight. "Did everyone get away safe?"

"Sadly, not everyone on board could be saved that night," said Compass gently. "But look there, Maya."

Far off, a tiny light bobbed on the dark horizon.

Maya spotted it first. "A ship! Compass, look — a ship is coming!"

"That's the **Carpathia**," said Compass. "She raced all night long. Starting the next morning, she pulled every single person from those lifeboats to safety."

Maya watched the little boats row toward the growing light, and finally let herself smile. "They found them. They're okay."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: New Rules for the Sea
chapters.text:
Sunlight warmed Maya's shoulders as the compass light shifted, soft and gold now instead of blue-green.

"Did grown-ups fix it," Maya asked, "so this wouldn't happen to another ship?"

"They did," said Compass. "Remember what you said — that everyone should get a seat in a lifeboat?"

Maya nodded. "I remember."

"After Titanic, a new rule was made," said Compass. "Every ship must now carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No exceptions."

Maya's eyes lit up. "That was my idea!"

"It was everyone's idea, once they saw what happened," said Compass kindly. "And one more thing — ships started watching out for icebergs on purpose, with a special iceberg patrol, so captains would know when ice was near."

Maya pumped her fist. "So ships got safer because of her."

"Exactly," said Compass. "Something hard happened, and people learned from it. That's a kind of bravery too."

Maya drew a new boat in her notebook — rows and rows of lifeboats, enough for every tiny passenger she'd drawn.

"There," she said proudly. "Now nobody gets left behind."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Finding Her Again
chapters.text:
The light shifted again, turning deep and dark. Maya floated — somehow — in cold, silent water, far below any waves.

"Where are we now?" she whispered.

"**1985**," said Compass. "Deep under the ocean, about **12,500 feet** down — far deeper than any sunlight reaches."

A small glowing screen floated nearby, showing fuzzy shapes on the dark seafloor. Maya squinted at it.

"There!" she said suddenly, pointing. "That shape — it's the front of a ship!"

"You found her," said Compass, voice warm with pride. "**Robert Ballard** and his team found this very wreck — the broken ship resting on the seafloor — on **September 1, 1985**, about **370 miles** off the coast of **Newfoundland, Canada**. She split into two main pieces."

Maya pressed her hand to the glass. "Hi again," she whispered to the ship.

"People built a whole museum for her, shaped like a ship's front, in **Belfast**, back in **2012**," said Compass. "There was even a famous movie made about her, back in **1997**. And plates, shoes, all sorts of little things from the ship are kept safe in museums today."

Maya smiled. "Someday I want to visit. I'll draw everything I see."

The light swelled bright blue-green, and the deep sea melted away.

Maya blinked. She was back on her bedroom carpet, pencil in hand. Her drawing now showed the whole story — shipyard, voyage, lifeboats, and the ship resting quietly on the seafloor, found at last.

The compass settled on her shelf, its needle finally still, glowing soft and low like a nightlight.

"Thank you, Compass," Maya murmured, climbing into bed.

"Anytime," it creaked. "Sweet dreams, little sailor."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. The sea is calm, the compass is quiet, and you are safe and warm. Sleep well, little sailor.

Her **keel**, the bottom bone of the ship, was laid down on **March 31, 1909**, and she was launched with a splash on **May 31, 1911**.
At **882 feet long**, Titanic was the biggest ship in the whole world.
She left **Southampton, England**, on **April 10, 1912**, heading for **New York City**.
Titanic had **four funnels**, but only **three** of them ever puffed real smoke.
Inside the ship, sixteen **watertight compartments** could seal shut like a row of sealed boxes, to keep water from spreading.
Two small **Pomeranian** dogs were carried safely aboard the lifeboats.
Passenger **Molly Brown** rowed her own lifeboat and was nicknamed the **"Unsinkable Molly Brown."**
There were lifeboats for about **1,178 people**, which was not quite enough for everyone aboard.
At **11:40 p.m.** on **April 14, 1912**, Titanic struck an iceberg.
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued the people from the lifeboats the next morning.
The wreck was found on **September 1, 1985**, by explorer **Robert Ballard**, resting about **12,500 feet** deep.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Puddle
story.subtitle: A splashy bedtime adventure about sun, rain, and color.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Puddle
chapters.text:
Ivy painted a big yellow sun on her paper.

Rain went tap, tap, tap on her window.

She peeked outside in her pajamas. A puddle by the step gave a tiny, shiny glow.

"Ooh!" said Ivy. She pulled on her boots and tiptoed out. SPLASH!

Up popped a cheerful droplet with a wobbly smile. "Hi, Ivy! I'm Splash," he said.

"Want to see where rainbows hide?" Ivy nodded fast. She grabbed her paintbrush for luck.

Splash spun like a little wheel. WHOOOOSH! The puddle lifted them both into the sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Sun at Your Back
chapters.text:
They floated above the wet yard. Soft rain kept falling.

"Look around, Ivy," said Splash. "Where is the sun hiding?"

Ivy turned and turned. She found a warm, bright patch right behind her.

"The sun has to be behind you," said Splash, "and the rain has to be in front."

Ivy giggled. "Like a sandwich! Sun in back, rain in front!"

"Exactly," said Splash. "That's the very first rainbow rule."

A thin stripe of color flickered up ahead, just waiting to grow.
chapters.shout_line: SUN IN BACK, RAIN IN FRONT!

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Splash floated Ivy close to one plump, round raindrop.

"Peek inside," he said. Ivy pressed her nose near the drop.

Sunlight zoomed in, bending like it was sliding down a slide.

"It bends!" said Ivy, pointing with her paintbrush.

"Light bends when it goes into a raindrop," said Splash, "just like you bend down a slide."

Ivy clapped. She loved slides. This was the very best slide, just for sunbeams.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Bounce Off the Back
chapters.text:
Inside the drop, the sunlight zoomed to the very back wall.

"Watch!" said Splash. The light bounced off, like a ball off a wall.

"BOING!" shouted Ivy, bouncing on her tiptoes.

"That's right," said Splash. "It bounces off the back, then bends again on its way out."

Out shot a tiny stripe of color, red on top, purple on the bottom.

Ivy gasped. "It's painting the sky!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Man Named Newton
chapters.text:
Splash floated Ivy down to a cozy old room.

A curious man sat by a window, holding a clear glass shape.

"That's Isaac Newton," said Splash. "He lived a long, long time ago."

Newton held his glass shape, called a prism, up to a sunbeam.

White light went in one side. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple came out the other.

"Sunlight was hiding all those colors!" said Ivy, dabbing her own paper to match.

Newton smiled at her. "Clever girl."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sun AND Rain Together
chapters.text:
Back in the sky, Splash spun slower now.

"Remember," he said, "rainbows need sun AND rain, both at the very same time."

"Like right now!" said Ivy, feeling warm sun and soft rain together.

"Right after a rain shower, when the sun peeks out, a rainbow can appear," said Splash.

Ivy looked up. A big, bright arch bloomed across the sky.

"THERE IT IS!" Ivy cheered, waving her paintbrush like a wand.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Home Again
chapters.text:
Splash floated Ivy gently down to her puddle by the step.

"Time for bed," he said softly. "You helped make a real rainbow today."

Ivy looked down at her paper. Her yellow sun now had a bright arch beside it.

She hadn't painted that part. Or had Splash helped, just a tiny bit?

"Goodnight, Splash," she whispered. The puddle gave one last glow, then went still and quiet.

Ivy climbed into bed, her paintbrush resting right beside her pillow.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Splish, splash, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: Sunlight bends when it goes into a little raindrop.
Inside the drop, the light bounces off the back, like a ball off a wall.
The light bends again as it leaves the drop, and colors come out.
Sunlight hides lots of colors — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple — until it bends and splits apart.
To see a rainbow, the sun needs to be behind you.
Rain needs to be in front of you so you can see the colors.
Rainbows need sunshine and rain at the very same time.
Rainbows often show up right after a rain shower, when the sun peeks out.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ivy flew home with Splash the Puddle Sprite and found her painted sun now had a bright rainbow arch beside it, her paintbrush resting by her pillow as she fell asleep.

story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Express
story.subtitle: A nighttime ride with Hoot the Owl, to find out why everybody sleeps

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Hoot Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Leo lay in bed. The room felt very dark tonight.

He pulled his blanket up to his chin.

On his shelf sat Hoot, his toy owl. Hoot's eyes always glowed soft gold.

Tonight, Hoot blinked all on his own. His wings opened wide. WHIRRR!

Leo's toy train began to glow too. CHUFF, CHUFF! Real steam puffed out.

"Climb aboard," hooted Hoot. "The Sleepy Express will show you why everyone sleeps."

Leo was still a little scared of the dark. But Hoot's glow felt warm, like a tiny sun. He hopped on.

The train rolled to a cozy room from long ago. A boy slept there. Two scientists watched his closed eyes flick fast, side to side.

"That quick-eye sleep is called **REM sleep**," said Hoot. "Scientists first spotted it in **1953**."

Leo grinned. "My eyes do that too?"

"Every single night," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Loop-the-Loop Track
chapters.text:
CLACKETY-CLACK! The train rolled onto a track shaped like a big loop.

"Why does it loop?" asked Leo.

"Because sleep loops too," said Hoot. "Each loop is about **ninety minutes** long."

The train dipped down into quiet, slow sleep. Then it swooped up into busy **REM sleep**, where dreams happen.

"During REM, your brain gets busy, almost like daytime," said Hoot. "But your arms and legs go floppy, like a rag doll. That way you can't act out your dreams."

Leo let his arms flop on the seat.

"Floppy dream arms!" he shouted, giggling.

"Your whole body does that, every loop, every night," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Grow Big Station
chapters.text:
The train stopped by a tall, striped measuring pole.

A little seedling slept in a pot nearby. Overnight, it had grown taller.

"Deep sleep is when bodies grow the most," said Hoot. "A tiny helper called **growth hormone** gets busy then, telling your body to grow bigger."

Leo pressed his back against the pole. "Will I be taller tomorrow?"

"A little bit," said Hoot, "if you sleep nice and deep tonight."

Leo stood extra tall and proud.

"That's why sleep helps you grow," hooted Hoot, and the train chugged on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Clock Tower
chapters.text:
A tall clock tower stood beside the tracks, its hands glowing in the dark.

"Who runs this clock?" asked Leo.

"A tiny clock inside your own brain," said Hoot. "It tells your body when to sleep and when to wake."

"Does it have a name?" asked Leo.

"Scientists call it your **circadian clock**," said Hoot. "Circadian just means 'about a day,' because it ticks around once every day."

The tower's bell rang softly. BONG!

"So that's why I get sleepy every bedtime?" Leo asked.

"Exactly," said Hoot. "Your little clock keeps ticking, even in the dark."

Leo patted his own chest, happy to have a clock inside.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Sleepy Potion Car
chapters.text:
The train rolled into a car full of glowing jars.

One jar glowed soft purple and hummed like a lullaby.

"What's in there?" asked Leo, leaning close.

"A sleepy helper called **melatonin**," said Hoot. "It tells your body, 'nighttime is here, time to rest.' Scientists first found it in **1958**."

"Does everyone have some?" asked Leo.

"Every person, every night," said Hoot. "It's like your own tiny bedtime bell, ringing quietly inside you."

The jar glowed bright, then dim, like a sleepy yawn.

Leo yawned too. "I think mine's ringing," he giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Memory Sorting Yard
chapters.text:
CHUFFA-CHUFFA! The train passed a yard full of little cars, each one holding a memory.

A worker sorted the cars onto different tracks.

"What's happening?" asked Leo.

"While you sleep, your brain sorts your memories," said Hoot. "It keeps the important ones, like a song you practiced or a new word you learned."

Leo spotted a car with a little owl painted on it. "That one's you!"

"Sleep helped you remember me," said Hoot, puffing proudly.

Leo laughed and waved as the cars rolled by, click-clack, click-clack.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Animal Sleepover Car
chapters.text:
The train rolled past a window full of sleepy animals.

A tiny baby slept in short little bursts. "Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours** a day," said Hoot, "with lots of dreaming."

A dolphin swam by with one eye open. "Dolphins sleep with half their brain resting, so one eye watches for trouble."

A giraffe dozed standing up. "Giraffes barely sleep at all, sometimes under two hours a day!"

A tiny bat hung upside down, snoozing. "Some bats sleep almost all day, up to **twenty hours**!"

Leo pointed at each one. "Everybody sleeps differently!"

"Every animal finds their own way to rest," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home on the Sleepy Express
chapters.text:
The train began rolling home, slow and gentle.

"Hoot, could I just stay awake all night, forever?" asked Leo.

"A boy once tried staying awake a very long time, just to see what would happen," said Hoot. "Doctors say that's not a good idea. Sleepy brains get grumpy and forgetful."

Leo shook his head. "No thank you. I like sleeping."

The train slowed. CHUFF... chuff... chuff.

It rolled right back into Leo's room, tracks glowing soft and warm.

Hoot's eyes dimmed to a gentle glow, just like always.

Leo snuggled into bed, not scared of the dark anymore.

On his pillow sat one tiny glowing feather, a keepsake from the Sleepy Express.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Hoot softly, sleep soundly.

true_facts.text: Scientists first spotted **REM sleep**, the quick-eye-moving kind, by watching a sleeping boy's eyes in **1953**.
A night of sleep goes in loops about **ninety minutes** long.
During **REM sleep** your brain gets busy, but your arms and legs go floppy so you can't act out dreams.
Deep sleep is when a helper called **growth hormone** gets busy, helping bodies grow.
A tiny clock inside your brain tells your body when to sleep and when to wake.
That body clock is called **circadian**, which means 'about a day.'
A sleepy helper called **melatonin** tells your body nighttime has come. Scientists first found it in **1958**.
While you sleep, your brain sorts the day's memories and keeps the important ones.
Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours** a day, with lots of dreaming.
Dolphins sleep with half their brain resting, keeping one eye open for trouble.
Giraffes barely sleep at all, sometimes under two hours a day.
Some bats sleep almost all day, up to **twenty hours**.
A boy once tried staying awake a very long time, but doctors say that's not a good idea.

story.title: Rosa and Isla and the Wall-Climbing Bugs
story.subtitle: A sticky, stompy, slurpy bedtime adventure up the garden wall

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Ladybird
chapters.text:
Rosa sat on her bed with her favorite ladybird toy. She gave it a squeeze. Squeak, squeak!

Isla lay on the floor with a book about rock climbing. She loved climbing walls at the gym.

Then the little toy ladybird began to glow. It glowed soft and green, right there on the windowsill.

"Whoa," said Isla. "Rosa, look!"

The glow swirled and popped into a tiny, twinkly ladybird named Pip. Pip had six legs and a big friendly smile.

"Hello!" said Pip. "Want to see how bugs and lizards climb walls? Even upside down!"

"YES!" shouted Rosa and Isla together.

Pip tapped their noses. POOF! Rosa and Isla shrank down, tiny as bugs, and zoomed up to the window glass.

A little lizard called a gecko was already there, stuck flat to the glass.

"How does he not fall?" asked Isla.

Rosa pressed her tiny hand on the glass. "My hand is not sticky," she said.

"His feet have millions of tiny hairs," said Pip. "So many hairs, they grab on tight, like Velcro."

Isla watched the gecko peel one toe up, then another. "It's not glue," she said. "He just peels his toes off, like tape!"

"Exactly," said Pip. "Nothing sticky left behind. Just clever toes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Fly's Tiny Glue Drops
chapters.text:
BUZZZZ! A fly landed on the glass right next to them.

Rosa giggled. "He's walking upside down!"

Isla leaned close. "Look at his feet, Rosa. Something shiny is under there."

Tiny, wet drops glistened under the fly's feet, like little dots of syrup.

"Flies and some beetles have sticky drops that squeeze out of their feet," said Pip. "Like tiny glue, fresh every step."

"So that's his trick," said Isla. "Not hairs. Drops!"

Rosa tried to copy the fly, pressing her sticky fingers together. "Am I a fly now?" she asked.

"Almost," laughed Pip. "You just need six legs and smaller shoes."

The fly buzzed off, leaving tiny shiny footprints that faded in the sun.

"Bye, fly!" waved Rosa.

Isla grinned. "One sticky trick down. Bet there's more."

"Oh, so many more," said Pip, zooming them higher up the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Friendly Spider
chapters.text:
A shadow moved across the glass. Rosa gasped. "A SPIDER!"

"It's okay," said Pip quickly. "She's just climbing. Watch her feet, not her legs."

Rosa peeked. The spider's feet were covered in hairs even tinier than the gecko's.

"Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too," said Pip. "That's why so many spiders can climb smooth glass, just like the gecko."

"So gecko hairs and spider hairs are cousins?" asked Isla.

"Sort of," said Pip. "Same clever idea, tiny size."

The spider waved one leg, almost like hello, then scuttled sideways and away.

Rosa waved back, brave now. "Bye bye, spider! Nice hairy feet!"

Isla laughed so hard she nearly slid off the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Ants Pick Their Tools
chapters.text:
Tap, tap, tap. An ant marched up the rough brick wall below the window.

"That wall is bumpy," said Isla. "But the glass is smooth. Same ant?"

"Watch," said Pip.

On the bumpy brick, the ant used sharp little claws, like tiny hooks, to grab every bump.

Then the ant reached smooth glass. It switched to sticky pads on its feet instead.

"It changed its tools!" said Isla. "Claws for bumpy, sticky pads for smooth!"

"Ants and cockroaches both do that," said Pip. "Smart bugs pick the right trick for the right wall."

Rosa clapped. "Like picking the right shoe!"

"Just like that," said Pip, smiling.

Isla nodded, thinking of her climbing shoes with their grippy bottoms. "Smart bugs," she said. "Smarter than my shoes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goats on a Cliff
chapters.text:
Pip waved a wing and the window scene changed. Suddenly they stood on a windy, rocky cliff.

A mountain goat stood calmly on a ledge no wider than a book.

"How is he not falling?" Isla breathed, amazed.

"Look at his hooves," said Pip. "Hard on the outside, squishy and soft in the middle."

The goat's hoof pressed down, and the soft middle squashed flat against the rock, gripping tight.

"It's like my climbing shoes!" said Isla. "Hard edge, grippy bottom!"

"Climbers really do copy animal feet for ideas," said Pip. "Scientists study gecko and bug feet to make better climbing gloves and shoes."

Isla's eyes went huge. "I want to invent climbing shoes someday," she said.

Rosa pointed at the goat. "He's a very good climber too!"

The goat hopped to another ledge. TAP! Steady as ever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Scratchy Squirrel
chapters.text:
Back in the yard, a squirrel zipped straight up the big oak tree.

SCRATCH, SCRATCH, SCRATCH!

"How does he climb so fast?" asked Rosa.

"Look close," said Pip. "His claws are sharp and curved."

Isla squinted. The bark looked smooth from far away, but up close it had tiny cracks and bumps.

"His claws dig into bumps we can't even see!" she said.

The squirrel paused on a branch, looked at them, and flicked its tail.

"Hi, squirrel!" said Rosa. "Nice scratchy toes!"

The squirrel scampered higher, leaves rustling, and vanished into the branches.

"Claws for bark," said Isla, counting on her fingers. "Hairs for glass. Drops for flies. So many tricks!"

"And we're not done yet," said Pip, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Froggy Feet
chapters.text:
PLIP, PLOP! Rain began to fall, and a little tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf.

Rosa loved frogs almost as much as ladybirds. "Can he climb when it's wet?" she asked.

"Watch his toes," said Pip.

The frog's toe pads were flat, wet, and covered in tiny shapes like a honeycomb.

"Those little shapes grip the wet leaf," said Pip. "So his feet don't slip, even in the rain."

Isla touched her own climbing shoes, which had bumpy patterns too. "Grippy shapes everywhere," she said.

The frog hopped from leaf to leaf, never slipping once.

"Boing, boing, boing!" sang Rosa, hopping in place.

Pip laughed so hard they wobbled in the air.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Slow Slimy Snail
chapters.text:
On the garden wall, something shiny left a silvery trail.

"A snail!" said Rosa. "He's so slow."

"Slow but clever," said Pip. "He glides on slippery slime, and his squishy foot ripples like little waves."

Isla watched closely. "No claws, no hairs, no sticky drops. Just slime!"

"Every climber has their own trick," said Pip. "Hairs, drops, claws, hooves, or slime. All of them clever."

The snail reached the top of the wall and tucked into his shell for a rest.

"Goodnight, snail," whispered Rosa.

Pip's glow began to shrink, and the garden wall faded into soft darkness.

POP! Rosa and Isla were back on the bedroom floor, their own normal size again.

The little ladybird toy sat glowing gently on the windowsill, like it was keeping one tiny secret.

"Best climb ever," yawned Isla, pulling her blanket up.

Rosa hugged her ladybird toy tight. "Night night, sticky toes," she whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Play well.

true_facts.text: A gecko's toes have millions of **tiny hairs** that help it grip glass and walk on ceilings.
A gecko's sticky feet are **not glue** — it peels its toes off one by one, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles have **tiny sticky drops** that squeeze out of their feet to help them climb.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, which is why many can climb smooth glass.
Ants use **sharp little claws** on bumpy walls and **sticky pads** on smooth ones, switching tools as needed.
Mountain goats have hooves that are **hard on the outside** and **soft and squishy in the middle**, so they grip rocky cliffs.
Squirrels climb using **sharp, curved claws** that dig into tiny bumps and cracks too small to see.
Tree frogs have **flat, wet toe pads** with tiny honeycomb-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves.
Snails climb walls by gliding on a layer of **slippery slime**, rippling their squishy foot like little waves.
People who study climbing have looked at gecko and bug feet to get ideas for better **climbing shoes and gloves**.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Went Back in Time
story.subtitle: A tiny red brick. A great big adventure with dinosaurs.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Back to the Very Beginning
chapters.text:
It had been a few sleeps since the big LEGO tower went **CLICK** and finally held.

Now Milo lay on the carpet building a LEGO shark. Juno sat next to him, lining up her dinosaur toys in a row.

"Stomp, stomp, stomp," said Juno, marching her triceratops across the rug.

Then the little red brick on the shelf began to glow. It glowed bright red, then it went **CLICK**.

"It's doing the thing!" said Juno. She had spotted it first.

Milo grabbed Juno's hand. "Let's go see!"

The brick went **WHOOOOSH**, and the bedroom melted into green and brown. When the swirly feeling stopped, they were standing in a strange, misty world. Ferns as tall as Dad grew all around.

A small toy triceratops tumbled out of Milo's pocket and landed on its feet. It blinked, and it was not a toy anymore. It was real, and it could talk.

"Hello," it said. "My friends call me Trike."

Juno giggled and patted the ground, not the dinosaur, because you never touch a wild animal, even a friendly one.

A small, quick creature scurried past on two legs.

"Is that a dinosaur?" asked Milo, pointing.

"It sure is," said Trike. "The very first dinosaurs showed up **230 million years ago** — so long ago that even your grandma's grandma wasn't born yet."

"Two hundred THIRTY million!" shouted Juno, even though she wasn't totally sure how big that number was. It just felt enormous, and it was.

"Let's see them ALL," said Milo.

Trike grinned a dinosaur grin. "Hold onto your brick. Here we go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Terrible Lizard Name
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH** again, and they landed in a room full of old bones laid out on tables.

A man in a stiff old coat was staring hard at one giant bone.

"Who are you?" asked Milo.

"Richard Owen," said the man, not looking up. "I study bones. And I have a problem. These old lizard bones need a name."

Juno tipped her head. "What's a dinosaur, anyway?"

Milo guessed first, because that's just how Milo is. "Is it... a big lizard?"

Richard Owen smiled. "Close! I made up a brand new word in **1842**. Dinosaur means 'terrible lizard' — not scary-terrible, just awesome-terrible, like really, really impressive."

Juno stood up tall and roared it out like a cheer.

"TERRIBLE LIZARD!"

Trike laughed so hard his frill wobbled. "That's the spirit."

Richard Owen wrote the word down carefully in his notebook, and it has stuck around ever since.

"Good name," said Milo, nodding like a builder checking his work. "Strong. Clicks right into place."

"High praise from a LEGO builder," said Trike.

The bones on the table seemed to rattle a little, almost like they were happy to finally have a name.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Teeth Like Shark Teeth
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, and the ground began to shake.

**BOOM. BOOM. BOOM.**

A giant animal stomped out from behind the trees. Its head alone was as big as a bathtub.

"T. rex," whispered Milo, and he did not whisper small, because Milo knows sharks and teeth and this was impressive.

The huge mouth opened. Inside were teeth as long as bananas.

"How big ARE those teeth?" asked Milo, who really, really loves teeth, especially shark teeth.

"Up to **30 centimeters** long, counting the root that's hidden in the jaw," said Trike. "That's about as long as your arm from your elbow to your hand."

Milo held up his arm and compared. "Whoa. My biggest shark tooth at home is tiny next to that!"

"Sharks grow new teeth their whole lives," said Milo, showing off a little. "Does T. rex do that too?"

"It sure does," said Trike.

The T. rex sniffed the air, decided they weren't lunch, and lumbered off into the ferns.

Juno let out a breath. "That was loud."

"And now it's gone," said Trike gently. "All safe."

"Can we see a SMALLER one now?" asked Juno.

"Funny you should ask," said Trike, "because the next one might surprise you."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: A Dinosaur the Size of a Turkey
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, and they landed by a rocky cliff.

Something small darted between the rocks. Juno expected a monster, because that's what the movies show.

But this dinosaur was little.

"That's a Velociraptor?" said Milo, squinting. "It's TINY."

"About the size of a turkey," said Trike. "Much smaller than it looks in movies."

Juno burst out laughing. "A turkey dinosaur!"

"And look closer," said Trike. "What's on its arms?"

Milo leaned in. "Feathers? Is that... FEATHERS?"

"Lots of dinosaurs had feathers," said Trike. "Even ones we used to think were just scaly."

Juno ran little circles, flapping her arms like wings. "I'm a dinosaur chicken!"

"Technically," said Milo, giggling, "chickens kind of ARE dinosaurs. Sort of. Right, Trike?"

Trike's eyes twinkled. "You're getting ahead of me. Hold that thought — it's a good one."

The little feathered dinosaur cocked its head at them, then scurried off after a bug, not scary at all, just quick and curious, like a very determined chicken on a mission.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Spikes, Horns, and a Big Frill
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, into a sunny field.

A huge dinosaur walked by with square plates sticking up along its back, and spikes on the end of its tail.

"Stegosaurus!" shouted Juno, pointing with both hands.

"Count the spikes on its tail," said Trike.

Juno counted slowly. "One, two, three, four!"

"Those spiky bits even have their own silly name," said Trike, grinning.

Then another dinosaur trotted up — Juno's favorite kind, with three horns on its face and a big bony shield around its neck, called a **frill**, like a built-in shield to keep its neck safe.

"Triceratops!" Juno yelled, and she counted its horns too. "One, two, three!"

"Correct both times," said Trike. "You're a natural."

The Triceratops lowered its big frilled head and let out a friendly snort, then went back to munching on ferns.

Milo studied the frill carefully. "It's like a LEGO shield piece. Snap-on armor."

"Built right onto its head," agreed Trike. "No assembly required."

Juno hugged her own arms around her neck, pretending she had a frill too. "Mine protects ME!"

Everyone laughed, and the Triceratops gave one more snort, as if laughing along.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Dinosaur Who Tucked In Her Babies
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, and they landed near a hillside covered in round little nests.

"Careful where you step," said Trike. "These are important."

Juno peeked into one nest and gasped. "Eggs!"

A gentle, long-necked dinosaur was curled nearby, watching over the nests like a mother keeping an eye on her kids at the park.

"That's Maiasaura," said Trike. "Her name even means 'good mother lizard.'"

"She takes care of her babies?" asked Milo.

"People found nests just like this one in a place called Montana," said Trike, "and it showed them dinosaur moms stuck around to look after their babies, instead of leaving them alone."

Juno counted the eggs in the closest nest. "One, two, three, four, five!"

"Five eggs, five future dinosaurs," said Trike.

Milo crouched down quietly. "That's kind of sweet, actually."

"Dinosaurs weren't all stomping and roaring," said Trike. "Some of them were really good parents."

The mother dinosaur nudged one egg gently back into place with her nose, and Juno nudged an invisible pretend egg of her own, copying her exactly.

"Goodnight, baby dinosaurs," Juno whispered to the nest.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Big, Big Change
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, and the sky looked strange — a little dusty, a little dim.

"What happened?" asked Milo.

"About **66 million years ago**, a giant rock fell from way out in space," said Trike. "It was like the biggest cannonball you can imagine, and it changed everything, fast."

Juno grabbed Milo's hand, just a little.

"Were the dinosaurs okay?" she asked.

Trike spoke gently. "Most of the big dinosaurs couldn't find enough food anymore, and they didn't live on. That part is a little sad."

Milo squeezed Juno's hand back. "But you're still here, Trike."

"Some small, feathery dinosaurs made it through," said Trike, brightening. "And over a very long time, they turned into something you already know."

A bird fluttered down and landed on a branch nearby, chirping away.

"A bird," whispered Juno.

"Birds today," said Trike, "are the dinosaurs who never really left. Every robin outside your window is a tiny dinosaur, saying hello."

Milo looked at the bird with brand new respect. "So dinosaurs are still around. They just got small and learned to fly."

"Exactly," said Trike. "Not every ending is really an ending."

Juno waved at the bird, and the bird, quite politely, seemed to bob its head right back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Digging Up Clues
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH**, and now it was today again — a sandy, sunny dig site with little brushes and tiny shovels waiting on the ground.

"Where are the dinosaurs?" asked Juno, looking around.

"Gone a long time now," said Trike. "But they left clues. People called **paleontologists** — that's scientists who study old bones — dig them up very carefully."

Milo spotted a shape pressed into a hard patch of ground. "Is this... a footprint?"

"A footprint turned to rock," said Trike. "People have found old dinosaur footprints like that in places like Texas and China."

Juno counted the toe marks. "One, two, three toes!"

Milo brushed sand off a buried bone, bit by bit, just like Trike showed him. "How do bones even turn into rock?"

"Bit by bit, over thousands and thousands of years, the bone gets swapped out for stone," said Trike. "We call the rocky bone a **fossil**."

"One of the biggest T. rex fossils ever found is nicknamed Sue," said Trike, "dug up in South Dakota in **1990**."

"And way over in the **Gobi Desert**," Trike added, "people have found more dinosaur fossils than almost anywhere else on Earth."

"There's even a story," said Trike, smiling, "that a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur fossil. That one might be a bit made up, but it's a fun story to tell."

Milo held his own little fossil up to the sun like a trophy. "I found a clue!"

"You sure did," said Trike. "Welcome to the club."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The little red brick went **CLICK**, and the world swirled green and brown and then settled into something very familiar: their own bedroom carpet.

Milo looked down at his hand. His little rock fossil was still there, real as anything.

"We get to keep it?" he asked.

The brick on the shelf gave one last friendly **CLICK**, as if to say yes.

Juno flopped onto the rug next to her dinosaur toys and lined them up again, this time in the right order, Triceratops first because it was still her favorite.

"Terrible lizards," Juno murmured happily.

"Awesome-terrible," Milo corrected, yawning. "Remember?"

Their half-finished LEGO tower from before stood quietly on the carpet, still clicked together, still holding strong.

Milo set his little rock fossil carefully on the very top brick, like a tiny trophy for the whole tower.

"Goodnight, Sue," Juno whispered to the fossil, because apparently that was its name now.

Outside the window, a bird chirped once in the dark, a tiny dinosaur saying goodnight of its own.

Milo pulled his blanket up. "Best adventure yet."

"Turkey dinosaur was my favorite," said Juno, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: The very first **dinosaurs** showed up about **230 million years ago**.
A scientist named **Richard Owen** made up the word **dinosaur** in **1842**. It means 'terrible lizard.'
A **T. rex** tooth can be up to **30 centimeters** long, about as long as your arm to your elbow.
A real **Velociraptor** was only about the size of a **turkey**, much smaller than in movies.
Lots of dinosaurs, even scary-looking ones, had **feathers**.
**Birds** today are the dinosaurs that never really left.
**Stegosaurus** had plates on its back and spikes on its tail.
**Triceratops** had three horns and a big bony **frill** to protect its neck.
A dinosaur called **Maiasaura** took care of her babies in nests full of eggs, found in **Montana**.
About **66 million years ago**, a giant rock fell from space and changed everything for the dinosaurs.
Old bones can slowly turn into rock over thousands of years — that rocky bone is called a **fossil**.
One of the biggest T. rex fossils ever found is nicknamed **Sue**, found in **South Dakota** in **1990**.

new_recurring.name: Trike
new_recurring.rule: A small toy triceratops that comes to life whenever the magic red brick glows; a gentle, encouraging guide who explains facts and confirms the kids' discoveries. Keeps his toy form when not on an adventure.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Back home, Milo kept the little fossil he found and set it on top of their still-standing LEGO tower, and Juno named it Sue before falling asleep.
