Rework the Chapter 8 opening so Sam discovers the paddles before Tok explains them. Cut or soften the name-and-date lecture for a 5-year-old (e.g. 'Real scientists copied gecko toes').
Fix the Chapter 7 heading (a woodpecker isn't upside down), add a shout line to Chapter 6, and replace the brief-like opening lines with an action showing Sam's love of bugs.

story.title: Sam and the Night of Sticky Feet
story.subtitle: A climb-the-walls bedtime adventure with Tok the gecko

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Tok Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Sam liked spiders best.

He liked geckos too. He picked up every bug in the garden. Even the squirmy ones. Even the crawly ones.

Tonight, Sam was supposed to be asleep.

Instead, he lay on his bedroom floor. Nose to nose with his night-light.

The night-light was a small green gecko. It stuck to the wall, all by itself. No tape. No glue. Just stuck.

"Lights out, Sam," called Mom from the hall.

"Okay, Mom!" Sam called back. He did not turn the light off.

The gecko night-light blinked. Its eyes glowed bright green.

"Psst," it said. "Sam. Want to see how I really stick?"

Sam sat up fast. "You can TALK?!"

"I'm Tok," said the gecko. "Grab my tail. Let's climb."

Sam grabbed the tiny tail. WHOOSH! The wall turned warm and buggy and full of stars.

Sam and Tok stood on one big smooth wall, outside, under the night sky. Tok's feet stuck tight. Sam pressed his own hand flat. It did not stick one bit.

"Why do you stick and I don't?" Sam asked.

"Look close," said Tok, and lifted one toe.

Sam looked. Tok's toes were covered in teeny tiny hairs. Millions of them. So many, nobody could ever count them all.

"Those little hairs grab onto tiny bumps," said Tok. "Bumps too small for your eyes to see."

"It's not glue?" asked Sam.

"Nope! No glue, no mess," said Tok. "When I want to let go, I just peel my toes up. One. By. One. Like peeling off a sticker."

Sam grinned and peeled an imaginary sticker off his own arm, toe by toe, giggling the whole time.

"And watch this," said Tok. He shook one foot. A speck of dirt flew off. "My feet shake the dirt away all by themselves. Clean feet, every single step."

"COOL FEET!" Sam shouted.

Tok puffed up proudly. "Come on," he said. "There's more climbers to meet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spider on the Window
chapters.text:
A little shadow moved across the glass ahead.

"Spider!" Sam whispered. He loved spiders best of all.

The spider walked straight up the window. Upside down, then sideways, then up again.

Sam reached a hand out, the way he always did in his own garden.

"Careful," said Tok gently. "She's climbing to work. Let's just watch."

Sam pulled his hand back. He cupped his fingers near the glass instead, looking close without touching.

"Does she stick like you?" Sam asked.

"Sort of," said Tok. "Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too. Not exactly like mine. But the same clever idea."

"Tiny hairs for everybody!" Sam said.

The spider paused right above their heads, legs spread wide, perfectly still.

"Why doesn't she fall?" Sam asked.

"Those hairs," said Tok. "They grip the glass, even upside down."

Sam watched the spider scoot sideways, quick as a wink, then stop again.

"She's not stuck stuck," Sam said slowly. "She's choosing where to go. Like you."

"Exactly like me," said Tok, pleased. "You're getting good at this."

The spider disappeared around a corner, off to wherever spiders go at night.

"Bye, spider," Sam whispered. "Sleep well."

Tok chuckled. "Spiders don't really sleep much. But she'll say thanks anyway."

Sam waved at the empty spot on the glass, just in case she was watching.

"Next stop," said Tok, "somebody with real glue on its feet. Actual glue."

Sam's eyes went wide. "Glue feet? Let's GO!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Fly's Secret Glue
chapters.text:
CLICK. A fly landed on the ceiling above them, upside down, calm as anything.

Sam stared. "How is that not falling on its head?"

"Guess," said Tok. "You're good at guessing."

Sam thought hard. "Maybe... its feet are sticky? Like actual glue?"

Tok's eyes lit up. "You got it! Flies and some beetles have tiny pads on their feet. The pads ooze out a sticky liquid. Like little glue drops, every step."

"EW! Glue feet!" Sam laughed. "That's so weird. I love it."

The fly buzzed and walked a slow loop on the ceiling, leaving no mess behind at all.

"Does the glue run out?" Sam asked.

"Nope," said Tok. "It just keeps making more. Handy, huh?"

Sam tried to imagine glue coming out of his own feet. He wiggled his toes inside his socks.

"I'd stick to my blanket every single night," Sam said.

"You'd never fall out of bed again," Tok laughed.

Sam laughed so hard he snorted, which made Tok laugh too, a little creaky gecko laugh.

The fly buzzed off into the dark, happy and sticky and unbothered.

"Where next?" Sam asked, catching his breath.

"Somewhere wet," said Tok. "Somewhere green. Follow me."

Sam hopped onto Tok's back, and SPLOOSH, they landed somewhere brand new.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Hexagon Frog
chapters.text:
They landed by a pond, cool and damp and loud with croaking.

A little tree frog sat on a wet leaf, then hopped onto the glass of a greenhouse nearby. It did not slip one bit.

"Look at its toes," Tok said.

Sam leaned close, careful not to touch. The frog's toe pads were flat, and covered in tiny shapes.

"They're shaped like little honeycombs," Sam said. "Six sides each. I counted!"

"Those honeycomb shapes are called hexagons," said Tok. "Six-sided shapes, just like you found. They help the frog grip wet, slippery leaves and glass."

"Its feet are wet too," Sam noticed.

"A thin layer of slime," said Tok. "Slippery stuff that somehow helps it stick, instead of slide."

"Slime that grips instead of slips," Sam repeated slowly. "Wild."

The tree frog blinked its big round eyes at them, then hopped higher up the glass.

"Go, little frog, go!" Sam cheered.

The frog gave one more hop and vanished into a leafy bush.

"You counted those sides all by yourself," said Tok. "Nice work, scientist."

Sam puffed his chest out. "I'm a scientist now?"

"Tonight you are," said Tok, grinning.

"SIX SIDES!" Sam shouted at the pond, just because it felt good to shout it.

Somewhere in the dark, a real frog croaked back, like it agreed completely.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Slow Snail Trail
chapters.text:
A silvery trail glittered across a garden wall nearby.

"Whoa, who drew that line?" Sam asked.

"Follow it," said Tok.

At the end of the shiny trail sat a small snail, inching straight up the brick wall.

"A snail? Climbing a wall?" Sam said. "Snails are so slow and squishy!"

"Slow, yes," said Tok. "But snails are excellent climbers. Want to guess their trick?"

Sam looked at the shiny trail again. "Is it... the slime?"

"It's the slime," Tok confirmed. "The snail glides along on it. Its squishy foot ripples in little waves, under and under, pushing it forward."

Sam watched closely. The snail's foot really did ripple, like a slow-motion wiggle dance.

"It's doing the worm!" Sam giggled, wiggling his own body to copy it.

Tok laughed his creaky laugh. "Close enough."

The snail reached the top of the wall and tucked halfway into its shell for a rest.

"Good job, snail," Sam said. "Slow and sticky wins the race."

"That's not quite how the saying goes," said Tok, "but I like your version better."

Sam left a tiny leaf by the snail, just in case it got hungry later, then waved goodbye.

"Up for somewhere higher?" Tok asked. "Much, much higher."

"HOW HIGH?" Sam asked, bouncing on his toes.

"Mountain high," said Tok, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Goat Hooves and Squirrel Claws
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The wall turned into a steep, rocky mountain.

Wind whistled past. A mountain goat stood calmly on a ledge no wider than a shoe.

"That looks scary," Sam said, "but the goat looks totally fine."

"Goats are great climbers," said Tok. "Look at its feet."

Sam peeked at the goat's hooves, the hard, round feet goats stand on.

"The outside is hard," Tok explained, "like a tough little shoe. But the inside is soft and squishy. It molds right onto the bumpy rock."

"Hard outside, squishy inside," Sam repeated. "Like a taco!"

Tok snorted. "Sure. Like a taco."

A squirrel scurried past them, straight up a nearby cliff, fast as lightning.

"That one doesn't have hooves," Sam noticed.

"Nope," said Tok. "Squirrels use sharp, curved claws. They dig into tiny cracks and bumps you and I could never even see."

Sam watched the squirrel zip up and out of sight in two blinks.

"So the goat uses squishy hooves," Sam said slowly, thinking hard, "and the squirrel uses sharp claws. They don't climb the same way at all!"

Tok beamed. "That's exactly right, Sam. Every climber uses the right tool for their own wall."

"Different tools for different walls," Sam said proudly, like he had just solved a great big puzzle.

"The biggest idea yet," said Tok. "Come on. Two more climbers to meet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bats and the Upside-Down Bird
chapters.text:
They ducked into a cool, cozy cave. Soft squeaks echoed all around.

Rows of bats hung from the ceiling, fast asleep, upside down.

"Are they stuck like geckos?" Sam whispered.

"Nope," said Tok. "Bats can't stick like me. They hang on with curved claws on their feet, hooked tight onto the rock."

"Like tiny hangers," Sam said.

"Like tiny hangers," Tok agreed, smiling.

Outside the cave, a woodpecker hammered on a tree trunk. TAP TAP TAP!

Sam watched it climb straight up, without ever sliding down.

"How does it stay up there?" Sam asked.

"Look at its feet," said Tok. "Two toes point forward, two point backward. Extra grip, all around the branch."

"And look at its tail," Sam said, pointing. "It's pushing against the trunk!"

"Its stiff tail feathers prop it up," said Tok, "like a little kickstand."

"A tail-chair!" Sam declared. "That's the best one yet."

The woodpecker paused, looked right at them, and tapped once more before flying off.

Sam waved at the sleeping bats. "Night night, hangers."

A few bats shuffled, but stayed fast asleep, upside down and snug.

"One more stop," said Tok. "The best one. It's about climbers just like you."

"Climbers like ME?" Sam asked, eyes wide.

"People," said Tok. "People who climbed glass, using gecko tricks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sam Climbs Too
chapters.text:
They landed in a bright room full of glass and shiny machines.

"A scientist named Kellar Autumn once studied gecko feet so closely," said Tok, "he finally figured out their whole sticky secret."

"Because of him," Tok went on, "other clever people built something amazing."

Tok handed Sam two small, flat paddles. Each one was covered in rows of tiny bumps, just like gecko toes.

"In 2014," said Tok, "scientists built paddles like these. A person pressed them on glass and climbed straight up a wall."

"A whole PERSON?" Sam gasped. "Climbing like a gecko?"

"A whole person," said Tok. "Want to try a tiny climb yourself?"

Sam pressed one paddle flat against the glass wall. He pulled. It held! He pressed the other paddle a little higher and pulled himself up, just a few inches off the ground.

"IT STICKS! I'M CLIMBING!" Sam shouted, wobbling happily in the air.

"Careful, champ," Tok laughed, steadying him gently back down.

"People even made sticky tape, copying the bumps on gecko feet," Tok added. "All from watching one little lizard's toes."

Sam set the paddles down, grinning so wide his cheeks hurt.

"That was the best night ever," Sam said, yawning right in the middle of his sentence.

"Climb well, Sam," Tok said softly. "Time to go home."

WHOOSH. The bright room melted away. Sam was back on his bedroom floor, blanket rumpled, night-light glowing soft green on the wall.

Tok was just a little gecko night-light again, feet stuck tight, not saying a word.

But on Sam's nightstand sat one small sticky paddle, the one he'd used to climb.

Sam smiled, tucked it under his pillow, and climbed, sleepily, into bed.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well.

true_facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk on ceilings because their toes are covered in millions of teeny tiny hairs.
A gecko's stickiness isn't **glue** — it peels its toes off one by one, just like pulling up a sticker.
A gecko's feet shake the dust off all by themselves, so its toes stay clean every single step.
**Spiders** can walk up glass because their feet have thousands of tiny hairs too.
**Flies** and some beetles climb using tiny foot pads that ooze real sticky glue, step after step.
A tree frog's toe pads are covered in tiny **hexagon** shapes, six-sided patterns that help it grip wet leaves and glass.
A **snail** climbs a wall by gliding on its own silvery slime, its squishy foot rippling in little waves.
A mountain **goat**'s hooves are hard on the outside and soft and squishy inside, molding right onto bumpy rock.
A **squirrel** climbs using sharp, curved claws that dig into tiny cracks too small to see.
**Bats** hang upside down from cave ceilings using curved claws, like tiny hangers.
A **woodpecker** climbs straight up tree trunks with two toes forward and two toes back, propped up by its stiff tail feathers.
In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles copied from gecko feet, and a person used them to climb straight up a glass wall.
People even made **sticky tape** by copying the tiny bumps on gecko feet.

new_recurring.name: Tok the gecko night-light
new_recurring.rule: Tok is Sam's small green gecko night-light who glows and comes alive at bedtime, pulling Sam into true animal adventures, and always signs off with 'Climb well' before sending Sam home.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam returned to his bedroom with a tiny sticky paddle tucked under his pillow, proof of his climb, while Tok glowed quietly on the wall once more.

story.title: Finn and Nell and the Buzzy Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A sweet nighttime flight to the hive

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Jar
chapters.text:
Finn lay on his bedroom floor with his last bite of honey toast. A little drop of honey hung off the edge, wobbling.

Nell lay next to him. She held her favorite yellow flower from the garden, close to her nose.

The honey drop fell. PLOP! Right onto the little jar on the shelf.

The jar began to glow. It glowed gold, just like Nell's flower.

Then it started to hum. BZZZZZZZ.

"Finn! Look!" Nell said. "The jar is singing!"

A tiny bee zoomed out of the glow. She had shiny gold wings.

"Hello," said the bee. "I'm Buzzlet. I'm a scout bee. I find flowers for my whole hive."

"A real bee? In my room?" Finn said, sitting up fast.

"Want to see how bees make honey?" Buzzlet asked. "The same honey on your toast?"

"YES!" said Finn and Nell together.

Buzzlet touched the jar with one tiny foot. The glow grew brighter and brighter.

WHOOOOSH! Gold light swirled all around Finn and Nell.

They felt small. Then smaller. Then smaller still.

When the light stopped, Finn and Nell had tiny wings, just like Buzzlet!

"We're bee-sized!" Nell laughed, wobbling on her new wings. "And I still have my flower!"

"Follow me," said Buzzlet. "Our first stop is a flower field."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Into the Flower Field
chapters.text:
They flew out the window together. FLAP FLAP FLAP went their brand new wings.

Below them stretched a whole field of flowers. Yellow ones, purple ones, pink ones too.

"My favorite color!" Nell said, and dipped down toward a big yellow flower.

"This is nectar," Buzzlet said, pointing inside the flower. "It's sweet juice, hiding deep down."

Finn peeked inside too. "How do you even drink it? You don't have a mouth like mine."

Buzzlet unrolled a long, bendy tongue. It looked just like a tiny straw.

"This is how," she said. "I slurp the nectar up, like a straw."

SLURRRRP! She sucked up the sweet juice.

"Where does it go?" Nell asked, watching Buzzlet's round little tummy.

"Into my honey stomach," said Buzzlet. "It's a second tummy, just for carrying nectar. Not for eating."

Finn giggled so hard he nearly tipped over. "A second tummy? I want one, for extra honey toast!"

Nell pointed to another bright yellow flower nearby. "Try that one next, Buzzlet!"

Buzzlet flew over and slurped again. Her honey stomach filled up, round and full and heavy.

"Time to bring it home," she said. "Follow me to the hive, bee-sized friends!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Passing It Along
chapters.text:
The hive buzzed loud, even from outside. Thousands of bees zoomed in and out.

"How many bees even live here?" Finn asked, peeking through the entrance.

"Lots and lots!" said Buzzlet. "In summer, our hive can hold **twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees**."

Nell's eyes went wide and round. "That is SO many bees!"

Inside, a house bee flew right up to Buzzlet. They touched their mouths together, gently.

"What is she doing?" Nell asked, tilting her head.

"Sharing my nectar," Buzzlet said. "Mouth to mouth, like sharing a drink with a friend."

The house bee took the nectar into her own tummy, carefully.

"Her spit has tiny helpers inside it," Buzzlet said. "They work on the nectar, bit by bit, turning it into honey."

Finn tried to picture tiny spit helpers like little cooks, stirring a pot. "Spit that makes honey? That is so wild."

"Pass it, Finn!" Nell said, giggling and cupping her hands. "Pretend you're a bee too!"

Finn cupped his own hands and pretended to pass invisible nectar over to Nell. They both laughed until they wobbled.

The house bee buzzed off to finish her job.

"Where does the nectar go now?" Nell asked, already following.

"To its brand new room," said Buzzlet. "Come see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Buzzlet led them deeper into the warm, buzzing hive.

Finn gasped. "Look at all these tiny little rooms!"

The walls were covered in small holes, each one shaped just the same.

"This is honeycomb," Buzzlet said. "Every little room is called a cell."

Nell landed on one and counted its sides with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six! Six sides!"

"Good counting!" said Buzzlet, impressed. "We build every cell with **six sides**, so no space gets wasted."

"What are the walls even made of?" Finn asked, tapping one gently with a wing.

"Wax," said Buzzlet. "We make it ourselves, right out of our own bodies."

"Bees build their own walls?" Finn said, shaking his head. "That is amazing."

A house bee flew past and spread nectar into one of the empty cells.

"She's putting the nectar into its new home," Buzzlet said softly.

Nell pointed at an empty cell nearby. "Can we help fill one up?"

Buzzlet smiled. "Not this time, little bee. But you can watch the very next step. It's my favorite part of all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Fan Those Wings!
chapters.text:
Rows and rows of bees lined up beside the full cells. Then they all began to flap.

FLAP FLAP FLAP FLAP FLAP!

"What are they doing?" Nell asked, covering her ears just a little.

"Fanning," said Buzzlet. "Nectar starts out watery. Fanning dries it out, so it turns thick and sticky."

Finn leaned in close. "So it's turning into real honey?"

"Exactly right," Buzzlet said. "Watery nectar slowly becomes sweet, sticky honey."

The buzzing grew louder and louder. BZZZZZZZZZZZZ!

"Why is it getting so loud?" Finn asked, grinning wide.

"Our wings flap about **two hundred times every single second**," said Buzzlet. "That's what makes the buzzing sound."

Nell tried flapping her own tiny wings as fast as she possibly could. She wobbled sideways and giggled.

"I can't go that fast!" she laughed, bumping gently into Finn.

"Nobody can, except a real bee," said Buzzlet, chuckling along with her.

Finn sniffed the warm air. "It smells like my toast!"

"That's the honey," Buzzlet said, smiling. "Almost, almost ready."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sealing the Sweetness
chapters.text:
A house bee flew over to a full cell. She patted a thin, shiny cover of wax across the top.

"What's she doing now?" Nell asked, watching closely.

"Sealing it," Buzzlet said. "A wax cap keeps the honey clean, and safe, and sweet."

Finn tilted his head sideways. "Why do you even need so much honey?"

"For winter," said Buzzlet. "When it gets cold, there are no flowers to visit. No nectar to slurp at all."

"So the honey is like a snack you saved for later!" Finn said, bouncing a little.

"That's exactly right," Buzzlet said. "Just like you saving your very last bite of toast."

Nell smiled wide. "I save my flowers in water so they last longer too!"

"Smart little bee thinking," said Buzzlet, gently patting Nell's wing.

Rows and rows of capped, golden cells shined softly in the dim light.

"It's like a whole pantry made of honey!" Finn said, spinning around to see it all.

"It is," Buzzlet said, smiling. "Now, come meet the bee who started this whole hive."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Meet the Queen
chapters.text:
Buzzlet led them right to the very middle of the hive.

A very, very big bee walked slowly across the comb.

"Whoa," Finn whispered. "She's huge!"

"That's our queen," Buzzlet said. "She's the mom of almost every single bee here."

Nell watched the queen dip low into an empty cell. "What is she doing?"

"Laying an egg," said Buzzlet. "She can lay more than **a thousand eggs** in just one day."

"A THOUSAND?!" Finn shouted, his eyes going huge.

"Yes!" Buzzlet laughed. "She stays very, very busy."

"Are you her kid too?" Nell asked, curious.

"I am," said Buzzlet. "Almost all of us here are her daughters. We're the worker bees. We do everything. Flying, cleaning, making the honey."

Finn counted bees walking past them. "So many sisters, all in one hive!"

"All girls?" Nell asked, delighted, bouncing on her toes.

"Almost all of us," said Buzzlet. "Us girls keep the whole hive running, every single day."

Nell puffed up proudly, chest out. "Girls doing every job. I really love that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Waggle Dance
chapters.text:
Outside the hive, another bee was dancing in tight little circles.

"Why is she wiggling like that?" Nell asked, already wiggling along with her.

"That's a waggle dance," Buzzlet said. "A wiggly dance that tells other bees where to find good flowers."

"She's talking, but with dancing?" Finn said. "That is so cool."

"The way she wiggles tells the others which direction to fly," Buzzlet said. "And how far away the flowers are."

Nell tried copying the dance, wiggling her little wings side to side.

"Am I doing it right?" she asked, giggling so hard she snorted.

"You're telling everyone there's a flower right behind you!" Buzzlet laughed.

Finn joined in too, wiggling right beside Nell. They both laughed so hard they toppled right over, into a soft pile of pollen.

"I think it's time," Buzzlet said gently, still smiling, "for two tired little bees to fly home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home Again
chapters.text:
Buzzlet flew them back toward the glowing jar, slow and steady.

"Before we go," she said, "one more thing. Do you know how much honey it takes **twelve bees** their whole life to make?"

Finn shook his head, waiting.

"Just **one teaspoon**," said Buzzlet. "That's why honey is so special. So many bees help make just a little bit."

Finn looked ahead at his honey toast, waiting back in his room. "I'll never waste a single drop again."

"And here's something neat," Buzzlet said. "If you keep honey sealed up tight, it never ever goes bad. Not ever."

"Not even after a hundred years?" Nell asked, amazed.

"Not even then," said Buzzlet, smiling.

"People called beekeepers take care of hives like ours," she added. "They borrow a little honey sometimes, but they always leave us plenty."

"Like you shared your whole story with us," Finn said softly.

"And guess what else," Buzzlet said. "While we fly between flowers, we carry yellow flower dust called pollen. That helps new flowers grow, and fruit too."

Nell looked down at her own yellow flower, held tight the whole trip. "You help all the flowers grow?"

"Every single day," Buzzlet said warmly.

The jar's golden light swirled around them once more. WHOOOOSH!

Finn and Nell grew bigger, and bigger, back to their very own size.

They landed softly on the bedroom floor. The jar sat quiet on the shelf, glowing just a little.

Nell set her yellow flower right beside the jar. Finn took one last, happy nibble of his honey toast.

"Goodnight, Buzzlet," Finn whispered.

The jar gave one tiny hum, then went dark and still, and sweet, and quiet.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz off to sleep, little bees.

true_facts.text: Bees use a long, bendy tongue like a straw to slurp sweet **nectar** from flowers.
Bees carry nectar in a special second tummy called a **honey stomach**.
Bees pass the nectar mouth to mouth, like sharing a drink with a friend.
Bees store nectar in little rooms with **six sides**, called cells.
Bees flap their wings to dry the nectar until it turns into sticky honey.
A bee's wings flap about **two hundred times every second**, making the buzzing sound.
Once honey is ready, bees cover it with a thin cap of wax to keep it safe.
Bees save up honey so they have food to eat all through the winter.
A bee hive can hold **twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees** in the summer.
The queen bee lays the eggs, sometimes more than **a thousand** in just one day.
Most bees in the hive are girls, called worker bees, and they do every single job.
Scout bees do a wiggly waggle dance to tell the others where good flowers are.
It takes **twelve bees** their whole life to make just **one teaspoon** of honey.
As bees fly between flowers, they carry yellow flower dust called pollen, which helps new flowers grow.

story.title: Ada and Bolt the Magnet-Bot
story.subtitle: A wiggly, buzzy bedtime trip through the invisible pull of magnets.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Humming Fridge Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada lay on her bedroom floor, lining up fridge magnets in a wobbly row.

Her favorite was a little robot magnet named Bolt, shiny and silver.

She pushed two magnets together. CLICK! They snapped tight.

She flipped one around and pushed again. The magnets would not touch. They slid apart, like they were shy.

Bolt's tiny eyes blinked, then glowed bright green.

"That's not weird," said a small, buzzy voice. "That's just magnets being magnets."

Ada sat up fast, hair flopping. "Bolt? You're talking?"

"Every magnet has two ends," Bolt said. "We call them **poles** — just a fancy word for ends."

"One north end pulls a south end close. But two north ends push each other away, like grumpy twins fighting over a window seat."

Ada flipped her magnet back and forth. North to south — SNAP! North to north — SCOOT!

"Want to find more magnet stuff?" Ada asked.

Bolt's chest popped open like a tiny door. "Climb in. Let's go find out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spinning Parade
chapters.text:
WHOOOSH! Ada zoomed down through Bolt's chest hatch, smaller than a crumb.

Inside the magnet, tiny glowing dots spun in circles all around her.

"Those are **electrons**," Bolt said. "Teeny tiny spinning bits inside everything, even you."

"Each one is a little bit magnetic, all by itself," Bolt explained.

Ada watched the dots spin every which way, pointing all different directions. Messy, like a dance class with no teacher.

"In iron, though," Bolt said, "the spinning dots can team up. We call a team a **domain** — just a group that all points the same way."

Ada clapped. "Like a parade! Everybody marching the same direction!"

"Exactly," said Bolt. "Line up enough parades, and you get one strong magnet."

Ada reached out and spun a wobbly dot to face the others. The whole crowd snapped into line, humming louder.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Wood That Wouldn't
chapters.text:
POP! Ada landed back on her bedroom rug, Bolt tucked under her arm.

"Let's test things," Bolt said. "Not everything has a parade inside."

Ada held the magnet near a wooden block. Nothing. Near a plastic toy. Still nothing.

"In wood and plastic," Bolt said, "the tiny dots point every which way, all mixed up. No parade, no pull."

Ada tried a spoon from her nightstand. CLINK! It stuck fast.

"Spoons are often iron, or a metal that's friends with iron," Bolt said. "That's why it snapped right on."

Ada tapped her chin. "So only some things have the parade?"

"Only some," Bolt agreed. "Iron does. So do nickel and cobalt. Most everything else just doesn't."

Ada lined up the wood, the plastic, and the spoon like a tiny trial. Guilty, guilty, and one big fat STICK.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
"Magnets have a secret," Bolt said, wiggling closer. "An invisible hug around them."

"We call it a **magnetic field**," Bolt said. "It's the space around a magnet where its pulling power still works, even without touching."

Ada squinted. "I can't see a hug."

"You can, actually," Bolt said. "Shake some tiny metal bits onto paper, then slide the magnet underneath."

Ada sprinkled little iron flecks onto a sheet of paper and slid her magnet beneath it.

The flecks jumped. They curved into loops, swooping from one end of the magnet to the other.

"WHOA," Ada gasped. "The hug has lines!"

"Curvy lines, pole to pole," Bolt said. "Now you've seen the invisible."

Ada traced the loopy pattern with her finger, careful not to smudge it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rock from Magnesia
chapters.text:
Bolt's hatch popped open again. "Want to meet the very first magnet-finders?"

"Yes!" Ada dove in.

They landed on a rocky hillside, long, long ago, near a place called **Magnesia**.

A shepherd stared down at his sandal, stuck fast to a black rock.

"That rock is called **lodestone**," Bolt said. "It's magnetic all on its own — no parade needed, it already has one."

"Folks found it right here," Bolt added, "and some people think that's even where the word 'magnet' comes from."

Ada held a pretend lodestone near her magnet. It pulled right in, snug as a hug.

"Lucky shepherd," Ada said. "Free magnet shoes."

Bolt let out a buzzy little laugh. "Let's see what people did with rocks like these."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Floating Needle
chapters.text:
They landed next in a quiet room full of scrolls, long ago in China.

A traveler floated a sliver of lodestone on a leaf, in a bowl of water.

Ada leaned in. "Why's it just... spinning there?"

"That's an early **compass**," Bolt said. "A tool that always points the same way, to help people find north."

The sliver stopped wobbling and pointed steady, one end always facing the same direction.

"More than two thousand years ago," Bolt said, "people used stones just like this to find their way on long trips."

Ada spun the little leaf gently. It wobbled... and swung right back.

"It always goes home," Ada whispered. "Like it knows the way."

"Everything does," said Bolt. "Even the whole entire Earth."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Earth, the Giant Magnet
chapters.text:
"Wait — Earth is magnetic?" Ada asked, eyes wide.

"The whole planet," Bolt said, "acts like one giant bar magnet."

"Deep, deep inside Earth, there's swirly melted metal," Bolt explained. "That swirling makes the whole planet magnetic, from top to bottom."

Ada pulled a real little compass from her pocket — Bolt had tucked one in for her.

The needle wiggled, then settled, pointing one steady way.

"It's pointing toward Earth's magnetic north," Bolt said. "That little needle is just a tiny magnet, lining up with the biggest magnet of all."

Ada walked in a slow circle, holding the compass flat. The needle always swung back to the same spot.

"It's like Earth is giving everybody a hug too," Ada said.

Bolt beeped happily. "Best hug on the planet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Ada's Electro-Crane
chapters.text:
Back in her bedroom, Ada found wire and a battery in her robot kit.

"Let's make our own magnet," Bolt said. "One you can switch on and off."

Ada wound the wire round and round a nail, like coiling a shoelace.

She touched both wire ends to the battery.

CLICK — the nail turned magnetic! It snatched up a paperclip.

"That's an **electromagnet**," Bolt said. "Wire coiled up, with electricity — we call that **current** — running through it."

"Real cranes use giant ones," Bolt added, "to lift whole cars at junkyards. Doorbells use tiny ones too, to go DING!"

Ada pulled the wire off the battery. The nail dropped the paperclip at once.

She yawned a huge yawn. Bolt's glow dimmed to a soft, sleepy green, settling back onto the fridge magnet on her nightstand.

Ada lined her magnets back into a neat little row, Bolt right in the middle.

"Goodnight, Bolt," she whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Stick together!

true_facts.text: A magnet has two **poles**, a north end and a south end, where its pull is strongest.
Opposite ends pull together, but two ends that match push each other away.
Tiny spinning bits called **electrons** live inside everything, and each one is a little bit magnetic.
In iron, groups of tiny spinners called **domains** line up like a parade to make one strong magnet.
In wood and plastic, the tiny spinners point every which way, so those things aren't magnetic.
The invisible pulling space around a magnet is called a **magnetic field**.
Sprinkling tiny metal bits near a magnet shows curvy lines looping from one end to the other.
Long ago, people near a place called **Magnesia** found a naturally magnetic rock called **lodestone**.
More than two thousand years ago, people in China floated lodestone slivers to make early **compasses**.
Deep inside Earth there's swirly melted metal, which makes the whole planet act like a giant magnet.
A compass needle swings around and points toward Earth's magnetic north.
Wrapping wire into a coil and running electricity through it makes an **electromagnet** you can switch on and off.
Giant electromagnets lift whole cars at junkyards, and tiny ones make doorbells go DING!

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow Squirt Gun
story.subtitle: A splash of light turns into a whole new world.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Opened a Door
chapters.text:
Priya was drawing a comic on her bedroom floor. Dev lay under the blanket fort, water pistol loaded, aiming at his flashlight beam.

"Watch this," he said, and squeezed the trigger.

A thin stripe of color flashed across the wall — red, orange, yellow, green, blue — glowing like someone had unzipped the air.

Priya dropped her pencil. "Dev. Do that again."

He squirted again. The colors stretched wider, until a tiny door of light stood open in their room. Out popped a round, shiny droplet with a huge grin.

"Finally!" said the droplet. "I'm Dewey. You two just made a baby rainbow. That means you get to see a real one."

"Rainbows need two things at once," Dewey said, hopping onto the flashlight. "Sunshine, and water drops, at the very same moment. That's why they show up when it's raining and the sun peeks out."

"And the sun has to be behind you, with rain out in front," Dewey added. "Just like you two, squirting away from the flashlight."

Dev squirted the beam once more. **WHOOSH**. The door grew big enough to step through.

"Well?" said Dewey. "Want to see how I'm made?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Rolling Raindrop
chapters.text:
They stepped through the door, and — **WHOOSH** — shrank down to drop-size, inside something round and wobbly.

Priya pressed her hand against the curved wall. The light inside fizzed and brightened, like it noticed her.

"Welcome to a raindrop," said Dewey. "Watch what happens when sunlight comes knocking."

A beam of white light zoomed through the wall. The moment it hit the water, it bent sideways, like a car taking a sharp turn.

"Light goes slower in water than in air," Dewey explained. "That makes it bend. The fancy name is refraction, but you can just call it the big turn."

The beam bounced off the very back of the drop, like a ball off a wall, then bent again on its way out.

"Bend, bounce, bend," said Dev, counting on his fingers. "That's the whole trick."

"That's the whole trick," said Dewey, beaming so hard he sparkled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Inside Sunlight
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, something odd sat glowing on a cloud: a triangle made of glass.

"That belonged to a scientist named Isaac Newton," said Dewey. "Back in the **1660s**, he shone plain sunlight through it, just like this."

Priya aimed the flashlight beam through the triangle. White light went in one side — and seven colors marched out the other, like a tiny parade.

"Whoa," said Dev. "The white light was hiding colors the whole time?"

"The whole time," said Dewey. "Sunlight only looks white. It's really every color, mixed together. Each color bends by its own amount, so they peel apart in glass, or in water."

Priya grinned. "Sunlight's basically wearing a disguise."

"Best disguise in the sky," said Dewey.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Red First, Violet Last
chapters.text:
Back at the real rainbow, the colors wiggled, refusing to line up straight.

"Every rainbow wears its colors the same way," Dewey said, nudging them into order. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and two colors close to blue, called indigo and violet."

"Roy G. Biv," said Priya, remembering it from art class. "That spells a name!"

"It does," said Dewey. "Red bends the least, so it ends up outside. Violet bends the most, so it tucks in close."

Dev squinted at the arc. "So red's the lazy one, and violet's the show-off?"

"That's one way to put it," laughed Dewey.

Priya sketched the stripes fast, before they faded. "Got it. Now I can draw a rainbow that's actually right."

"ROY G. BIV!" they shouted together, just because it was fun to yell.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow That's Actually a Circle
chapters.text:
Dewey led them onto a floating cloud, shaped like a diving board.

"From up here, look down," he said.

Dev leaned over and gasped. The rainbow wasn't an arch at all — it was a whole circle, like a hula hoop made of color.

"Rainbows are always circles," Dewey said. "On the ground, the dirt blocks the bottom half, so you only see the top arch."

"So where's the bottom half hiding?" Dev asked.

"Right under your feet," said Dewey. "People flying in airplanes sometimes see the whole circle, since there's no ground to block it."

Priya pictured it from a plane window and clapped. "A hula hoop in the sky. I'm telling everyone at school."

"IT'S A CIRCLE!" Dev yelled, so loud a nearby cloud wobbled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Rainbow's Quiet Twin
chapters.text:
As they floated back down, Priya spotted something faint above the first rainbow.

"Dewey, is that... another one?"

"Good eye," said Dewey. "Sometimes light bounces twice inside a raindrop instead of once, and that makes a second, fainter rainbow above the first."

Dev squinted. "It looks backward!"

"It is backward," said Dewey. "Red's on the inside this time, and violet's on the outside. Flipped, like a mirror."

"Two for the price of one," said Priya. "That's a good deal."

"Light's generous that way," said Dewey. "Most of the time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bridges, Promises, and Pots of Gold
chapters.text:
The rainbow arch seemed to hum, like it was keeping a secret. Dewey hopped up onto the very top.

"People have told stories about rainbows forever," he said. "Long ago, Norse stories called it Bifrost, a bridge of light to the home of the gods."

"A bridge for gods," said Dev. "Cool commute."

"In another old story," Dewey went on, gentler now, "after a great flood, a rainbow showed up as a promise that things would be okay."

Priya was quiet a second. "A promise in the sky. I like that."

"And in Irish stories," said Dewey, brightening, "people say there's a pot of gold at the end of every rainbow."

Dev's eyes went huge. "Let's go get it!"

He ran toward the end of the arch — and it slid away from him, exactly as far as before.

"No use running," laughed Dewey. "A rainbow moves wherever you move. You can never actually touch one. That pot of gold is only a story, but a fun one."

Dev shrugged. "Worth a try."

Priya elbowed him. "Worth a try, after chasing gold for ten whole minutes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Rainbows Made of Moonlight
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Dewey, as the sky began to dim. "Rainbows don't only come from the sun."

He pointed to a waterfall glowing under a round, silver moon. A pale arch floated above the spray.

"That's a moonbow," said Dewey. "Moonlight is so much dimmer than sunlight that moonbows usually look white or gray to your eyes."

"No colors at all?" asked Priya.

"Barely any," said Dewey. "But a camera can catch the colors hiding inside, even when our eyes can't."

Dev squirted his water pistol once more, right through a moonbeam. A faint, pale stripe shimmered, then faded.

"Sleepy rainbow," said Dev, yawning for real this time.

Dewey smiled. "Time to go home, you two."

The door of light opened again, and — **WHOOSH** — they were back on the bedroom carpet. The flashlight rolled in a slow circle. The water pistol sat empty.

On the floor lay Priya's comic. Without her noticing, the rainbow she'd drawn earlier was now colored perfectly: red outside, violet tucked in close.

"Catch you on the next color," said a tiny, fading voice.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Catch you on the next color.

true_facts.text: Sunlight **bends** into a raindrop, bounces off the back, and bends again on its way out — that's what makes a rainbow.
Rainbows only show up when **sunshine and rain** happen at the very same time.
Light takes a big turn, called **refraction**, when it moves from air into water.
A scientist named **Isaac Newton** shone sunlight through a glass triangle in the **1660s** and showed it hides seven colors.
Sunlight only looks white, but it's really every color mixed together.
Rainbow colors always line up the same way, spelling the name **Roy G. Biv**.
**Red** always ends up on the outside of a rainbow, and **violet** tucks in closest to the inside.
A rainbow is really a whole circle, but the ground blocks the bottom half, so we only see the top arch.
Sometimes a fainter **second rainbow** shows up above the first, with its colors flipped backward.
In old Norse stories, people called the rainbow **Bifrost**, a bridge of light to the home of the gods.
Irish stories tell of a **pot of gold** at the end of a rainbow, but since a rainbow moves whenever you move, nobody can ever really reach it.
Rainbows can show up in waterfalls and even moonlight, where they're called **moonbows**.

new_recurring.name: Dewey the Raindrop
new_recurring.rule: A cheerful droplet guide who appears whenever sunlight and water mix (prism light, mist, hose spray). Loves gentle puns, calls refraction 'the big turn,' and always signs off with 'Catch you on the next color.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Priya and Dev return to the bedroom carpet with the flashlight rolling in a circle and the water pistol empty, and Priya discovers her comic's rainbow is now colored perfectly, red outside and violet tucked in close.

story.title: Jack, Ellie and the Shell That Hummed
story.subtitle: A nighttime swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Shell That Hummed
chapters.text:
Jack lay on his bedroom floor, turning his new shark-tooth necklace over and over in his fingers. He had found it on the beach that very morning, buried in the sand up to its point.

Across the room, Ellie spun in her mermaid-tail blanket, practicing her best mermaid flip on the carpet. "Mermaids don't need teeth necklaces," she said. "We have shiny scales instead."

"Sharks had scales too, actually," Jack said. "Tiny ones. I read it."

On the windowsill between their beds sat an old curly shell. Neither of them had ever heard it make a single sound. Tonight, it hummed.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "Is that shell glowing?"

It was glowing, soft blue-green, like moonlight caught underwater. Jack picked it up, and the hum turned into a voice, bubbly and warm.

"Well now," said the shell. "Two ocean-lovers in one bedroom. I'm Pearl. Fancy a swim?"

Before either of them could answer, the walls melted into blue. Sunlight rippled down through water above their heads.

"Quick fact before we start," said Pearl. "A shark's skeleton isn't hard like yours. It's soft and bendy, like the top part of your ear."

Ellie tugged her own ear and giggled. "Squishy! Like me!"

Something enormous drifted past, spotted like a night sky, its mouth open wide as a doorway. Ellie grabbed Jack's arm. "IS IT GOING TO EAT US?"

"Look closer," said Pearl. "What's it swallowing?"

Jack squinted. Tiny specks, smaller than rice, drifted into that huge mouth. "It's not eating fish. It's eating the specks!"

"Plankton," said Pearl, "tiny floating bits of food. That is a **whale shark**, the biggest fish in the sea — over **40 feet long**, longer than a school bus. All it wants is your snack-sized specks, not you."

"Gentlest giant ever," Ellie said. "Almost as nice as a mermaid."

"COOLEST FISH EVER," Jack yelled, and the whale shark swam on into the blue, unbothered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Older Than the Trees
chapters.text:
The water around them turned murky green, and the fish swimming past looked all wrong — long and strange, fins in the wrong places.

"Where are we?" Jack asked.

"Further back than you've ever been," said Pearl. "Watch the shore."

Ellie peered through the water at the land beyond. She frowned. "Pearl, there's nothing growing there. No trees. No grass. Just rocks."

"Good eyes," said Pearl. "Sharks were swimming in this ocean more than **400 million years** ago — before trees grew on land, and long before any dinosaur ever took a step."

Jack tried to picture a number that big and gave up. "That's older than Grandpa."

"Much older than Grandpa," Pearl agreed.

One of the strange fish drifted close, small and slow, nothing like the giant they had just met. Ellie waved at it gently, keeping her hands to herself.

"That little one," said Pearl, "is an early relative of every shark alive today. Sharks have changed so little over all that time, they still look a lot like that now."

"OLDER THAN TREES," Jack announced, loudly enough that the little fish flinched and darted off.

Ellie laughed so hard she swallowed a mouthful of make-believe seawater, which Pearl assured her was perfectly fine, since none of it was real water at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
Something huge and shadowy drifted far off in the deep, and Ellie froze. "Pearl? What is THAT?"

"Only a picture," said Pearl gently. "A memory the ocean remembers. Nothing here can touch you."

The shadow came closer, a giant shark bigger than a school bus, bigger even than their whale shark friend. Then, just as quickly, it faded like smoke.

"That was **Megalodon**," said Pearl. "One of the biggest sharks that ever lived. It swam in oceans a very long time ago, and it isn't around anymore — not here, not anywhere."

"What happened to it?" Jack asked.

"Nobody saw it happen," said Pearl. "It just isn't part of our ocean today. But it left something behind."

Something glinted in the sand below. Jack swam down and picked it up: a huge, pointed tooth, triangle-shaped and heavy in his palm.

He held it against his hand. The tooth stretched from his wrist past his fingertips. "It's as big as my WHOLE HAND!"

"That's about right for a megalodon tooth," said Pearl. "Soft parts of old animals, like skin, mostly rot away over time. Hard teeth last much longer, slowly turning into stone shapes buried in rock. That's almost all we have left of megalodon — its teeth. Everything we know about it, we learned from teeth just like that one."

Ellie peeked at the tooth, keeping a careful distance. "Good thing it's just a memory."

"The best kind," said Pearl. "One with no bite left in it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek grey shark cut through the water ahead, smooth and fast, with a mouth full of triangle teeth.

"Great white shark," said Pearl. "Grows up to about **20 feet long**. Those teeth have jagged little edges, like a steak knife, perfect for seals and fish."

Ellie counted from a safe distance, pointing at row after row behind the front teeth. "Pearl, there's teeth behind the teeth!"

"Sharp eyes," said Pearl. "Sharks lose teeth all the time — snapped off, worn down, just lost. New teeth are always waiting in rows behind, moving forward to take their place."

"So they never run out?" Jack asked.

"Never," said Pearl. "A shark can go through thousands of teeth in one lifetime."

"Thousands," Jack repeated, delighted. "Imagine losing a tooth and getting ANOTHER one tomorrow, and ANOTHER one the day after."

"I'd never have to visit the tooth fairy," Ellie said. "Though I bet she'd be thrilled. Think of the pocket money."

The great white swam a slow, unbothered circle around them and disappeared into deeper blue, its spare rows of teeth tucked away for later.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sandpaper Skin and Secret Dots
chapters.text:
A smaller shark glided alongside them, close enough that Jack could see every detail without reaching out to touch it.

"Its skin looks shiny," he said, "but kind of bumpy?"

"Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny points," said Pearl, "like little teeth all over its body. It feels rough, like sandpaper, and it helps the shark slip through water with hardly any splash."

"Sandpaper shark," Ellie said. "Mermaids would never. We like things smooth."

Jack pointed at a cluster of small dots scattered across the shark's snout. "What are those? Freckles?"

"Even better," said Pearl. "Those are tiny jelly-filled holes that let the shark feel electricity — the faint kind that buzzes from every living creature's body. With those dots, a shark can find a fish hiding under the sand without even seeing it."

"Like a superpower," Jack breathed.

"A snout superpower," Pearl agreed. "Though I wouldn't recommend trying it on your sister."

"Too late," said Ellie, smirking. "I already know exactly where he hides the last cookie."

The shark flicked its tail and vanished into a cloud of sand, superpower and all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Shark With the Strange Head
chapters.text:
Ahead, a shadow swam by shaped like nothing Ellie had ever seen — a wide, flat head, stretched out on both sides like a hammer.

"Pearl, its head is WRONG," Ellie said.

"Just different," said Pearl, laughing. "That's a **hammerhead shark**. Its eyes sit way out on each end of that flat head."

Ellie thought about it, tilting her own head side to side. "So it can see more?"

"Exactly right," said Pearl. "With its eyes spread so far apart, a hammerhead gets an almost all-the-way-around view of the water, which helps it spot things hiding nearby."

Jack tried tilting his head like the shark, looking left and right at once, and immediately bonked his forehead on Pearl's shell-light. "Ow. Okay. I see why I only get one normal head."

Ellie laughed so hard a stream of bubbles escaped her mermaid flip. "Smooth, Jack. Very smooth."

The hammerhead swung its strange, wonderful head side to side, scanning the water, and swam unhurried into the deep.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Mermaid's Purses
chapters.text:
Something small and dark drifted past, snagged on a bit of swaying seaweed. It was leathery, rectangle-shaped, with curly strings at each corner.

Ellie's eyes went huge. "Pearl. Is that a tiny purse?"

"Close," said Pearl, smiling in her bubbly way. "Some sharks don't have babies the way you might think. They lay eggs, tucked safe inside a case just like that one. People who find them washed up on beaches nicknamed them **mermaid's purses**."

"MERMAID'S PURSES," Ellie repeated, hugging the word to herself like treasure. "I KNEW mermaids were real somewhere in this."

"Not every shark lays eggs, mind you," said Pearl. "Plenty of shark mothers have live babies instead, called pups, no purse required."

Jack peered at the little case, careful not to touch it. "So there's a baby shark curled up inside?"

"There could be," said Pearl. "Snug and safe, until it's ready to wriggle out into the big wide ocean."

Ellie cupped her hands near it, not touching, just admiring. "Best purse I've ever seen. Better than any mermaid's, and I didn't think that was possible."

"High praise," said Pearl, as the little purse drifted gently on, tucked safe in its seaweed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady and the Way Home
chapters.text:
A new shape swam into view ahead — not a shark this time, but a woman in old-fashioned diving gear, grinning behind her mask, clipboard in hand.

"Pearl!" Jack said. "Who's that?"

"That," said Pearl, "is **Eugenie Clark**. People called her the Shark Lady. She spent years studying sharks up close, and she proved something important — sharks are curious, clever animals, and they can even be trained to do tricks, like dogs learning a new game."

Ellie watched the Shark Lady scribble notes, utterly unafraid, as a nurse shark glided calmly beside her. "She's not scared at all."

"She didn't need to be," said Pearl. "People getting hurt by sharks is extremely rare. It almost never happens. Sharks mostly just want to be left alone to swim."

"So all the sharks we met tonight..." Jack started.

"...were never going to bother you," Pearl finished. "Sharks sit right at the top of the ocean's food chain. By eating sick or weak fish, they help keep every other animal in the sea healthy and balanced. The whole ocean needs them."

"Guardians," Jack said. "Not monsters."

"Guardians," Pearl agreed. "Now. Bedtime, I think."

The blue water melted away, and the bedroom walls came rushing back. Jack and Ellie landed softly on their own carpet, the shell glowing gently between them.

"Swim well," Pearl whispered, dimming to a soft flicker, "until next tide."

Ellie clutched her mermaid blanket tight, grinning. Jack set his shark tooth carefully on the windowsill, right beside the shell.

"Best swim ever," he whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.

story.title: Nora and the Mosaic Tile of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A gold tile, a buried town, and a loaf of very old bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gold Tile
chapters.text:
Nora was lying on her bedroom carpet, sorting tiny colored tiles into piles. Red tiles. Blue tiles. One gold tile that wouldn't stop shining.

She picked it up. It felt warm, like a little sun.

"Ooh," she whispered. "Hello?"

The gold tile blinked — actually blinked, like an eye — and a tiny voice popped right out of it.

"Hello, Nora," said the tile. "My name is Tessa. Want to see where mosaic tiles come from?"

Before Nora could answer, the carpet rippled like water. The tile glowed brighter and brighter, until — WHOOSH — her room melted into bright sunshine and dusty stone streets.

Nora blinked. She was standing in an ancient town, people in togas bustling past, pots balanced on their heads.

"Where are we?" Nora asked.

"Welcome to Pompeii," Tessa said, glowing proudly from her palm. "A busy Roman town, near where the city of **Naples** is today."

Nora looked down. The street had big flat stones laid across it, like stepping stones over a puddle.

"Why are there rocks in the road?"

"Clever catch," said Tessa. "Those are **stepping stones**. People hopped across to keep their sandals dry, and carts rolled right through the gaps."

A cart rattled by, its wheels fitting neatly through a gap, just like Tessa said.

"This town's name might mean something, too," Tessa added. "Some people think **Pompeii** comes from an old word for **'five'** — maybe because five little villages joined into one big town."

"Five villages becoming one town," Nora said slowly. "Like five colors of tile becoming one picture."

"Exactly like that," said Tessa. "Ready to see more?"

Nora grinned and started walking. "Lead the way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Water on Every Corner
chapters.text:
SPLASH. Nora jumped back from a fountain spraying water across the stones.

"Sorry!" laughed Tessa. "Pompeii loves water."

Nora peeked over the fountain's edge. Pipes ran along the street, right into the stone bowl.

"Where does the water come from?"

"Pompeii had a clever water system," Tessa explained. "Pipes carried water all around town, right to **public fountains** like this one, so everyone could fill a jug."

Nora counted fountains down the street. One, two, three — she lost count after five.

"There's so many!"

"That's the idea," said Tessa. "Nobody had to walk far for a drink."

They turned a corner and found a steamy building.

"A bathhouse," Tessa said. "People came here to get clean, chat with neighbors, and warm up."

Nora pressed her hand to the window. Warm.

"It's like a giant bathtub for the whole town!"

"Kind of," Tessa giggled. "Though I wouldn't bring your rubber duck."

Nora laughed so hard she nearly dropped Tessa in the fountain.

"Careful!" Tessa squeaked. "I'm a mosaic tile, not a fish!"

Still laughing, Nora wiped her hands and looked down. Something glittered at her feet — bits of colored stone, making a tiny picture on the ground.

"Tessa, look! A mosaic — just like mine!"

"The Romans loved mosaics too," Tessa said warmly. "That's where I come from, you know."

Nora grinned at the shining floor. "Small world."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Great Oval
chapters.text:
A distant roar rumbled through the street.

"What was that?" Nora asked.

"Follow me," said Tessa.

They rounded a corner and Nora gasped. A giant oval building rose over the rooftops, bigger than her whole school.

"Whoa. What is that?"

"Guess," said Tessa. "Look at the shape."

Nora studied it. Round walls. Rows and rows of stone benches, circling all the way around.

"It's like a stadium," she said. "For watching something."

"Exactly right," said Tessa. "This is the **amphitheater** — a big oval building for watching contests and games. It was built around **70 BC**."

"Seventy BC?" Nora's eyes went wide. "That's SO old."

"One of the oldest ones we know about," Tessa said proudly.

Nora climbed a few steps to peek inside. Thousands of empty stone seats faced a sandy floor.

"How many people fit in here?"

"Thousands," said Tessa. "The whole town could practically show up."

Nora imagined the roar of a packed crowd, cheering down at the sand.

"I bet it got loud," she said.

"Loud enough to hear from the next town over," Tessa agreed.

Nora sat on a sun-warmed bench, just where an ancient Roman kid might have sat, cheering for the very same show.

"I like this seat," she said.

"Good choice," said Tessa. "Front row, two thousand years early."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Walls That Talk
chapters.text:
Nora stopped in front of a wall covered in painted words.

"Tessa, people wrote on the walls?"

"All the time," said Tessa. "Painted right onto the outside of buildings."

Nora squinted at red letters. "What does it say?"

"That one is asking people to vote for someone running the town," said Tessa. "Like a poster, painted straight onto stone."

"A wall full of ads," Nora said. "Like a billboard!"

"Good word for it," Tessa laughed.

They walked on, and Nora spotted an open doorway with bright paint peeking through.

"Can we look inside?"

Tessa nodded, and Nora stepped into a cool room. Walls covered in paintings — people in deep red robes, dancing figures, swirling gold and black.

"Whoa," Nora breathed. "It's beautiful."

"These are **frescoes**," said Tessa gently, "paintings made right onto wet wall plaster, so the color sinks in and lasts and lasts. This room is part of the **Villa of the Mysteries** — mysterious pictures nobody's fully explained yet."

Nora leaned close to a painted face, its eyes still bright after so long.

"It's like the house is keeping a secret."

"Maybe it is," said Tessa. "That's part of the fun."

Nora traced the colors with her finger, careful not to touch.

"Someday," she whispered, "I'm going to paint a room exactly like this."

"I believe you," said Tessa. "You've already got the mosaic practice."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wobble
chapters.text:
The ground gave a sudden shiver under Nora's feet.

"Whoa!" She grabbed a wall. "Did you feel that?"

"A little wobble," said Tessa calmly. "Don't worry — it's already over."

Nora looked around. A nearby building had a long crack running up one wall, patched with fresh plaster.

"What happened here?"

"Years before now," said Tessa, "a strong earthquake shook Pompeii and cracked up lots of buildings."

"Is that why there's new plaster?"

"Good eye," said Tessa. "People fixed things up, and kept right on living here."

Nora pressed her palm against the patched wall. It felt solid now.

"So the ground wobbles sometimes around here?"

"Sometimes," Tessa admitted. "There's a big volcano close by. **Mount Vesuvius**. Earthquakes happen when it gets restless underground."

Nora looked up. In the distance, a huge green mountain rose over the rooftops, calm and quiet, a thin wisp of cloud at its very top.

"That doesn't look scary," she said.

"Most days, it isn't," said Tessa. "People built their whole lives right here, next to it, for hundreds of years."

Nora watched the mountain a moment longer, then shrugged.

"Well," she said, "if the ground's done wobbling, I want to see more."

"That's my girl," said Tessa, bobbing happily. "Onward."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Mountain Wakes Up (79 AD)
chapters.text:
The sky turned strange. A thick gray cloud shot up from the mountain, shaped like an enormous umbrella.

"Tessa! Look!"

"Time to watch from somewhere safe," said Tessa quickly. The world blurred, and they landed across the water, on a hill far from the mountain.

Boom. A low rumble rolled across the bay.

"On **August 24th**, in the year **79**," Tessa said, "**Mount Vesuvius** erupted — all at once, and hard."

Nora watched ash drifting down from the giant cloud, dusting rooftops far below like gray snow.

"Is everyone okay?" she asked quietly.

"Many people got away safely," said Tessa. "Some sailed off across the water. A brave commander named **Pliny the Elder** even sailed his ships toward the danger, to help people escape."

Nora nodded, relieved. "That was brave."

Beside them, a young man stood scribbling on a scroll — a rolled-up paper book — watching the cloud with careful eyes.

"That's **Pliny the Younger**," Tessa whispered. "He's writing down everything he sees, like a reporter."

"What's he writing it for?"

"So people far in the future — like you — would know exactly what happened," said Tessa. "Scientists still use his letters today. They even named this kind of eruption after him: a **Plinian eruption**, which just means a huge, fast one, shaped just like this cloud."

Nora watched the ash drifting, thicker and thicker, until it had piled up deep enough, Tessa said, to bury a whole house.

"As much as **twenty feet deep**," Tessa said softly. "The town disappeared under the ash, almost overnight."

Nora was quiet a moment. "I'm glad we're writing it down too," she said. "Just like him."

"Me too," said Tessa.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Frozen in Time
chapters.text:
The ash cleared, and years and years blinked by in a blink.

Nora found herself in a quiet, roofless room, open to the sky. Dust covered everything, but underneath, the walls still held their paint.

"Where are we now?" Nora asked.

"Same town," said Tessa, "a long, long time later. The ash fell so fast and thick, it froze this place almost exactly how it was."

Nora peeked into a little stone oven in the corner. Something round and lumpy sat inside.

"Tessa! Is that... bread?"

"Look closer," said Tessa.

Nora leaned in. The loaf still had score marks across the top, and even the baker's little stamp.

"It's actual bread," she whispered. "From thousands of years ago!"

"IT'S REAL BREAD!" Nora yelled, and then clapped a hand over her mouth, giggling.

"The ash kept it safe the whole time," said Tessa. "Paintings too, and even words people scratched onto walls — like notes left for us."

"People back then wrote notes, just like me and my friends?"

"Just like that," said Tessa.

"What about the town next door?" Nora asked. "Did it get buried too?"

"**Herculaneum**," said Tessa. "A smaller town by the sea, buried the same day, but under a different kind of material — one that kept wood, and even old scrolls, from crumbling away."

"Wooden furniture, surviving all this time?" Nora shook her head in wonder. "That's wild."

"The whole area turned into a giant time capsule," said Tessa. "Everything just... waiting."

Nora touched the edge of the oven gently. "Waiting for someone to find it."

"Exactly," said Tessa. "And someone did."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Digging Up a Secret
chapters.text:
Clink. Clink. Nora heard shovels hitting stone.

"What's that?" she asked.

"Fast forward again," said Tessa, and the world shimmered.

They landed beside workers, digging carefully in loose dirt.

"In **1748**," said Tessa, "people digging right here found old walls and jars, buried deep underground. That's how the whole town got found again."

"After all that time?" Nora said. "Nobody remembered it was even here?"

"Almost nobody," said Tessa. "The ash hid it that well."

Nora watched the diggers brush dirt from a stone step, slow and careful.

"They're being so gentle."

"Archaeologists — people who dig carefully to learn about the past — work like that," said Tessa. "Slow and careful, so nothing gets broken."

"Is it all dug up now?"

"Not even close," said Tessa. "The mountain's still watching over it all, too. **Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano, and scientists keep a close eye on it, since so many people live nearby now."

"Good," said Nora. "Somebody should watch."

Tessa glowed warmly. "Can we go home now?" Nora asked. "I want to finish my mosaic."

"Thought you'd never ask," said Tessa.

The dusty dig blurred into gold light, and the carpet rushed up under Nora's knees again.

She was back in her room, holding the little gold tile, now glowing soft and low.

Scattered across the carpet, the tiles she'd been sorting earlier had somehow arranged themselves — red, gold, and blue — into a tiny stepping-stone street.

"Did you do that?" Nora whispered.

Tessa just winked, and stopped glowing.

Nora smiled at the little mosaic street glittering on her floor, scooped up Tessa, and tucked her into the small wooden box where she kept her favorite tiles.

"Goodnight, Pompeii," she whispered. "Thanks for the trip."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Keep piecing it together.

true_facts.text: Pompeii was a real Roman town near where the city of **Naples** is today.
The name Pompeii might come from an old word for **'five'** — maybe because five villages joined together.
Pompeii's streets had **raised stepping stones** so people could cross without wet feet, with gaps left for cart wheels.
Pipes carried water all around town to **public fountains**, so everyone could fill a jug.
Pompeii's huge oval **amphitheater** was built around **70 BC**, one of the oldest ever found.
Colorful wall paintings called **frescoes** still decorate a building called the **Villa of the Mysteries**.
On **August 24, 79 AD**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried the town.
A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption and wrote it all down in letters, which is why this kind of huge, fast eruption is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
Ash and rock piled up as deep as **twenty feet**, burying the whole town.
A loaf of **bread**, complete with the baker's stamp, was found perfectly preserved inside an oven.
The nearby town of **Herculaneum** was buried too, but its ash kept even **wooden furniture** safe.
Pompeii was forgotten until workers digging found old walls in **1748**.
**Mount Vesuvius** is still an active volcano today, and scientists keep watching it closely.
