story.title: Maya and the Race to the Stars
story.subtitle: A bathtub, a beep, and a whole sky of firsts.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beeping Beach Ball (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya was drawing boats on the foggy bathroom mirror with her finger. It had been one whole week since the bridge hummed its last rivet into place, and she still missed the clank of it.

She slid into the warm bath and made little waves with her toes. Then the water began to glow, soft and silver, like a night-light under the bubbles.

**SPLOOSH!** Up popped a round, whiskery face. "All aboard, Maya," said Barnacle the harbour seal, water dripping off his nose. "Ready to sea the stars?"

Maya giggled. "That's not even how you spell it."

"Puns don't need spelling," said Barnacle, and the bathwater opened into a round glowing window, like a porthole on a ship. Through it, Maya saw black sky and tiny white dots.

They stepped through together. Far below hung a blue ball of a planet, and near it floated something small and shiny.

"Listen," said Barnacle. A thin beep-beep-beep came from the little shiny ball.

"It's counting!" said Maya, tilting her head. "Like a heartbeat."

"Good ears," said Barnacle. "That's **Sputnik 1**, the first man-made satellite — a machine that circles a planet instead of landing on it. The Soviet Union sent it up on **October 4, 1957**."

"How big is it?" Maya asked, spreading her hands.

"About as wide as a beach ball," said Barnacle. "But that little beep-beep went round and round Earth, and anyone with a radio could hear it."

Maya watched it sail past, smooth and steady, the way a toy boat glides around a bathtub island.

"It's going around and around," she said. "Like my boats go around the soap dish."

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle. "We call that going into **orbit**."

Maya grinned so wide her nose scrunched. "IT BEEPS!" she shouted, and the beep seemed to answer back, beep-beep-beep, all the way around the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika Goes Up (1957)
chapters.text:
The glowing porthole shimmered, and the scene changed. A bigger rocket stood tall, smoke curling at its feet.

"Something's different," said Maya, pressing her nose near the glow. "I hear something else. Not a beep."

She was right. A soft bark floated through the dark.

"Good catch," said Barnacle. "On **November 3, 1957**, just one month after the beach-ball satellite, the Soviets sent up **Sputnik 2**. This time somebody rode along."

"Somebody who barks?" asked Maya, eyes wide.

"A dog named **Laika**," said Barnacle gently. "She was the very first living creature to circle the Earth from way up here."

Maya watched the little capsule swing past, round and steady, and waved both hands at the window even though she knew Laika couldn't see her.

"She's brave," Maya said softly.

"The bravest," agreed Barnacle. "People everywhere heard her story and cheered for her."

Maya reached into her pocket — she always kept a stub of crayon there, just in case — and sketched a quick dog shape on her damp palm before it faded. "For Laika," she said. "So I remember her."

Barnacle's whiskers twitched like he was smiling. "That's exactly the kind of thing worth remembering, Maya."

The little capsule sailed on, round and round, a small brave shape against all that dark and all those stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Catches Up (1958)
chapters.text:
The window fizzed and flickered, and suddenly they were looking down at a busy office full of papers and chalkboards.

"Everyone looks worried," Maya noticed, pointing at the scribbling grown-ups below.

"They were," said Barnacle. "That beeping beach ball gave America quite a jolt. So the United States built its own space team."

"A team for going up?" asked Maya.

"Exactly. It's called **NASA**, and it started working on **October 1, 1958**."

Maya watched rockets being wheeled out on carts, like boats going down a ramp into water.

"Did they launch something too?" she asked.

"They sure did. Just before NASA started, on **January 31, 1958**, America sent up its own satellite, called **Explorer 1**."

Maya squinted at a little pencil-shaped shape zooming past the window. "It's skinnier than the beach ball one!"

"Sharp eyes again," said Barnacle. "Explorer 1 was long and thin, built to carry instruments instead of just beeping."

Maya pressed her palm to the glowing porthole, watching both rockets — Russian and American — swirl through the dark like two boats racing around the same pond.

"They're not even looking at each other," she said, "but they're still racing."

"That," said Barnacle, "is the whole Space Race in one sentence."

Maya beamed, proud of her own words, and the porthole glowed brighter, ready for the next stop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The First Person in the Sky (1961)
chapters.text:
The porthole swirled into deep blue, and a strange round capsule spun gently into view, a tiny window on its side.

"Is someone inside that one?" Maya asked, nose nearly touching the glow.

"Someone very important," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, a Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human being to ever fly into space."

Maya's mouth fell open. "The actual first person? Ever?"

"The actual first," said Barnacle. "He flew all the way around Earth once, in a little capsule called **Vostok 1**. The whole trip took about **108 minutes** — shorter than one of your swim meets."

Maya tried to picture it: one whole lap around the entire planet, done before bedtime snack time was even over.

"Was he scared?" she asked.

"People say he smiled the whole way," said Barnacle.

Maya watched the little capsule zip past, tiny against the huge dark, and she smiled back at it, even though Gagarin couldn't see her either.

"One lap," she whispered. "One whole lap around the world."

She traced the capsule's circle shape in the fog on the porthole glass with one finger, round and round, just like the shape a boat makes coming home to the same dock.

"All aboard for the next stop, Maya?" asked Barnacle.

"All aboard," Maya answered, and the window glowed brighter still.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: An American Flies, and a Big Dare (1961)
chapters.text:
The glow flickered again, and now a different rocket stood waiting, shorter and stubbier.

"Is this one American?" Maya guessed, pointing at its flag.

"Good eye," said Barnacle. "On **May 5, 1961**, an astronaut named **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, riding a little capsule called **Freedom 7**."

"Did he go all the way around too?" Maya asked.

"Not quite," said Barnacle. "His flight was shorter and didn't loop all the way around Earth like Gagarin's did. But it still made him a hero back home."

The porthole shimmered again, and now they floated above a crowd listening to a man in a dark suit speak from a podium.

"Who's that?" Maya asked.

"**President Kennedy**," said Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, he stood up and dared his whole country to do something enormous."

"What did he dare them to do?"

"Land a person on the Moon," said Barnacle, "and bring them home safe, before the end of the decade."

Maya looked up at the pale Moon hanging nearby, round as a dinner plate.

"That's really far," she whispered.

"It really is," said Barnacle. "But sometimes the biggest dares are the ones worth keeping."

Maya nodded slowly, watching the crowd below cheer and clap, and she felt a little shiver of excitement, the good kind, the kind before a big swim race.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Woman Orbits the Earth (1963)
chapters.text:
The window swirled, showing a capsule gliding smooth and quiet, far steadier than the last.

"This one looks calm," Maya said. "Who's flying it?"

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle, "a Soviet cosmonaut — that's the Russian word for astronaut. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever to fly in space."

Maya pressed both hands to the glass. "A girl went to space?"

"A grown-up girl," said Barnacle, smiling, "who used to work in a factory before she trained to fly."

"That's so cool," said Maya. "Did she go around a lot?"

"She circled the Earth in her capsule, **Vostok 6**, again and again," said Barnacle.

Maya watched the little ship swing past, steady as a sailboat tacking back and forth across a bay.

"She's doing laps," Maya said. "Like me in the pool."

"Just like you," said Barnacle, "only her pool was the whole sky."

Maya laughed and waved both arms at the tiny capsule as it passed, pretending she was cheering from the poolside.

"Go, Valentina!" she shouted, and for just a second the little ship seemed to wobble its wings in reply, though Barnacle only winked and said nothing at all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Walk Outside the Ship (1965)
chapters.text:
The porthole glowed again, and this time Maya gasped. A person floated completely outside a spaceship, tethered by a long cord, arms spread wide against the stars.

"He's OUTSIDE!" Maya cried. "With nothing around him!"

"On **March 18, 1965**," said Barnacle, "a Soviet cosmonaut named **Alexei Leonov** became the very first person to float outside his spacecraft. We call that a **spacewalk**."

"Isn't that scary?" Maya asked, gripping the edge of the porthole.

"He was tied on with a cord the whole time," said Barnacle calmly, "so he couldn't float away. He floated out there for about **ten minutes**."

Maya watched Leonov turn slowly, like a diver doing a lazy somersault underwater, except with stars instead of fish.

"It's like swimming," she said, "but way, way up."

"That's exactly how he described it afterward," said Barnacle.

Maya let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding, and grinned. "He's okay though. Right?"

"Right as rain," said Barnacle. "Back inside, safe and sound, in time for dinner."

Maya giggled at that, picturing an astronaut peeling off his big puffy suit and asking what was for dinner, same as anybody else.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Picture of Our Whole Planet (1968)
chapters.text:
The window shifted to show gray, dusty ground sliding by below a round window.

"Are we at the Moon?" Maya asked, leaning close.

"Almost over it," said Barnacle. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts on **Apollo 8** became the first people to ever circle the Moon."

Maya watched the gray ground curve away, and then, over its edge, something blue and bright rose up.

"Whoa," she breathed. "What IS that?"

"That," said Barnacle softly, "is Earth. One of the astronauts, **William Anders**, took a photograph of it rising over the Moon, right at that very moment."

Maya stared at the little blue marble, swirled with white clouds, hanging all alone in the black.

"It looks so small," she whispered.

"It holds every person you know," said Barnacle, "and every boat you've ever drawn."

Maya reached for her crayon stub and pressed it to her palm again, drawing a tiny circle with squiggly blue lines. "For everybody," she said quietly.

Barnacle didn't make a joke this time. He just floated beside her, watching the little blue Earth rise, and let the quiet sit for a moment before the porthole glowed on to the next stop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Boots on the Moon (1969)
chapters.text:
The ground below turned pale and bumpy, close enough to touch. A ladder led down from a boxy little ship.

"Someone's climbing down!" Maya said, pointing hard.

"On **July 20, 1969**," said Barnacle, "astronaut **Neil Armstrong** became the very first person to ever step onto the Moon."

A boot touched the dust. Little puffs floated up, slow and dreamy, like bubbles underwater.

"It's floaty!" Maya said. "Like swimming!"

"The Moon pulls much softer than Earth does," said Barnacle, "so everything floats a little extra up there."

A second astronaut climbed down to join the first. "That's **Buzz Aldrin**," said Barnacle. "A third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above them the whole time, flying the ship **Columbia** in big slow loops."

"So one person stayed in the boat," said Maya, "while two people went exploring?"

"Exactly like a boat trip," said Barnacle, pleased. "And do you know what carried all three of them up there? A rocket called the **Saturn V**, taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya's jaw dropped. "That's SO tall."

"Two men built that whole dream," Barnacle added. "**Wernher von Braun** led the American rocket team, while a Soviet engineer named **Sergei Korolev** had led the Soviet rockets in secret, his name kept hidden for years."

Maya watched the two bouncing shapes on the dusty ground, taking slow, floaty, giant steps.

"A giant leap," she murmured, remembering the words Barnacle had taught her to listen for.

"A giant leap," Barnacle agreed, "for every single one of us."

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Handshake in Space (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The porthole flickered, and this time something looked wrong. A cramped little ship drifted sideways, lights blinking.

"What happened?" Maya asked, worried.

"In **1970**, a tank carrying oxygen — the air astronauts need to breathe — broke apart on the **Apollo 13** ship, on its way to the Moon," said Barnacle, steady as ever. "It gave everyone quite a scare."

"Are they okay?" Maya asked quickly.

"They are," said Barnacle. "Engineers back on Earth figured out a clever fix, and the crew flew safely home."

Maya let out a breath. "That's good. I don't like scary parts."

"Good thing this story has a happy middle," said Barnacle, "same as it has a happy end."

The window glowed once more, warmer now, golden instead of black. Two spaceships floated close together, one from America, one from the Soviet Union.

"They're touching!" Maya said.

"On **July 17, 1975**," said Barnacle, "the two ships docked together in orbit, and the astronauts from both sides reached out and shook hands."

Maya watched the tiny figures clasp hands through their round helmets, floating together above the little blue Earth.

"That's better than racing," she said softly. "That's being friends."

"Best ending there is," said Barnacle, and the porthole began to shrink, water swirling gently back toward the bath.

**SPLOOSH!** Maya landed back in the warm water with a happy splash, her toes wrinkly, her crayon stub still clutched tight in one damp hand. On her palm, faint and smudged, was a tiny blue Earth, a tiny dog, and one tiny rocket, all drawn together.

"Goodnight, stars," Maya whispered, and pulled the plug, letting the water — and the whole Space Race — swirl quietly away.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreams, and SPLOOSH — sweet dreams among the stars.

true_facts.text: The **Sputnik 1** satellite was about the size of a beach ball and sent out a beep-beep sound people could hear on the radio, starting **October 4, 1957**.
On **November 3, 1957**, a brave dog named **Laika** became the first living creature to circle the Earth, aboard **Sputnik 2**.
America started its own space team, called **NASA**, on **October 1, 1958**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person ever to fly in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 5, 1961**, **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, flying the capsule **Freedom 7**.
On **May 25, 1961**, **President Kennedy** dared America to land someone on the Moon and bring them safely home.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, circling Earth in **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his spaceship, a **spacewalk** that lasted about **ten minutes**.
In **December 1968**, the **Apollo 8** astronauts were the first to circle the Moon, and one of them photographed Earth rising over it.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap.
While Armstrong and **Buzz Aldrin** walked on the Moon, **Michael Collins** stayed above, flying the ship **Columbia** alone.
In **1970**, a broken oxygen tank put the **Apollo 13** crew in danger, but clever fixes brought them safely home.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spaceships docked together in orbit, and their crews shook hands.

new_recurring.name: The Starlight Porthole
new_recurring.rule: A glowing round window that appears in water wherever Maya is — bathtub, puddle, pool — and opens onto a true moment in history or science. It always opens and closes with a SPLOOSH.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Maya returned to her bath with a faint, damp crayon drawing on her palm — a tiny Earth, a tiny dog, and a tiny rocket — as the Starlight Porthole swirled closed behind her.

story.title: Zara and the Humming Geode
story.subtitle: A journey through the fiery, rumbling, rock-making world of volcanoes

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Humming Geode
chapters.text:
Zara sat crisscross on her bedroom floor, sorting her rock box by color. Red jasper. White quartz. A plain gray lump she wasn't sure about yet.

She picked up the gray lump and turned it over. It felt warm, almost like sunshine. But her room was dark and cold, long past bedtime.

Then the lump began to hum. A low, round sound, like a sleepy bee. Cracks of orange light leaked out between its bumps.

"Whoa," Zara whispered. She held her breath and waited.

CRACK! The rock split open like a tiny door. Warm golden light spilled onto the carpet. Inside sat a small, round crystal with a friendly, crinkled face.

"Finally!" the crystal said, stretching two tiny crystal arms. "I've been waiting inside that rock for ages. I'm Ember. I'm a geode — that's a rock with a hollow middle, full of crystals."

Zara blinked. "You talk."

"I do, for the right rock-lover," Ember said, winking. "And you, Zara, have excellent taste in rocks. Want to see where rocks like me really come from?"

Zara didn't need to be asked twice. "Yes!"

Ember glowed brighter, until the light swallowed the whole room.

When it faded, Zara stood on warm black ground. Steam puffed between her sneakers. Ahead of her, a mountain breathed gray smoke into the sky.

"Where are we?" Zara asked.

"A volcano," said Ember. "That's an opening in the ground, where hot melted rock, ash, and gas come bursting out from deep underground."

Zara peered at a bright orange river oozing down the mountainside. "Is that lava?"

"Close! While it's still underground, we call it magma," said Ember. "The second it reaches the surface, where we can see it — that's when it becomes lava."

"Magma below, lava above," Zara repeated, testing the words.

"Exactly," said Ember. "You're already a volcano expert. Let's go find out why they're here at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
The ground gave a tiny shiver under Zara's sneakers. BRRRM.

"Did you feel that?" Zara asked, grabbing Ember's warm little hand.

"That's the Earth stretching," said Ember. "Most volcanoes sit along the edges of giant puzzle pieces called plates. They float around so slowly, you'd never notice. Sometimes they push together. Sometimes they pull apart. Sometimes they slide right past each other."

Zara looked down, half expecting the ground to slide. It stayed put.

Ember rose into the air, and the whole mountain shrank beneath them. Up and up they went. Soon Zara could see a huge curve of ocean, dotted with smoking mountains along its edge, like beads on a necklace.

"Look at that shape," said Ember. "It curls all the way around the Pacific Ocean, like a horseshoe. People call it the Ring of Fire."

Zara traced the curve in the air with one finger. "It goes on forever."

"About three out of every four of the world's active volcanoes live right along this ring," said Ember.

Zara counted on her fingers. "Three out of four. That's almost all of them!"

"Almost," laughed Ember. They swooped lower, toward a green island crowded with more smoking peaks than Zara could count.

"Try counting these," said Ember.

Zara tried. She ran out of fingers fast. "There's so many!"

"This is Indonesia," said Ember. "It has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" Zara's eyes went wide.

"Anywhere," said Ember. Below them, farmers worked fields of deep, healthy green. "People have lived alongside these volcanoes for a very long time."

"Why would anyone live so close?" Zara asked. "Isn't that scary?"

"Hang onto that question," said Ember. "We'll answer it before bedtime. For now, just remember this. It's the volcano capital of the whole planet."

Zara tucked the fact into her pocket, right next to her favorite piece of quartz. "Got it. Where next?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hotspot Under Hawaii
chapters.text:
Warm wind. Blue water. A mountain so wide and gentle, Zara almost didn't notice it was a mountain at all.

"This one looks different," Zara said, squinting at its long, easy slopes.

"Good eye," said Ember. "This one didn't form at the edge of a plate at all. It formed over a hotspot — a spot deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising up, like a candle flame that never moves."

Zara watched orange fountains spray gently from a crack in the ground. No big bang, just a steady fizz. "It's not even scary."

"This one's called Kilauea," said Ember. "It's one of the most active volcanoes on Earth. It's been erupting on and off for decades, like a slow, steady fountain instead of one giant boom."

They flew higher, over an enormous dark shape rising out of the sea.

"And that is Mauna Loa," said Ember. "It's the biggest active volcano on Earth, measured by how much rock it's made of. It rises more than four thousand meters above the ocean."

"Four thousand?" Zara tried to picture it. "That's taller than anything I've ever seen."

"Mountains like these are called shield volcanoes," said Ember. "Wide, with gentle slopes, like a warrior's shield laid flat on the ground. Not every volcano looks like that, though. Some are tall and pointy, with steep sides, like Mount Fuji in Japan. Those are called stratovolcanoes."

Zara looked from the wide, gentle mountain below to the pointy smoking cone they'd seen earlier. "So volcanoes come in different shapes."

"Just like rocks," said Ember, nudging the quartz in Zara's pocket. "Some smooth, some spiky, some shaped like nothing else on Earth."

Zara grinned and watched the lava fountain fizz away, bright against the blue water. "I like that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Writer Who Watched
chapters.text:
Gray flakes drifted down from the sky, soft as snow, but warm.

Zara caught one on her hand. "Is this... ash?"

"It is," said Ember. "Welcome to a very old day near a mountain called Vesuvius."

Below sat a busy stone town, full of people in togas, market stalls, and barking dogs.

"In the year seventy-nine, this mountain erupted," said Ember gently. "It covered two Roman towns, called Pompeii and Herculaneum, under thick, heavy ash."

Zara watched townspeople point at the smoking mountain, gathering their things. "What happened to everyone?"

"Many people got away safely," said Ember. "And because of what happened here, we learned so much about how volcanoes like this one work."

Across the bay, a man stood scribbling onto a scroll, never taking his eyes off the mountain.

"Who's that?" Zara asked.

"Pliny the Younger," said Ember. "He watched the whole eruption from far away and wrote it all down in letters to a friend. His careful notes are still studied by scientists today."

Zara watched the man write, fast and focused, even as ash drifted onto his scroll. "He wasn't scared?"

"He was curious," said Ember. "Curious enough to write it all down, so people thousands of years later — like you — could understand it."

Zara thought of her own rock notebook at home, where she wrote down where she found each stone. "I do that too. I write down my rocks."

"Then you and Pliny would have gotten along very well," said Ember, smiling, as the last gray flakes settled gently around them like a quiet, warm snow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Boom
chapters.text:
Far across the ocean, something went BOOM — so loud Zara's ears rang, even though the mountain was tiny on the horizon.

"Whoa!" Zara covered her ears. "What was that?"

"That," said Ember, "was Krakatoa, erupting in 1883."

"It's so far away, though," said Zara, staring at the tiny smoking dot.

"That's the wild part," said Ember. "The sound was so loud, people heard the boom about three thousand miles away, on an island called Rodrigues."

Zara's mouth fell open. "Three thousand miles? That's... that's basically everywhere."

"THAT'S SO LOUD!" Zara shouted, grinning behind her own cupped hands.

"One of the loudest sounds anyone has ever recorded," said Ember.

Zara pressed her hands tighter over her ears, just in case another boom was coming. None did. The sky stayed calm. The ocean stayed blue.

"It's okay," said Ember softly. "That boom already happened, a long time ago. We're just visiting the memory of it."

Zara let her hands drop slowly, feeling her heartbeat settle back down. "Good. One boom like that is enough for me."

"One boom is usually plenty," Ember agreed, grinning. "Ready for somewhere a little chillier?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Year Without a Summer
chapters.text:
Zara shivered. "Why is it snowing? Isn't it supposed to be summer?"

They stood in a leafy green field, except the leaves were dusted white, and everyone around them wore thick coats.

"Good catch," said Ember. "This is 1816, and people called it the Year Without a Summer."

"Because of a volcano?" Zara guessed.

"Exactly right," said Ember. "The year before, in 1815, a volcano called Tambora, in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption ever recorded."

"Bigger than Krakatoa?" Zara asked, remembering her ringing ears.

"Even bigger," said Ember. "It sent so much ash into the sky. That ash blocked some of the sun's warmth, all the way on the other side of the world."

Zara looked up, trying to imagine tiny ash specks floating so high they could cool the whole Earth. "One mountain did all that?"

"One very, very big eruption," said Ember. "Fields froze. Snow fell in the middle of summer. Many people far away never even knew why."

"That's kind of amazing," said Zara. "And kind of wild."

"Both can be true," said Ember. "Volcanoes don't just change the ground around them. Sometimes they change the whole sky."

Zara pulled her sleeves down over her cold hands. She watched snowflakes settle onto green summer leaves like they belonged there. "I believe you now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The whole side of a mountain began to slide, like a giant scoop of ice cream sliding off a cone.

"Whoa, is that supposed to happen?" Zara asked, stepping back.

"Watch," said Ember. "This is May 18th, 1980. That's the largest landslide ever recorded, sliding right off Mount St. Helens."

The instant the slide let go, the mountain answered. A tremendous gray blast shot sideways and up into the sky.

"It blew the whole top off!" Zara gasped.

"IT BLEW ITS TOP!" she shouted again, just to say it twice.

"About thirteen hundred feet of mountaintop, gone in moments," said Ember.

Zara spotted a man with notebooks and instruments, standing at a lookout spot some distance away. "Who's that?"

"David Johnston," said Ember. "A scientist who studied volcanoes to help keep people safe. He had been watching this mountain closely for weeks, trying to understand it better."

Zara watched the ash cloud roll outward, gray and enormous, and felt glad the area below had been kept clear of people. "People listened to him?"

"Many did," said Ember. "That's exactly why scientists still study volcanoes so carefully today, so fewer people are ever caught by surprise."

Zara nodded slowly, watching the ash settle like gray snow over the broken mountain. "I'm glad someone was paying attention."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Brand New Island
chapters.text:
The ocean itself seemed to be boiling. Bubbles. Steam. Then, slowly, black rock poked up out of the waves.

"Is the sea... making land?" Zara asked, amazed.

"It is," said Ember. "This is near Iceland, in 1963. An underwater volcano has been erupting for so long, it's building a brand new island, right here, out of nothing. People named it Surtsey."

"IT'S MAKING A NEW ISLAND!" Zara shouted, bouncing on her toes.

Zara watched steam hiss off the freshly cooled rock. "A whole island, just... made?"

"Iceland has lots of volcanoes," said Ember, "because it sits right where two of Earth's puzzle-piece plates are pulling apart from each other. New land keeps bubbling up through the gap."

Zara crouched by the water's edge, where dark volcanic dirt crumbled between her fingers. It looked plain, almost boring. "Wait — is this the stuff the farmers near Indonesia liked?"

"You remembered!" said Ember. "Volcanic ash breaks down into wonderful dirt for growing food, rich and full of everything plants need. That's why people are willing to live near volcanoes, even risky ones. The ground grows the best crops around."

"So that's the answer," Zara said, grinning. "I knew you'd tell me eventually."

"I always do," said Ember. "And here's one more secret. Scientists don't just wait for volcanoes to explode and hope for the best. They watch for tiny earthquakes with special shaky-ground machines, and they use satellites in space to check if the ground is puffing up like a balloon. Both are warning signs that a volcano might be waking up."

Zara looked at the baby island, steaming quietly under the stars. "So people can get ready."

"Exactly," said Ember. "Ready, and safe."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Biggest Mountain Anywhere
chapters.text:
Ember's light shifted from gold to deep, starry purple, and the ground beneath Zara's feet turned rusty red.

"Where are we now?" Zara asked, looking at a sky with no blue in it at all.

"Mars," said Ember. "Look up."

Zara tipped her head back, and back, and back. A mountain rose so high it disappeared into the pink sky.

"That's Olympus Mons," said Ember. "The biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere. It's about thirteen and a half miles high. Almost three Mount Everests, stacked on top of each other."

"Three Everests," Zara whispered. "That's not even a mountain. That's basically a whole planet's worth of mountain."

"Pretty close," laughed Ember. "Ready for one more stop before bed?"

They landed in a grassy park full of steaming pools and bubbling mud.

"This is Yellowstone," said Ember. "It sits on top of something called a supervolcano, an extra-giant volcano, buried mostly underground. Its last huge eruption happened about six hundred and forty thousand years ago."

Zara watched a puddle of mud plip and plop, lazy and warm. "Is it going to erupt now?"

"Scientists watch it closely," said Ember, "and right now, there's no sign it's getting ready to erupt anytime soon. It's just quietly steaming, like it has for ages."

Zara let out a breath. "Good. I like it better quiet."

Ember's glow turned warm and gold again, the color of home. "Speaking of quiet, I think it's time for bed, rock star."

The light wrapped around Zara like a blanket. When it faded, she sat right back on her own bedroom carpet. The gray geode sat closed in her lap, warm, humming softly one last time before going still.

Zara looked at her rock box, suddenly seeing every stone differently. Each one had a story written inside it, waiting for someone curious enough to ask.

She placed the little geode gently on her windowsill, right where the moonlight would find it. "Goodnight, Ember," she whispered. "Thanks for showing me."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Dig deep, shine bright.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is an opening in the ground where hot melted rock, ash, and gas burst out from deep underground.
Underground, melted rock is called **magma**. Once it flows out and you can see it, it becomes **lava**.
Most volcanoes sit along the edges of Earth's giant **plates**, which push together, pull apart, or slide past each other.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe-shaped loop around the Pacific Ocean, holding about **three out of every four** of the world's active volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes grew over a **hotspot**, a place deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising, instead of at the edge of a plate.
Wide, gentle volcanoes like Hawaii's are called **shield volcanoes**. Tall, pointy ones like Mount Fuji are called **stratovolcanoes**.
A Roman writer named **Pliny the Younger** watched the Vesuvius eruption from far away and wrote it all down in letters.
**Krakatoa's** 1883 eruption made a boom so loud it was heard about **three thousand miles** away.
**Tambora's** 1815 eruption sent so much ash into the sky that it helped make 1816 the **Year Without a Summer**.
On **May 18, 1980**, the largest landslide ever recorded slid off **Mount St. Helens**, right before it erupted.
The Mount St. Helens eruption blew about **thirteen hundred feet** off the top of the mountain.
A brand new island named **Surtsey** rose out of the sea near Iceland in **1963**, built by an underwater volcano.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returned the now-quiet geode to her windowsill, glowing warm in the moonlight, after learning how volcanoes shape mountains, islands, and even the sky.

story.title: Ben and Blip: The History of Video Games
story.subtitle: Ben finds a glowing controller — and plays through the whole history of video games.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Glow in the Toy Bin
chapters.text:
Ben sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor, flashlight tucked under his chin. Pixel-art dragons and blocky green hills covered the walls around him — some drawn on paper, some built from LEGO bricks, some glowing right there on his tablet.

He was finishing one last dragon, pixel by pixel, wings colored dragon-scale green. Beside him, his stuffed raccoon stood guard, the self-appointed boss of bedtime. It was way, way past bedtime.

Under his bed, something hummed.

Ben set down the tablet and dug through his old toy bin. Deep at the bottom, under action figures and loose socks, he found a boxy controller, dusty and forgotten. He blew the dust off in one big puff.

The controller blinked. Green, then white, then green again — like a tiny screen waking up from a long nap.

"Ben!" said a crackly voice. A tiny pixel face popped up on the controller's one round button. Two blinking eyes. A wide, happy mouth. "You found me. I'm Blip."

Ben nearly dropped it. "You're... alive?"

"I'm every game that ever was," Blip said, "all rolled into one dusty old controller. Want to see where games began?"

Before Ben could answer, the controller buzzed. His bedroom wall filled with wiggly green lines, like TV static gone wobbly. A loading bar stretched across the middle, filling up pixel by pixel.

"Where are we going?" Ben asked.

"Level one," Blip said. "Hang on."

The bar filled all the way. The green lines folded back like a curtain, and Ben stepped through.

"Brookhaven, New York," Blip said. "The year is **1958**."

A man in a lab coat leaned over a big machine with a round screen. A glowing dot bounced across it, back and forth, like a tiny ball of light.

"That's **William Higinbotham**," Blip said. "He built that round screen. It's called an **oscilloscope** — a machine that draws wobbly green lines. He made it just to give lab visitors something fun to try."

Ben squinted at the bouncing dot. "Is that... tennis?"

"**Tennis for Two**," Blip said. "The very first video game anybody built, just for fun."

Ben grabbed the little twisting knob and turned it. The glowing ball arced over a glowing net and bounced back with a soft BOOP.

"I'm playing the first video game EVER!" Ben whispered.

"Nineteen fifty-eight," Blip said. "Nobody even called it a video game yet. They didn't have the word."

Ben turned the knob again, harder. The ball zipped straight into the net. He laughed so loud, a lab assistant glanced up, startled, like he'd heard a cat sneeze.

"LEVEL ONE, CLEARED!" Blip shouted, and the wiggly green wall folded up like paper.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Spinning Spaceships
chapters.text:
A loading bar stretched across the air, filled up, and popped. The green lines vanished.

Now Ben stood in a room full of humming metal cabinets, each one taller than his dad.

"Whoa," Ben said. "Did someone build a computer out of refrigerators?"

"Computers used to be huge," Blip said. "This one fills a whole room all by itself."

A college student tapped switches on a panel, grinning like he'd just scored a goal in overtime.

"That's **Steve Russell**," Blip said. "The year is **1962**. He and his friends go to a school called **MIT**. They just taught this giant computer to play a game."

On a round screen, two tiny spaceships spun in circles, shooting little dots at each other.

"**Spacewar!**" Ben read off a scrap of paper taped to the machine.

"You got it," Blip said. "One of the very first games anyone ever played on a real computer."

Steve Russell flicked a switch. His spaceship spun wildly off course, heading right for a dot.

"He's gonna crash!" Ben said.

Without thinking, Ben reached over and flicked the switch back the other way. The ship spun straight, dodged the dot, and sailed clear with room to spare.

Steve Russell blinked at the screen. Then he laughed. "Huh. Thanks, kid."

"Nice flying," Blip said, nudging Ben with a pixel elbow. "You just helped make computer history. Not bad for a school night."

Ben grinned so hard his cheeks hurt. "Can we see more?"

"Patience," Blip said. "Every level unlocks the next one. That's just how it works."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box
chapters.text:
The loading bar filled, and the air changed. It smelled like sawdust and hot wires.

A man with glasses twisted a wire onto a plain brown box. Wires ran from the box to an old, bulky TV. Taped to the side of the box was a handwritten label: TV GAME, TAKE ONE.

Ben grinned. "Even new ideas start messy."

"**Ralph Baer**," Blip said. "Some people call him the father of video games. It's the late **1960s**. He's trying something nobody's done before — playing a game on your very own TV, at home."

"Not in a big lab?" Ben asked.

"Nope. Right in your living room, next to the couch."

The brown box buzzed. Two white squares popped up on the TV, batting a little white dot between them.

"Looks like Minecraft's great-great-great-grandpa," Ben said, and Blip laughed so hard his pixel face glitched sideways.

Ralph Baer frowned at a loose wire. The picture flickered and went dark.

Ben reached in and pressed the wire back in place, the way he'd seen his dad fix the flickering garage light.

The picture snapped back, steady and bright. Ralph Baer looked around, puzzled, then shrugged and kept working, humming to himself.

"Does it only play one game?" Ben asked.

"For now," Blip said. "Wait till you see what it turns into."

"Good hands," Blip added. "That brown box of his turned into the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the very first game machine you could buy for your home. It came out in **1972**."

"The first ever home game machine?" Ben said. "That's huge!"

"Huge," Blip agreed. "And it started with one guy, some wires, and a plain brown box nobody looked twice at."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters and Pong
chapters.text:
The loading bar filled, and DING. DING. DING. A room full of flashing machines surrounded them, packed shoulder to shoulder with kids.

"Welcome to the **arcade**," Blip said. "A whole room just for game machines. It's **1972** again — busy year for video games."

Two men stood by a wooden cabinet with a white glowing screen.

"**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney**," Blip said. "They started a company called **Atari**. This is their new game — **Pong**."

On the screen, two paddles batted a square dot back and forth. BEEP. BOOP. BEEP.

A kid dropped a coin in the slot and started playing, grinning like it was his birthday and Christmas combined. A little scoreboard above the cabinet ticked up with every hit, a number climbing fast.

"People went absolutely crazy for this game," Blip said. "One story says a machine got so stuffed with quarters, it actually jammed shut. That part might be a bit of a tall tale — nobody's totally sure — but it shows you how much people loved it."

Quarters clinked and overflowed right onto the floor.

"Can I play?" Ben asked.

"Go on," said Blip.

Ben grabbed the knob and batted the dot back, and back again, faster each time, his tongue poking out in concentration.

The dot zipped past the other paddle. BOOP! The scoreboard clicked up to one, bright as a win.

"POINT!" Ben yelled, and the whole arcade cheered along with him, like he'd won something real.

chapters.heading: Level 5: Cartridges and Invaders
chapters.text:
"New game, new box," Blip said, as the arcade melted into a cozy living room.

A kid on the carpet blew dust off a flat plastic rectangle. He slid it into a slot on a game machine. Stacked on a shelf nearby sat rows and rows of different cartridge boxes, like a tiny library just for games.

"That's called a **cartridge**," Blip said. "Kind of like the game cards you plug into a Nintendo Switch today. Before this, a machine could only play the games already built inside it. In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let you swap cartridges in and out whenever you wanted. Suddenly, one machine could play hundreds of different games."

Ben picked up a box with blocky aliens on the cover. "What's this one?"

"Try it and see," Blip said.

Ben slid the cartridge in. Rows of blocky aliens marched across the screen, dropping lower and lower each second.

"**Space Invaders**," Blip said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called **Taito**. It started a huge arcade craze. Everybody, everywhere, wanted to play it."

Ben grabbed the joystick and blasted the bottom row just as it dipped low. The aliens sped up, marching faster, beeping louder.

"They're getting quick!" Ben said, grinning, and cleared the last row with one final, satisfying shot.

"Nice shooting," Blip said. "One more stop before bedtime gets any further away."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Pizza with a Bite Missing
chapters.text:
The alien ship faded into a soft yellow glow.

A designer sat at his desk, staring down at a pepperoni pizza with one slice gone.

"**Toru Iwatani**," Blip said. "The year is **1980**. People say he looked at that missing slice and thought — that could be a character!"

On the screen, a yellow circle with a wedge for a mouth chomped its way down a maze of little dots.

"**Pac-Man**!" Ben said. "I KNOW this one! Grandma plays this on her phone!"

"Course you do," Blip said. "It's one of the most famous games ever made."

Ben grabbed the joystick. He steered Pac-Man around a corner, just missing a ghost by a single pixel.

"Close one!" Ben laughed, wiping imaginary sweat off his forehead.

But the glow flickered. The screen filled with stacks and stacks of game boxes, piling higher than Ben's head. Some wobbled, threatening to topple like a game of giant Jenga.

"Uh oh," Blip said. "This part's less fun. In **1983**, so many rushed, not-very-good games got made that shoppers stopped trusting new ones. Stores couldn't even give them away. People call it the video game crash."

Ben looked up at the leaning towers of boxes. "Did games just... stop?"

"Almost," Blip said. "But not quite. Hang on tight. It gets better, I promise."

chapters.heading: Level 7: Buried Treasure
chapters.text:
Dust and desert sand crunched under Ben's sneakers.

"New Mexico," Blip said. "Still **1983**. A company buried a bunch of unsold game cartridges out here, in a **landfill** — that's a huge pit where trash gets buried and covered over."

Diggers worked under the hot sun, a big yellow digger truck rumbling beside them, kicking up clouds of dust. The desert sun pressed warm on Ben's shoulders, and somewhere a cicada buzzed like a tiny warning alarm.

Ben spotted something poking out of the dirt.

"Blip, look!" He scraped away sand with the toe of his sneaker. A plastic cartridge, dusty but whole, sat right there in the dirt.

"People always wondered if that story was even true," Blip said. "Just a legend, some folks figured. But in **2014**, diggers came back and checked for real. They found cartridges — including some old **E.T.** games — buried just like the story said all along."

Ben held the dusty cartridge up like a trophy. "Buried treasure!"

"Sort of," Blip laughed. "Not gold. But still pretty amazing, if you ask me."

Ben tucked the cartridge carefully into his hoodie pocket. "Can I keep it?"

"We'll see," Blip said, winking a pixel eye. "Let's go find out who saved video games next."

chapters.heading: Level 8: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks
chapters.text:
A mushroom-shaped glow lit up the next room.

"**1985**," Blip said. "A company called **Nintendo** needed something big, and fast."

A round-faced designer sketched a little man in blue overalls on a notepad, humming as he drew.

"**Shigeru Miyamoto**," Blip said. "He made a jumping plumber named **Mario** the star of a brand-new game — **Super Mario Bros.** It came packed inside Nintendo's new game machine. It brought everybody back to games, all over again."

Ben grabbed the controller. He jumped Mario clean over a gap, grabbing a floating coin on the way down. CLINK! A turtle shell slid by below, and Ben hopped clean over that too.

"Nice hop," Blip said.

The screen shimmered sideways. Now colorful blocks rained down a narrow well, stacking up, waiting to be turned and slotted together just right.

"**Tetris**," Ben said instantly. "That's the one Dad plays on his phone at breakfast!"

"Made in **1984**," Blip said, "by a scientist named **Alexey Pajitnov**, in Moscow. He just wanted falling shapes to fit together neatly."

Ben twisted a long block sideways and dropped it into the gap. The whole bottom row vanished. FWOOSH!

"THAT'S the good stuff," Ben said, pumping his fist in the air.

"Pure puzzle magic," Blip agreed, pixel eyes sparkling.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Blue Blur and Shiny Discs
chapters.text:
A streak of blue zipped past so fast it left a blur in the air.

"Whoa — slow down!" Ben laughed, ducking out of the way.

"That's **Sonic**," Blip said. "A fast blue hedgehog. Made in **1991** by a company called **Sega**. They wanted their own speedy star, someone even quicker than Mario."

"Big rivalry, huh?" Ben said.

"The best kind," Blip said. "The kind that makes everybody try harder."

Sonic zipped through a loop-the-loop, grabbing golden rings along the way. Ben grabbed the controller and timed a jump perfectly over a row of spikes.

"Nice reflexes," Blip said.

The scene shimmered sideways into a room glowing with shiny silver discs, stacked like pancakes.

"**PlayStation**," Blip said. "Made by **Sony**, in **1994**. It used discs instead of cartridges. That meant games could look and sound way better than before."

Nearby, two kids sat side by side with headsets on, shouting friendly trash talk at each other across a glowing screen.

"They're playing together?" Ben asked.

"That's from a game called **Doom**, back in **1993**," Blip said. "It got people playing together on linked-up computers, at parties just for gaming. People called them LAN parties."

Ben grinned. "Like when I play with my cousins on the same server!"

"Exactly like that," Blip said. "Just... with a whole lot more wires."

chapters.heading: Level 10: Back Home, Game Saved
chapters.text:
The room shook gently, like a TV losing signal for a second.

"One more stop," Blip said, "before bedtime really, actually happens. I promise this time."

The air filled with blocky green hills and square trees, familiar as anything.

"This one you know," Blip said.

"MINECRAFT!" Ben shouted. "No way!"

"Made in **2011**," Blip said, "by a developer named **Markus Persson** — people call him **Notch**. It's become the best-selling video game of all time."

Ben reached out and placed one block, just to feel it click into the world, solid and square under his fingers.

The scene shimmered one last time into a bright museum hall. Glass cases glowed softly, full of old controllers and cartridges, lined up like treasures. Along one wall, Ben spotted a glowing Pac-Man cabinet, and down another, a plain brown box behind glass — the very same one he'd seen Ralph Baer building.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Blip said. "It opened in **2015**, at a museum called **The Strong**, in **Rochester, New York**. Every game we just saw has a little spot in here, somewhere."

Ben spotted an empty glass case with a small sign: SPACE RESERVED. "What goes there?"

"Maybe something you'll make someday," Blip said.

The controller buzzed one last time. The museum melted away into Ben's own bedroom, flashlight still warm on the carpet where he'd left it.

Ben blinked. Something crinkled in his hoodie pocket — the dusty old cartridge from the desert, right where he'd tucked it.

He set it gently on his windowsill, next to his finished pixel-art dragon.

"Night, Blip," Ben whispered.

The controller gave one last sleepy blink. "Night, Ben. Same time tomorrow?"

Ben grinned and pulled his blanket up to his chin. "Level eleven," he mumbled, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game over for tonight — but tomorrow, you press START again.

true_facts.text: **William Higinbotham** built **Tennis for Two** in **1958**, shown on a screen called an **oscilloscope** at a lab in **Brookhaven, New York**.
**Ralph Baer**, called the father of video games, built a plain brown box you could plug into your home TV in the late **1960s**.
That brown box became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first home game machine, which came out in **1972**.
**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started **Atari** and released the arcade game **Pong** in **1972**.
Legend says one Pong machine got so full of quarters it jammed shut — maybe a tall tale, but it shows how popular the game was.
**Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders** in **1978** for a company called **Taito**, starting a huge arcade craze.
**Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** in **1980**, said to be inspired by a pizza with one slice missing.
A famous story says unsold game cartridges were buried in a **New Mexico** landfill — and diggers really did find some in **2014**.
**Shigeru Miyamoto** created **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring the plumber **Mario**.
**Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** in **1984**, in Moscow.
**Sega** released **Sonic the Hedgehog** in **1991**, a fast blue character made to compete with Mario.
**Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft** in **2011**, and it became the best-selling video game ever.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** at a museum called **The Strong**, in **Rochester, New York**.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny pixel-faced guide who lives inside an old, boxy game controller. He glows green-white-green to start an adventure, narrates real video game history level by level, and always signs off with 'Same time tomorrow?'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ben returns to his bedroom with a desert-found game cartridge now resting on his windowsill beside his finished pixel-art dragon, and Blip blinks off to sleep until the next bedtime adventure.

story.title: Lena and the Keeper's Ball
story.subtitle: One goalkeeper, one glowing ball, and the whole history of soccer in one long night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Hum Under the Bed
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was on the floor, lining up bottle caps as free kicks and diving across the rug to tip them wide.

Under her bed sat the old leather ball her grandfather had given her — scuffed brown, stitched in a pattern she'd never seen on a new one. When her knee bumped it loose, the stitches lit up gold, and the ball started to hum like a kettle about to whistle.

Lena froze. Then, because she was a goalkeeper and goalkeepers do not flinch, she caught it.

**WHOOOSH.** The glow swallowed the room.

She landed on dry yellow grass. A group of kids her own age were kicking a leather ball toward a small hole in a net strung between two poles — feet, chests, heads, never hands.

"No hands," Lena said slowly. "Is this soccer?"

An older boy mimed zipping his hands behind his back, then pointed at his feet. Message received. This was **Cuju**, a kicking game played in China more than **2,000 years ago** — one of the oldest grandparents soccer ever had.

Lena asked for a turn in goal. When the ball arced toward the hole, she dropped and parried it wide with her shoulder. The kids cheered like she'd always belonged there.

The stitches on her own ball glowed brighter. Time to go.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ball in the Wall
chapters.text:
The glow dropped her somewhere colder: stone walls, a half-built ceiling, workers prying something dusty from a gap behind old wooden panels.

"Found behind the panels," one murmured, turning a leather ball over in his hands. "Who knows how long it's been hiding."

This part was real: a stitched leather ball dug out of **Stirling Castle** in Scotland, maybe from the **1540s** — which could make it the oldest football anyone's ever found. Nobody's totally sure of that date, so take it with a grain of salt. But hiding in a castle wall for centuries? That part held up.

Before Lena could ask more, the glow yanked her into a muddy English street, where it looked like an entire town was shoving a ball toward two rival church doors, elbows flying, a fence splintering somewhere behind her.

"This is soccer?" Lena shouted over the noise.

"**Mob football**," a man yelled back, dodging past. "Whole streets play. Sometimes whole towns!"

It got so out of hand that in **1314**, **King Edward II** banned it completely in London — too many broken fences for one king to stomach.

Lena watched the chaos from a doorway and said, "No wonder somebody finally wrote rules down."

The ball in her arms seemed to agree. It hummed, louder than before.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Rulebook
chapters.text:
The glow set her down in a tidy room at a university, where a handful of students argued over a chalkboard full of crossed-out rules.

"If every school plays differently," one said, "how can anyone play each other?"

In **1848**, students at **Cambridge University** wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — a first try at one shared rulebook everyone could use. It didn't fix everything, but it was a start.

Fifteen years later, Lena found herself in a London room full of serious men and fountain pens.

"Mr. Morley?" she guessed.

**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** looked up, surprised anyone knew his name. He was founding **The Football Association** — the **FA** — on **26 October 1863**, and personally writing football's first official **Laws of the Game**: the rulebook that finally said players couldn't carry the ball with their hands.

"Say the word for what you're making," Lena said. "Go on."

He wrote "association football." Years later, English schoolboys shortened "assoc" into a nickname — "**soccer**" — sometime in the **1880s**. Lena grinned; she'd wondered about that name her whole life.

The ball under her arm clicked, almost like applause.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Clean Sheet Heard Round the World
chapters.text:
Next stop: a muddy pitch, a trophy gleaming on a sideline table, a referee checking his pocket watch.

"The **FA Cup**," someone told her. "First played **1871 and 72**. Oldest football competition still running, anywhere in the world."

Lena barely got to admire the trophy before the glow moved her again — to Glasgow, cold air, two national teams lining up for the very first **international match** ever played, **Scotland against England**, in **1872**.

Someone shoved gloves into her hands and pointed at an empty goal. "You're in."

She didn't need telling twice. Shot after shot came at her — low, high, one that dipped wickedly — and she turned every single one away.

The final whistle blew. **0–0.**

"A clean sheet," Lena said proudly, "means nobody scored. Not one goal, the whole match."

The crowd cheered the scoreless draw like it was a final. Lena understood completely — some of her favorite games ended exactly like this one.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The League and the Letter F
chapters.text:
The next glow dropped her into a shouting argument about train schedules.

"If every town plays by different rules," a man was saying, "we need a proper league — same teams, same season, every year."

In **1888**, **William McGregor** organized exactly that: the **Football League**, the first league of its kind anywhere in the world.

Lena barely caught her breath before the glow spun her into a meeting room in Paris, full of men arguing in several languages at once about how different countries could agree on one set of rules.

In **1904**, seven countries founded **FIFA** — the organization that still runs world soccer today, deciding rules and setting up matches between nations.

"What's the big tournament everyone keeps mentioning?" Lena asked.

One of the men just smiled. "Give it time."

The ball hummed, impatient, like it already knew where they were headed next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Uruguay, 1930
chapters.text:
Lena landed in a stadium packed tighter than any she'd ever seen, flags waving, the air buzzing before kickoff.

"The first ever **World Cup**," a man beside her said, adjusting his hat. "**1930**. Right here in **Uruguay**."

"Who's playing?" Lena asked.

"Uruguay. Argentina. The final." He grinned. "Home team wins."

She watched Uruguay lift that very first World Cup trophy, the crowd roaring loud enough to shake her teeth. Later, in a quieter hallway, she met the man whose idea had made the whole tournament happen: **Jules Rimet**, the FIFA president who had pushed hardest for one true world championship. The first trophy would even carry his name.

"One tournament," Lena said. "Every country. Good idea."

Jules Rimet tipped his hat like she'd confirmed something he'd always suspected.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Women Who Wouldn't Stop
chapters.text:
This glow felt different — heavier, like it knew the next stop mattered.

Lena landed beside a packed field where a women's team was warming up, one player drawing stares with every towering kick.

"That's **Lily Parr**," a woman next to Lena said. "Best striker most people never heard of. Her team, the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, drew bigger crowds than plenty of men's games."

Then the cheering just stopped. A notice went up: women's soccer banned from major grounds across England, starting that year. No real reason given — just a decision that shut the door for decades.

"That's not fair," Lena said, and she meant it.

"No," the woman agreed. "It wasn't."

The glow pushed forward fast, skipping years like pages, until it landed on **1971** — the year the ban was finally lifted, fifty years after it began. Then it jumped again, to **1991**, and a stadium in China, where Lena watched the **first official Women's World Cup** — won by the **United States**.

Lena stood up straighter. "Fifty years is a long time to wait for a game."

"Worth it, though," the woman said, nodding at the field. "Look at them now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Dog Who Saved the Cup
chapters.text:
The next glow came fast and bright, like the ball itself was excited.

Lena landed on an English street in **1966**, right as a small mixed-breed dog nosed at a package wrapped in newspaper under a hedge.

"That's the World Cup trophy," a passerby gasped. "It's been missing a whole week!"

The dog, named **Pickles**, had found what half of London's police force couldn't. Lena laughed so hard she nearly missed the next jump — straight into a stadium where **England** lifted that same trophy, champions of the **1966 World Cup**, their only title so far.

Before she could cheer properly, the glow sped up, flickering through years like a highlight reel. A Brazilian forward in yellow danced past three defenders — **Pele**, the only player ever on **three** World Cup-winning teams, in **1958**, **1962**, and **1970**. A referee at that same 1970 tournament pulled a bright card from his pocket to warn a player — an idea borrowed straight from traffic lights, red to stop, yellow to slow down.

Lena's head was spinning with dates. The ball under her arm hummed once, low and warm, like it was done showing off.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home
chapters.text:
The glow faded gently this time, easing her down instead of yanking.

Lena blinked. She was back on her bedroom carpet, bottle caps scattered where she'd left them, the old leather ball warm and quiet in her hands, its stitching dark again like nothing had happened.

Except something had. Tucked against the laces, where there'd been nothing before, sat a small scrap of faded cloth — a tiny patch stitched with careful, old-fashioned letters: **FA 1863.**

Lena turned it over twice, grinning in the dark. Tomorrow at practice, she was going to tell her coach about a 0–0 draw that got a whole stadium cheering, and a dog who found a trophy nobody else could.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match couldn't come soon enough.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played without hands, was played in China more than **2,000 years ago**.
In **1314**, **King Edward II** banned the wild street game of **mob football** in London.
A stitched leather ball found hidden at **Stirling Castle** in Scotland might date back to the **1540s** — though nobody's completely sure.
**The Football Association** was founded in London on **26 October 1863**, and said players couldn't carry the ball with their hands.
The word **"soccer"** came from English schoolboys shortening "assoc" (for association football) in the **1880s**.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871–72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
The first official **international match** was a **0–0** draw between Scotland and England in Glasgow in **1872**.
**FIFA**, the group that runs world soccer, was founded in Paris in **1904** by seven countries.
The first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay** in **1930**, and the host team beat Argentina in the final.
England's soccer officials banned women's soccer from major grounds, then finally lifted that ban in **1971**, fifty years after it began.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in China in **1991** and won by the **United States**.
In **1966**, the stolen World Cup trophy was found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**England** hosted and won the **1966 World Cup** — still its only title.
Brazilian forward **Pele** is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962,** and **1970**.

story.title: Arjun and the Last Panel
story.subtitle: A midnight comic draws one boy through the real science of shut-eye.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Last Panel
chapters.text:
Arjun sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor, inking panel six of *Captain Boundary*, his homemade comic. The clock said 10:47. "Five more minutes," he told nobody, the way he always did.

His cricket-ball desk lamp — a gift from his uncle, stitched seams and all — flickered green instead of its usual yellow. He tapped it. It flickered again.

Then the last empty panel on his page, the one he hadn't drawn yet, started to glow.

A blot of ink peeled off the paper and folded itself into a small, scruffy shape with a speech-bubble for a head. "Finally," it said. "Someone who stays up enough to meet me."

"Who — what are you?"

"Inkling," said the blot, bowing. "I live in unfinished panels. Yours has been glowing for weeks, because you never finish the story. You always say five more minutes."

"I do not," Arjun lied.

Inkling grinned. "Want to know what those minutes are costing you? Climb in."

The panel widened like a doorway. Arjun, pencil still in hand, stepped through.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boy Whose Eyes Twitched
chapters.text:
They landed in a dim room full of wires, a boy asleep under cables taped near his eyes. Arjun ducked behind a desk. "Are we spying?"

"Watching," said Inkling. "A sleep lab in Chicago, **1953**."

A young scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky** leaned close to the sleeping boy, staring at his eyelids. They twitched fast, side to side — like a flipbook someone was fanning.

"His eyes are moving," Arjun whispered. "But he's asleep. That's actually kind of creepy."

"Or," said Inkling, "it's a discovery. Guess what it means."

Arjun studied the twitching lids. "He's... dreaming? Like watching something happen inside his own head?"

"Exactly," said a deep voice — Aserinsky's mentor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, stepping from the shadows. "We're calling it **REM sleep** — rapid eye movement. The eyes dart because the brain is busy."

Arjun grinned. "I called it. I actually called it."

"You did," said Inkling. "Not bad for a kid who should be asleep himself."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ninety-Minute Over
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into a cricket ground at dusk, floodlights humming.

"Why are we at a match?" Arjun asked, delighted anyway.

"Because you understand overs," said Inkling. "A night's sleep runs in laps too — about **ninety minutes** each, round and round till morning."

On the big screen above the pitch, a wavy line played: calm hills, then a wild spiky patch, then calm again. "That spiky bit is **REM sleep**," said Inkling. "Brain almost as busy as when you're awake. The calm bits are quiet, deep sleep."

Arjun spotted a sleeping fielder stretched on the boundary rope, part of the display somehow. "During the spiky bit, does he move around?"

"Try and wake him gently. Go on."

Arjun nudged the arm. It flopped, loose as a rag doll. "His muscles are... turned off?"

"Switched loose," Inkling said, "so sleepers can't act out whatever wild thing they're dreaming. Imagine bowling a yorker mid-dream."

Arjun laughed. "That would end badly."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Growing Stretch
chapters.text:
Back on solid ground, Arjun noticed his trousers stopped higher above his ankles than before. "Did I just grow?"

"Only a little," said Inkling, smirking. "But growing happens mostly while you sleep. In the deepest part of quiet sleep, your body releases extra **growth hormone** — a chemical message telling bones and muscles to get bigger."

Arjun lit up. "So if I want to bowl faster next season..."

"Sleep helps. A lot."

He thought about every time he'd begged for five more minutes of drawing instead of climbing into bed. "I've basically been sabotaging my own fast bowling."

"Mm-hm," said Inkling, not even trying to hide a grin.

Arjun flopped onto a patch of grass, testing a theory. "If I nap right now, will I wake up taller?"

"No instant results, champion. Go to bed on time for weeks, though, and you'll see."

He groaned — the groan of someone already caught.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Body's Clock
chapters.text:
They stepped into something like a planetarium, except the dome was a see-through model of a human brain, lit from inside.

"Right there," said Inkling, pointing to a pinhead spot above where two nerves crossed, "is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say that five times fast."

"No thank you. What does it do?"

"It's the body's master clock. It tells you when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake, roughly every **twenty-four hours**. Scientists call that rhythm **circadian** — old words meaning 'about a day.'"

Arjun squinted at the glowing dot, doing quick mental math like he did with run rates. "So it's not exactly twenty-four hours?"

"Close. Close enough that in **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, science's biggest medal, for finding the actual genes that keep that clock ticking."

"A prize. For a clock inside your head."

"The most important clock you own," said Inkling. "It never needs winding. Just darkness, and a bed you actually get into."

Arjun pointedly ignored that last part.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Potion
chapters.text:
Next they stood in a cluttered laboratory, shelves lined with small glass bottles. "**1958**," said Inkling. "A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team were hunting for a sleepy-time chemical."

"Hunting how?"

"They pulled it from a tiny part of the brain called the pineal gland — think of it as a chemical factory the size of a grain of rice." Inkling held up a bottle, a faint glow pulsing inside. "They named it **melatonin**. Your own factory makes it every night, once the lights go down."

Arjun thought about his bedroom lamp, how it always felt harder to sleep with it still glowing. "Is that why dark rooms make you sleepy?"

"Dead on. Darkness tells your factory to start the shift."

Arjun turned the little bottle like a comic panel he was about to ink. "Comic idea: Melatonin Man. Power: makes everyone yawn."

"Weakest superhero ever," said Inkling. "Draw him anyway."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Memory Vault
chapters.text:
The lab melted into a library where glowing boxes drifted like untethered balloons, each labeled with a date.

"What's in these?" Arjun reached for one marked yesterday.

"Memories," said Inkling. "Sleep sorts your whole day into boxes — what to keep, what to let fade. Ever notice you remember a cricket shot better after sleeping on it than right after you hit it?"

Arjun thought of his cover drive, practiced for weeks. "Actually... yeah."

A nearby box rattled. Through its glow he saw a boy, eyes shut, calmly walking across a room, moving a chair out of his own way.

"Is he going to walk into something?" Arjun asked, worried.

"He's **sleepwalking**. It happens during deep, quiet sleep — not during dreaming. He's not acting out any dream. His brain's just half-running the show."

Arjun watched the boy sit back down, safe, undisturbed. "That's less scary than I thought."

"Most of sleep is," said Inkling. "That's rather the point of it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Animal Sleep Safari
chapters.text:
The library dissolved into a warm night zoo, every enclosure glowing faintly.

"Round of quick ones," said Inkling. "Guess the sleepiest animal here."

Arjun studied a giraffe, legs folded, head bobbing. "Not him. Too uncomfortable."

"Good guess. Giraffes sleep under **two hours a day**, in short standing naps — shortest of any big animal."

A dolphin circled its pool, one eye shut, one eye open. "Wait, is it even asleep?"

"Half of it is. Dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, so one eye stays open — for danger, or just to keep swimming."

"That's basically keeping watch at a sleepover," Arjun said. "Smart."

Last, a glass case held a squirming newborn baby, fast asleep. "How much does a baby sleep?"

"**Fourteen to seventeen hours** a day, in short bursts, almost half of it the dreaming kind."

Arjun looked around the whole snoring zoo. "Did not expect homework at a zoo."

"Everyone's got a system," said Inkling. "Yours just involves ink and a bedtime you ignore."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Eleven Days Awake, and Home
chapters.text:
The zoo faded into an old photograph that came alive around them: a teenager beside a chart, eyes red, grinning anyway.

"This is **Randy Gardner**," said Inkling. "**San Diego, 1964**. Seventeen years old. For a science-fair project, he stayed awake about **eleven days** straight — one of the longest stretches ever recorded."

"Eleven days? No sleep at all?"

"He nearly fell apart by the end — mood crashed, memory foggy, couldn't focus." Inkling's voice went firm. "Doctors don't recommend anyone try to break that record. It's not a stunt. It's just hard on a person."

Arjun nodded slowly. "Noted. Not trying that."

"Good," said Inkling, softer now. "Because every night, while you sleep, your brain runs a kind of rinse cycle, flushing out the day's leftover waste. Skip sleep, and the wash never happens."

The photograph faded, the panel reopening behind them.

"People spend about a **third of their whole life** asleep," Inkling added. "Not wasted time. Maintenance."

Arjun stepped back through the glowing panel. His room was exactly as he'd left it — except panel six was no longer empty. It held a tiny inked figure, waving.

He looked at his cricket-ball lamp, glowing its ordinary yellow, and for once did not ask for five more minutes.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Captain Boundary would get his ending — but tonight, Arjun let his own story close first.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, a scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky** noticed a sleeping boy's eyes twitching fast under his eyelids, which led to discovering **REM sleep**.
A night's sleep runs in repeating laps about **ninety minutes** long, moving between quiet sleep and busier, dream-filled sleep.
During **REM sleep** the brain gets almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go loose so sleepers can't act out their dreams.
The deepest part of quiet sleep triggers extra **growth hormone**, a chemical message that helps growing kids get bigger.
A tiny spot in the brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** works like a master clock, telling the body when to feel sleepy or awake.
In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep the body's clock ticking.
In **1958**, scientist **Aaron Lerner** and his team pulled a sleepy-time chemical called **melatonin** from a tiny part of the brain.
Sleep helps sort the day's happenings into memories you can keep, which is why practiced things can feel clearer after a good sleep.
**Sleepwalking** happens during deep, quiet sleep, not during dreaming — sleepwalkers aren't acting out a dream.
Dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open for danger or to keep swimming.
Giraffes sleep under **two hours a day**, in short naps while standing — the shortest sleep of any big animal.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old **Randy Gardner** of **San Diego** stayed awake about **eleven days** for a science-fair project.
Doctors say nobody should try to copy Randy Gardner's experiment — going without sleep that long is hard on the mind and body.
People spend roughly a **third of their whole life** asleep.
